questions.q: Stokes' law gives drag on a small sphere as F = 6πηrv. What are the SI units of the viscosity η?
o: kg·m/s
That's momentum. It treats viscosity as force times time, which isn't what the formula gives.
N/m²
That's pressure (Pa). Dividing by speed adds an extra second, so viscosity is Pa·s.
kg/(m·s)
Correct: η = F ÷ (rv) = (kg·m/s²) ÷ (m²/s) = kg/(m·s), which is Pa·s.
kg/s
This divides force by speed but forgets to also divide by the radius, a length in m.
questions.note: η is often written Pa·s.
questions.x: To find the units of η (viscosity), get η by itself first: η = F ÷ (6πrv). The 6 and the π are plain numbers with no units, so only F, r and v matter. Write each in base units: F is a newton, 1 N = 1 kg·m/s²; r is a length in m; v is a speed in m/s. The bottom is m × m/s = m²/s. Dividing by m²/s is the same as multiplying by s/m², so η = (kg·m/s²) × (s/m²) = kg/(m·s). That's the same as a pascal times a second (Pa·s). N/m² is tempting, but that's pressure, missing the extra second.

questions.q: Vector A is 3 m east and vector B is 4 m north. What is A − B?
o: 5 m, pointing north of east
That's A + B. Subtracting B flips it from north to south.
5 m, pointing south of east
Correct: A − B = 3 m east + 4 m south; √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5 m, south of east.
1 m, pointing east
This subtracts the lengths (4 − 3). That only works when vectors lie along the same line.
7 m, pointing south of east
This adds the lengths (3 + 4). Vectors at right angles combine with the Pythagorean theorem.
questions.note: Subtracting a vector = adding its reverse.
questions.x: To subtract a vector, flip it around and add it: A − B = A + (−B). B is 4 m north, so −B is 4 m south. Now you have 3 m east plus 4 m south. Those two are at right angles, so the length comes from the Pythagorean theorem: c² = a² + b² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25, so c = √25 = 5 m. It points between east and south, so 5 m south of east. A + B has the same 5 m length but points north of east. Only the direction tells them apart.

questions.q: An object is dropped from rest. What is the ratio of the distance it falls during the 2nd second to the distance during the 1st second?
o: That's just the ratio of the times, 2 s to 1 s. Distance grows with time squared.
That's total distance after 2 s versus after 1 s (20 to 5). The 2nd second alone is 15 m.
A ratio of 1 means constant speed. A falling object keeps speeding up.
Correct: 5 m in the 1st second, 20 − 5 = 15 m in the 2nd, and 15 ÷ 5 = 3.
questions.note: Distances in successive seconds go 1 : 3 : 5 : 7.
questions.x: Something dropped from rest falls a total distance d = ½gt². Values: g = 10 m/s², and we check t = 1 s and t = 2 s. After 1 s: d = ½ × 10 × 1² = 5 × 1 = 5 m. After 2 s: d = ½ × 10 × 2² = 5 × 4 = 20 m. The 2nd second alone covers 20 − 5 = 15 m. So the ratio is 15 ÷ 5 = 3. A handy pattern: each second, a falling object covers distances in the odd-number ratio 1 : 3 : 5 : 7, because it keeps speeding up.

questions.q: A ball is thrown straight down at 10 m/s from a 15 m ledge. What is its speed just before hitting the ground (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: About 17 m/s
That's a ball dropped from rest (√300 ≈ 17.3). This one was thrown down at 10 m/s, so it lands faster.
20 m/s
25 m/s
This adds 10 m/s and 15 m. A speed and a distance can't be added, just like dollars and miles.
30 m/s
This adds the 10 m/s throw on top of 20 m/s. The throw is already counted in the 100.
questions.note: Speeds add in quadrature in v² = v₀² + 2ad, not linearly.
questions.x: Time isn't given here, so use the motion equation that leaves time out: v² = v₀² + 2ad. The ball starts at v₀ = 10 m/s, gravity speeds it up at a = 10 m/s², and it falls d = 15 m. Plug in: v² = 10² + 2 × 10 × 15 = 100 + 300 = 400. Take the square root: v = √400 = 20 m/s. You can't just add 10 m/s on top of a plain drop speed, because the equation adds the squares, not the speeds.

questions.q: A ball is kicked at 20 m/s at 30° above level ground. Approximately how far away does it land?
o: Correct: flight time 2 s, vₓ = 20 × cos 30° ≈ 17.3 m/s, and 17.3 × 2 ≈ 35 m.
This multiplies the vertical speed (10 m/s) by the flight time. Range needs the sideways speed.
This uses all 20 m/s as the sideways speed. Only the cos 30° part goes sideways.
This uses only 1 s, the time to the top. The ball also has to come back down.
questions.x: Split the launch speed into two parts. Vertical: v_y = v sin θ = 20 × sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 m/s. Gravity takes 10 m/s off each second, so it rises for 10 ÷ 10 = 1 s and falls for 1 s: 2 s in the air. Horizontal: vₓ = v cos θ = 20 × cos 30° ≈ 20 × 0.87 = 17.3 m/s, and nothing changes it. Range = vₓ × t = 17.3 × 2 = 34.6 ≈ 35 m. Using the full 20 m/s sideways gives 40 m, which is too far.

questions.q: Compared with the ideal (no-drag) case, how does air resistance affect the launch angle that gives maximum range on level ground?
o: The optimal angle rises above 45°
Higher arcs stay up longer and lose more speed to drag, so the best angle drops, not rises.
The optimal angle stays exactly 45°
45° is the best angle only when there's no air resistance.
The optimal angle becomes 90°
Straight up, the object comes back down where it started, so the range is zero.
The optimal angle drops below 45°
Correct: drag punishes long, high flights, so a lower path goes farther.
questions.x: With no air, the farthest launch on level ground is at 45°. Air resistance (drag, the push of air against a moving object) changes that. Drag steals speed the whole time the object is flying, so the longer the flight, the more it loses. A high arc stays up a long time and gets hit hardest. A lower, flatter path spends less time in the air, so it keeps more of its speed. That pushes the best angle below 45°. That's why real long throws and kicks usually go out at around 35 to 40°.

questions.q: A horse pulls a cart, and by Newton's third law the cart pulls back on the horse with an equal force. Why can the horse and cart still accelerate forward?
o: The horse pulls slightly harder than the cart pulls back
Third-law forces are always exactly equal. The horse never out-pulls the cart.
The paired forces act on different objects, and the ground pushes the horse forward
Correct: the pair acts on two different objects, and the ground's forward push on the hooves drives them.
Third-law forces cancel only when objects are at rest
Third-law pairs are equal and opposite whether things are moving or not.
The cart's reaction force is delayed by its inertia
Third-law forces happen at the same instant. Inertia affects acceleration, not timing.
questions.note: Trap: action–reaction forces act on different objects.
questions.x: Newton's third law says that if A pushes on B, B pushes back on A just as hard, in the opposite direction. The key is that those two forces act on DIFFERENT objects: one on the horse, one on the cart. Forces only cancel when they act on the same object, so this pair never cancels. To see if the horse speeds up, look only at forces on the horse: the cart pulls it back, but the ground pushes its hooves forward (friction), and that forward push is bigger. Thinking the horse pulls 'harder' is the classic mistake.

questions.q: Masses of 3 kg and 5 kg hang on opposite sides of a frictionless, massless pulley. What is their acceleration (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: 4.0 m/s²
This divides the 20 N difference by the heavier mass only (20 ÷ 5). Both masses move, so use 8 kg.
This uses the heavier weight, 50 N, instead of the difference, 50 − 30 = 20 N.
10 m/s²
That's free fall. The lighter mass holds the heavier one back, so a is less than g.
2.5 m/s²
questions.note: Atwood: a = (m₂ − m₁)g/(m₁ + m₂).
questions.x: This is an Atwood machine: two masses on a pulley moving together. The heavier side wins by the difference in weights, but that difference has to move both masses. Formula: a = (m₂ − m₁)g ÷ (m₁ + m₂). Values: m₂ = 5 kg, m₁ = 3 kg, g = 10 m/s². Plug in: a = (5 − 3) × 10 ÷ (3 + 5) = 2 × 10 ÷ 8 = 20 ÷ 8 = 2.5 m/s². Dividing by only one mass gives an answer that's too big, because both masses speed up together.

questions.q: Masses of 2 kg and 6 kg hang over a frictionless, massless pulley. What is the string tension (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That's the 2 kg mass's weight. Tension must be bigger to speed that mass upward.
That's the 6 kg mass's weight. Tension must be smaller so that mass can speed up downward.
That's the average of the two weights (or the net force). You need F = ma on one mass.
questions.x: Find the acceleration first, then use F = ma on one mass. Atwood formula: a = (m₂ − m₁)g ÷ (m₁ + m₂), with m₁ = 2 kg, m₂ = 6 kg, g = 10 m/s². So a = (6 − 2) × 10 ÷ (2 + 6) = 40 ÷ 8 = 5 m/s². Now the 2 kg mass: tension T pulls it up, its weight 2 × 10 = 20 N pulls it down, and it speeds up going up. So T − 20 = 2 × 5 = 10, and T = 20 + 10 = 30 N. Check with the 6 kg mass: 60 − T = 6 × 5 = 30, so T = 30 N. Tension always lands between the two weights.

questions.q: A book rests on a table. What is the Newton's third-law partner of Earth's gravitational pull on the book?
o: The book's gravitational pull on Earth
Correct: same kind of force (gravity), same two objects, just reversed: book on Earth.
The table's normal force on the book
Equal and opposite here, but it's a different force acting on the same object, the book.
The book's push on the table
That's the partner of the table's normal force on the book, not of gravity.
The table's weight
The table's weight is Earth pulling on the table. The book isn't part of that force.
questions.note: Third-law pairs: same interaction, two different objects.
questions.x: A Newton's third-law pair is two sides of one interaction. If A pulls on B, then B pulls on A with the same kind of force, the same size, in the opposite direction. Earth pulls the book down by gravity, so the partner is the book pulling Earth up by gravity. The table's normal force (the table's push up on the book) is also equal and opposite to the weight here, which makes it tempting. But it acts on the same object, the book, and it's a different kind of force, so it isn't the pair.

questions.q: A 10 kg box sits on a floor with μs = 0.4. A 25 N horizontal push does not move it. What is the static friction force (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That's the most static friction can be (0.4 × 100 N), not what it is right now.
0 N
With no friction, the 25 N push would make the box speed up. It stays still.
Correct: the box doesn't move, so friction exactly matches the 25 N push (below the 40 N limit).
This subtracts the push from the limit (40 − 25). Friction just balances the push.
questions.note: Trap: μsN is a ceiling, not the value.
questions.x: Static friction (the grip that keeps a resting object from sliding) is only as strong as it needs to be, up to a limit. The limit is f_max = μsN. Values: μs = 0.4, and on a flat floor N = mg = 10 × 10 = 100 N. So f_max = 0.4 × 100 = 40 N. The push is only 25 N, which is less than 40 N, so the box doesn't slip. It sits still, so the forces cancel: friction is exactly 25 N, pointing against the push. Plugging in μsN when the box isn't about to slip is the trap.

questions.q: Why do anti-lock brakes typically shorten a car's stopping distance?
o: They increase the normal force on the tires
ABS doesn't change the car's weight on the road, so the normal force stays the same.
They convert kinetic friction into rolling resistance
Rolling resistance is tiny and wouldn't stop a car faster. ABS works through tire-road friction.
They raise μk by heating the tires
ABS works by stopping the wheels from locking, not by heating the tires.
They keep tires rolling, so static rather than kinetic friction acts
Correct: rolling tires use static friction, and μs > μk, so the maximum braking force is bigger.
questions.x: There are two kinds of friction. Static friction acts when surfaces grip without sliding. Kinetic friction acts when they slide past each other. For tires on a road, the static coefficient μs is bigger than the kinetic coefficient μk, so gripping can give more braking force than sliding. A wheel that rolls without skidding touches the road with a patch that isn't sliding, so static friction acts. A locked wheel skids, so the weaker kinetic friction acts. Anti-lock brakes (ABS) keep the wheels just short of locking, so they stop the car with the stronger static grip. You also keep steering control.

questions.q: Two identical blocks slide from rest down frictionless ramps of the same height, one steep and one shallow. Which statement is correct?
o: Both arrive at the same time with the same speed
Same speed, yes, but not the same time. The shallow ramp is longer and accelerates the block less.
The steep-ramp block arrives first, and both have the same final speed
Correct: v = √(2gh) for both, but the steep ramp is shorter with bigger acceleration, so it's faster.
The steep-ramp block arrives first with greater speed
Final speed depends only on the height dropped, not the ramp's angle.
The shallow-ramp block arrives first
The shallow-ramp block travels farther with less acceleration, so it takes longer.
questions.x: Speed and time work differently here. Speed: with no friction, the block's stored energy from height (mgh) all turns into energy of motion (½mv²). Set them equal and the mass cancels: v = √(2gh). The angle never shows up, so both blocks reach the bottom at the same speed. Time: down a ramp, the acceleration is g sin θ, where θ is the ramp angle. A steep ramp has a bigger angle, so a bigger acceleration, and it's also shorter. So the steep-ramp block gets there first.

questions.q: A wheelchair ramp rises 1 m for every 12 m of horizontal run. Ignoring friction, about what force along the ramp is needed to push a 100 kg person and chair up at constant speed?
o: That's the full weight (100 × 10), needed only for a straight-up lift.
About 83 N
Correct: sin θ ≈ 1/12 on a gentle slope, and 1000 N × 1/12 ≈ 83 N.
This multiplies the weight by 12. A ramp makes the push smaller, so you divide.
About 500 N
That's the push for a 30° ramp (sin 30° = 1/2). This ramp is much gentler.
questions.x: On a ramp, only part of the weight pulls down the slope: F = mg sin θ. Values: m = 100 kg, g = 10 m/s², so mg = 100 × 10 = 1000 N. The ramp rises 1 m for every 12 m across. For gentle slopes, sin θ is about rise ÷ run, so sin θ ≈ 1/12. Plug in: F ≈ 1000 × 1/12 = 1000 ÷ 12 ≈ 83 N. At constant speed you push exactly that hard. A ramp trades force for distance: the work, mgh, is the same as lifting straight up, but it's spread over a path about 12 times longer.

questions.q: An object moves in a circle at constant speed. In what direction does its acceleration point?
o: Along the velocity, tangent to the path
A push along the motion would change the speed, and the speed here is constant.
Away from the center
Outward 'centrifugal force' is only felt from inside the spinning frame. The real acceleration points inward.
It has no acceleration
The direction keeps changing, so the velocity changes. That's an acceleration.
Toward the center of the circle
Correct: centripetal acceleration points to the center and turns the velocity's direction.
questions.x: Velocity means speed plus direction. In a circle at constant speed, the speed stays the same but the direction keeps changing, so the velocity is changing. Any change in velocity is an acceleration. This one points toward the center of the circle, and it's called centripetal, meaning 'center-seeking'. It's always at a right angle to the motion, so it turns the object without speeding it up or slowing it down. Its size is a = v² ÷ r, where v is the speed and r is the radius. The outward 'centrifugal force' you feel on a spinning ride isn't a real force; it only seems to exist from inside the spinning frame.

questions.q: A car crosses the top of a circular hill of radius 40 m at 20 m/s. What is the normal force from the road on the car?
o: Equal to the car's weight
Only on flat ground or at rest. Curving over a hill uses up some of the road's support.
Twice the car's weight
That's what you'd get at the bottom of a dip, not the top of a hill.
Zero
Correct: v² ÷ r = 400 ÷ 40 = 10 m/s² = g, so gravity alone does the turning and N = 0.
Half the car's weight
That would need v² ÷ r = g ÷ 2 = 5 m/s². Here it's 10 m/s².
questions.note: At a hilltop, N = m(g − v²/r).
questions.x: At the top of a hill, the center of the circle is below the car, so the net force on the car has to point down. Gravity (mg) pulls down and the road pushes up (the normal force, N). So mg − N = mv² ÷ r. Values: v = 20 m/s, r = 40 m, g = 10 m/s². First, v² ÷ r = 20² ÷ 40 = 400 ÷ 40 = 10 m/s². That's exactly g. So N = m(g − v² ÷ r) = m(10 − 10) = 0. Gravity alone is doing all the turning, and the car is just about to leave the road.

questions.q: A ball whirled on a string moves in a horizontal circle. If the string snaps, what path does the ball initially follow (seen from above)?
o: A straight line tangent to the circle
Correct: with no inward pull, the ball keeps its velocity at that moment, which points along the tangent.
A straight line radially outward
There's no outward force to push it that way. That's the 'centrifugal force' mix-up.
A continued circular path
Moving in a circle needs an inward pull, and the string was providing it.
A spiral outward
A spiral would need some ongoing sideways force. With none, the path is straight.
questions.x: A ball only moves in a circle while something keeps pulling it toward the center. Here that's the string. When the string snaps, that pull is gone. Newton's first law says an object with no net force on it keeps going in a straight line at the same speed. So the ball keeps the velocity it had at that instant, and that velocity points along the tangent: a straight line that just touches the circle at that point. It doesn't fly straight outward, because there was never a real outward force.

questions.q: What is the minimum speed a car needs at the top of a vertical loop of radius 10 m to stay on the track (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: 0 m/s
A stopped car at the top would just fall straight down off the track.
10 m/s
Correct: at minimum speed N = 0, so mg = mv² ÷ r and v = √(gr) = √100 = 10 m/s.
About 14 m/s
That's √(2gr) = √200, an energy-style result, not the condition for staying on.
That's gr = 100 without the square root. v² = 100, so v = 10.
questions.x: At the very top of the loop, the center of the circle is below the car, so gravity and the track's push (the normal force N) both point toward the center: mg + N = mv² ÷ r. The slowest the car can go is when the track just stops pushing, N = 0. Then gravity alone does the turning: mg = mv² ÷ r. The mass cancels, leaving v = √(gr). Values: g = 10 m/s², r = 10 m. Plug in: v = √(10 × 10) = √100 = 10 m/s. Any slower and gravity pulls the car down faster than the track curves, so it falls away.

questions.q: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 50 m where μs = 0.5. What is the maximum speed without skidding (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: About 16 m/s
25 m/s
That's μs × r = 0.5 × 50 = 25, leaving out g and the square root.
5 m/s
That's √(μs × r) = √25, leaving out g.
That's v² = 250. You still need the square root.
questions.note: Max speed on a flat curve is independent of mass.
questions.x: On a flat curve, the only thing turning the car is static friction, the grip of tires that aren't sliding. The most grip available is μsmg. To turn, the car needs mv² ÷ r. At top speed they're equal: μsmg = mv² ÷ r. Mass cancels, so v = √(μsgr). Values: μs = 0.5, g = 10 m/s², r = 50 m. Plug in: v = √(0.5 × 10 × 50) = √(5 × 50) = √250. Since 16 × 16 = 256, √250 is just under 16, so about 16 m/s.

questions.q: At what distance from Earth's center is the gravitational acceleration one-ninth of its surface value? (R = Earth's radius)
o: 9R
This forgets the square. At 9R, g drops to 1/81 of the surface value.
At √3 R, r² = 3R², so g is only cut to 1/3.
This squares the factor again. At 81R, g would be 1/6561 of the surface value.
3R
Correct: g goes as 1/r², and one-ninth needs r² = 9R², so r = 3R.
questions.x: Gravity weakens with the square of distance: g = GM ÷ r², where r is the distance from Earth's center. At the surface r = R, so g₀ = GM ÷ R². We want g = g₀ ÷ 9. Plug in: GM ÷ r² = (1/9) × GM ÷ R². Cancel GM and flip both sides: r² = 9R². Take the square root: r = 3R. Check: GM ÷ (3R)² = GM ÷ 9R², which is one-ninth. Note that 3R is measured from the center, so it's only 2R above the ground. Picking 9R treats gravity as if it fell off as 1/r.

questions.q: A uniform 4 m beam weighing 200 N rests on supports at each end. A 400 N person stands 1 m from the left end. What force does the left support exert?
o: That's the right support. The person stands nearer the left, so the left carries more.
Correct: about the right end, L × 4 = 200 × 2 + 400 × 3 = 1600, so L = 400 N.
This splits 600 N evenly, which works only if the load sits in the middle.
That's the whole load. Two supports share it.
questions.x: The beam isn't moving or turning, so the torques (turning effects, force × distance from a pivot) must balance. Put the pivot at the right support, so its unknown force drops out. Values: the beam is 4 m long, so the left support is 4 m from the pivot. The 200 N beam weight acts at its middle, 2 m away. The 400 N person is 1 m from the left, so 4 − 1 = 3 m from the right. Balance: L × 4 = 200 × 2 + 400 × 3 = 400 + 1200 = 1600, so L = 1600 ÷ 4 = 400 N. Check: total load is 600 N, so the right support carries 600 − 400 = 200 N.

questions.q: A 4 kg lamp hangs from two strings, each making 60° with the horizontal ceiling. What is the tension in each string (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: This splits 40 N in half and ignores the angle. Angled strings must pull harder.
This gives each string the full weight. Two strings share the job.
About 23 N
Correct: 2T sin 60° = 40 N, so T = 40 ÷ 1.73 ≈ 23 N.
About 46 N
This divides by sin 60° but forgets that two strings share the load.
questions.x: A tilted string pulls partly up and partly sideways. With the angle θ measured from the horizontal, the upward part is T sin θ. The two strings' sideways parts cancel, and their upward parts hold up the weight: 2T sin 60° = mg. Values: m = 4 kg, g = 10 m/s², so mg = 40 N; sin 60° ≈ 0.87 (that's 1.73 ÷ 2). Plug in: 2 × T × (1.73 ÷ 2) = 40, so 1.73 × T = 40, and T = 40 ÷ 1.73 ≈ 23 N. Each string pulls more than half the weight, because part of its pull goes sideways.

questions.q: A spring (k = 200 N/m) is already stretched 0.1 m. How much additional work stretches it to 0.2 m?
o: 1 J
That's the work for the first 0.1 m (0 to 0.1 m), not the second.
3 J
4 J
That's the total from 0 to 0.2 m. The first 1 J was already done.
2 J
This splits the 4 J total evenly, as if each 0.1 m costs the same.
questions.note: Spring work grows with x², not x.
questions.x: A stretched spring stores energy U = ½kx², and the work to stretch it further is the increase in that energy: W = ½k(x₂² − x₁²). Values: k = 200 N/m, x₁ = 0.1 m, x₂ = 0.2 m. Squares: 0.2² = 0.04 and 0.1² = 0.01. Plug in: W = ½ × 200 × (0.04 − 0.01) = 100 × 0.03 = 3 J. The first 0.1 m only took ½ × 200 × 0.01 = 1 J, so the second 0.1 m costs three times as much. The spring pulls back harder the more it's stretched.

questions.q: A 50 kg sledder starts from rest at the top of a 10 m high hill and reaches 10 m/s at the bottom. How much energy was lost to friction (g = 10 m/s²)?
o: That's all the starting energy. Half of it is still there as motion at the bottom.
This adds KE to PE. Energy lost is the difference, not the sum.
0 J
The sledder ends with less energy than it started with, so some was lost.
questions.x: Start with the energy at the top, then see how much is left at the bottom. At the top the sledder is at rest, so all the energy is potential energy (energy stored from height): PE = mgh. Values: m = 50 kg, g = 10 m/s², h = 10 m, v = 10 m/s at the bottom. PE = 50 × 10 × 10 = 5000 J. At the bottom it's all kinetic energy (energy of motion): KE = ½mv² = ½ × 50 × 10² = 25 × 100 = 2500 J. The difference, 5000 − 2500 = 2500 J, was turned into heat by friction.

questions.q: Total mechanical energy of a system is conserved when:
o: The net force is zero
In free fall the net force isn't zero, yet energy is conserved. Force and energy are different questions.
Friction is present but small
Any friction, however small, turns some mechanical energy into heat.
The object moves at constant speed
A block sliding down a rough ramp at constant speed loses height, so it loses mechanical energy.
Only conservative forces do work
Correct: friction and drag move energy out of KE + PE; gravity and springs don't.
questions.x: Mechanical energy is kinetic energy (energy of motion) plus potential energy (energy stored by position, like height or a stretched spring). It stays constant when only conservative forces do work. A conservative force, like gravity or a spring, stores energy and gives it all back. Nonconservative forces, like friction, air drag or your muscles, add or remove mechanical energy, usually turning it into heat. A net force is fine: in free fall, gravity is the net force and the ball speeds up, yet KE + PE stays the same.

questions.q: In a lab, a solid ball rolling without slipping down a ramp consistently has about 30% less translational KE at the bottom than mgh predicts. What best explains this?
o: The ball's mass was too large
Mass cancels when comparing KE to mgh, so it can't cause a percentage shortfall.
The local value of g is larger than assumed
A bigger g would make the KE bigger, not smaller.
Some energy goes into the ball's rotational kinetic energy
Correct: for a solid sphere, 2/7 of the energy (about 29%) goes into spinning.
The ramp height was underestimated
Underestimating h would make the measured KE look too big, not too small.
questions.x: A ball that rolls without slipping has to spin as well as move forward. So the energy from the drop, mgh, gets shared between two kinds of kinetic energy: translational (moving forward, ½mv²) and rotational (spinning, ½Iω², where I is the moment of inertia, an object's resistance to spinning, and ω is how fast it spins). For a solid sphere, I = ⅖mr², and that works out to 2/7 of the energy going into spin. 2 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.29, or about 29%, which matches the 30% shortfall.

questions.q: A 1 kg puck moving east at 3 m/s collides and sticks to a 1 kg puck moving north at 3 m/s. What is the velocity of the combined pucks?
o: 3 m/s toward the northeast
That's each puck's speed before. Twice the mass sharing the momentum moves slower.
About 2.1 m/s toward the northeast
Correct: 1.5 m/s east and 1.5 m/s north, so √(1.5² + 1.5²) ≈ 2.1 m/s northeast.
About 4.2 m/s toward the northeast
That's 3√2, the combined momentum, without dividing by the 2 kg total mass.
0 m/s
Momenta at right angles can't cancel. Only opposite directions cancel.
questions.note: Conserve each momentum component separately.
questions.x: Momentum (mass × velocity) is conserved in each direction separately. East: 1 kg × 3 m/s = 3 kg·m/s. North: 1 kg × 3 m/s = 3 kg·m/s. The stuck-together pucks have 1 + 1 = 2 kg, so v_east = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 m/s and v_north = 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5 m/s. Combine the two at right angles with the Pythagorean theorem: v = √(1.5² + 1.5²) = √(2.25 + 2.25) = √4.5 ≈ 2.1 m/s. Equal east and north parts mean it heads northeast.

questions.q: Cart A (1 kg) moves at 4 m/s toward stationary cart B (1 kg). Afterward, A moves at 1 m/s and B at 3 m/s, both forward. How should this collision be classified?
o: Perfectly elastic
Elastic means KE is kept. Here it drops from 8 J to 5 J.
Perfectly inelastic
Perfectly inelastic means they stick. They end at different speeds, so they separated.
Impossible, because momentum isn't conserved
Momentum is conserved: 4 before and 1 + 3 = 4 kg·m/s after.
Inelastic, but not perfectly inelastic
Correct: momentum stays at 4 kg·m/s, KE drops from 8 J to 5 J, and the carts separate.
questions.x: Check momentum first (mass × velocity). Before: 1 × 4 = 4 kg·m/s. After: 1 × 1 + 1 × 3 = 1 + 3 = 4 kg·m/s. It's conserved, so the collision is possible. Now kinetic energy, KE = ½mv². Before: ½ × 1 × 4² = ½ × 16 = 8 J. After: ½ × 1 × 1² + ½ × 1 × 3² = 0.5 + 4.5 = 5 J. KE dropped, so it isn't elastic. The carts end at different speeds, so they didn't stick, which rules out perfectly inelastic. That leaves plain inelastic.

questions.q: Two carts collide on a frictionless track with no external horizontal forces. What happens to the velocity of the system's center of mass?
o: It drops to zero at the moment of impact
The carts' pushes on each other are internal, and they can't change how the center of mass moves.
It increases if the collision is elastic
Elastic or not affects KE, not total momentum, so the center of mass can't speed up.
It remains constant
Correct: no outside force, so total momentum and center-of-mass velocity stay constant.
It reverses direction
Reversing would need an outside push. The carts only trade momentum with each other.
questions.x: The center of mass is the average position of all the mass in a system. Its velocity is the total momentum divided by the total mass. When the carts collide, they push on each other, but those are internal forces: equal and opposite, so they just move momentum from one cart to the other. The total momentum doesn't change unless an outside force acts, and there isn't one here. So the center-of-mass velocity stays exactly the same, whether the collision is gentle, violent, elastic or sticky.

questions.q: An ideal simple machine lets a person lift a load with a smaller effort force. Compared with lifting the load directly, which quantity is unchanged?
o: The effort force
It's smaller. Making the effort force smaller is the whole point of the machine.
The work required
Correct: W = Fd, and the smaller force acts over a longer distance, so work stays the same.
The distance the effort must move
It's larger. A smaller force has to act over a longer distance to do the same work.
The ratio of load force to effort force
That ratio is the mechanical advantage, and it goes above 1 for a useful machine.
questions.note: Machines trade force for distance, never saving work.
questions.x: Work is force × distance (W = Fd). An ideal simple machine, like a lever, pulley or ramp with no friction, can't create energy, so the work to lift the load is the same as lifting it directly: mgh. What the machine does is let you use a smaller force over a longer distance. Force goes down, distance goes up by the same factor, and the product stays the same: F_in × d_in = F_out × d_out. Real machines need a bit more work than this because friction wastes some.

questions.q: Lifting a box with a bent back, the erector spinae act about 5 cm behind the lumbar discs, while the upper body and box weight act about 40 cm in front. Why are disc forces so large?
o: The weight of the box acts directly on the discs only
The muscle force, not just the box's weight, is what loads the discs most.
Bending reduces the muscles' lever arm to zero
The lever arm is short (5 cm) but not zero. Zero would need an infinite force.
Gravity is stronger when the back is bent
g doesn't change with posture. What changes is how far the weight is from the spine.
The short muscle lever arm requires a muscle force many times the load
Correct: muscle force × 5 cm = load × 40 cm, so the muscles pull about 8 times the load.
questions.note: Bend the knees to bring the load closer.
questions.x: Torque is force × lever arm, where the lever arm is the distance from the pivot (here, the disc). To hold still, the muscle's torque must match the load's torque: F_muscle × d_muscle = W × d_load. Values: d_muscle = 5 cm, d_load = 40 cm. Plug in: F_muscle × 5 = W × 40, so F_muscle = W × 40 ÷ 5 = 8W. The back muscles must pull 8 times the load, and the disc gets squeezed by that muscle force plus the weight. Holding the load close shortens its lever arm and cuts the muscle force.

questions.q: A saline solution has a density of 1200 kg/m³. What is its specific gravity?
o: This flips the ratio: 1000 ÷ 1200. The substance goes on top.
Correct: SG = 1200 ÷ 1000 = 1.2, and the units cancel.
That's the density itself. You still have to divide by water's 1000 kg/m³.
1.2 kg/m³
Right number, but SG is a ratio of two densities, so it has no units.
questions.x: Specific gravity (SG) tells you how many times denser something is than water. Formula: SG = ρ_substance ÷ ρ_water, where ρ (ρ) means density. Values: ρ_substance = 1200 kg/m³ and ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³. Plug in: SG = 1200 ÷ 1000 = 1.2. The kg/m³ on top and bottom cancel, so SG has no units at all. So the saline is 1.2 times as dense as water. Writing 1200, or tacking kg/m³ onto 1.2, are both wrong.

questions.q: A patient's urine specific gravity rises from 1.005 to 1.030 after a day without drinking. This change indicates that the urine:
o: Contains more water per unit solute
More water per solute would dilute the urine and push SG down toward 1.000.
Has a lower mass per unit volume
A higher SG means more mass per volume, not less.
Contains more dissolved solute per unit volume
Correct: more dissolved solute per volume adds mass, so density and SG go up.
Has become less dense than water
Any SG above 1.000 means denser than water. 1.030 is denser, not less.
questions.x: Specific gravity (SG) is a liquid's density divided by water's density. Pure water is exactly 1.000. Dissolved stuff in urine, like salts and waste, adds mass without adding much volume, so the more of it there is per volume, the higher the SG. When you don't drink, the kidneys hold on to water and get rid of the same waste in less water. The urine gets more concentrated, and the SG climbs from 1.005 (nearly as dilute as water) to 1.030. So the change means more dissolved solute per volume.

questions.q: Equal masses of two liquids with densities 800 kg/m³ and 1200 kg/m³ are mixed (volumes additive). The mixture's density is:
o: 960 kg/m³
Correct: 1 kg each gives V = 5/2400 m³, and 2 kg ÷ (5/2400 m³) = 960 kg/m³.
1040 kg/m³
This leans toward the denser liquid. With equal masses, the lighter one takes up more space.
2000 kg/m³
Densities can't be added. The sum has no physical meaning.
1000 kg/m³
A simple average works only for equal volumes. Here the masses are equal.
questions.x: Density is mass ÷ volume, so for a mixture you add up the masses, add up the volumes, then divide. Don't just average the densities. Take 1 kg of each liquid. Volume = mass ÷ density: V₁ = 1 ÷ 800 and V₂ = 1 ÷ 1200 m³. Common bottom 2400: 1/800 = 3/2400 and 1/1200 = 2/2400, so total V = 5/2400 m³. Total mass is 2 kg. Density = 2 ÷ (5/2400) = 2 × 2400 ÷ 5 = 4800 ÷ 5 = 960 kg/m³. That's below the simple average of 1000 because the lighter liquid takes up more space.

questions.q: An open-ended mercury manometer is attached to a gas tank. The mercury on the open side stands 20 cm higher than on the tank side. The gauge pressure of the gas is about: (ρ(Hg) = 13,600 kg/m³)
o: That's gauge plus atmospheric pressure, which is the absolute pressure.
Negative would mean the tank is below air pressure. The open side is higher, so it's above.
Correct: ρgh = 13,600 × 10 × 0.2 = 27,200 ≈ 2.7 × 10⁴ Pa, positive.
That uses water's density (1000 kg/m³) instead of mercury's 13,600 kg/m³.
questions.x: Gauge pressure is how much a pressure is above the air pressure around us. In an open-tube manometer (a U-tube of liquid, one end open to air, the other on the tank), the height difference shows it: P_gauge = ρgh. The mercury is higher on the open side, so the gas is pushing harder than the air, and the gauge pressure is positive. Values: ρ = 13,600 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s², h = 20 cm. 1 m = 100 cm, so divide by 100: 20 cm = 0.2 m. Plug in: P = 13,600 × 10 × 0.2 = 13,600 × 2 = 27,200 Pa ≈ 2.7 × 10⁴ Pa.

questions.q: An open beaker of water sits in an elevator accelerating upward at 2 m/s². What is the gauge pressure 1 m below the water surface?
o: That's g − a, for an elevator speeding up downward.
That's the pressure with the elevator still or at constant speed. It ignores the acceleration.
This doubles g. You add the 2 m/s², you don't multiply by 2.
questions.x: Pressure under water comes from holding up the water above. In an elevator speeding up upward, everything feels heavier, water included, so the water pushes down harder. You handle that with an effective gravity: g_eff = g + a for upward acceleration. Formula: P = ρ(g + a)h. Values: ρ = 1000 kg/m³ (water), g = 10 m/s², a = 2 m/s², h = 1 m. Plug in: P = 1000 × (10 + 2) × 1 = 1000 × 12 = 12,000 Pa. Speeding up downward would give g − a, and free fall would make the gauge pressure zero.

questions.q: In a hydraulic lift with an area ratio of 1:25, the small piston is pushed down 50 cm. How far does the large piston rise?
o: 10 cm
This uses the radius ratio (5) instead of the area ratio (25).
This multiplies by 25. The big piston moves less, not more.
2 cm
Correct: the volumes match, so d₂ = 50 cm ÷ 25 = 2 cm.
50 cm
Equal distances would mean more volume came out than went in.
questions.x: Liquid can't be squeezed, so the volume pushed down on the small side is exactly the volume that lifts the big side. Volume = area × distance, so A₁d₁ = A₂d₂. Values: A₂ = 25 × A₁ (a 1:25 area ratio), d₁ = 50 cm. Solve for d₂: d₂ = (A₁ ÷ A₂) × d₁ = (1/25) × 50 = 50 ÷ 25 = 2 cm. This matches energy: the big piston pushes with 25 times the force but moves 1/25 as far, so the work in equals the work out.

questions.q: Ignoring gravity, cerebrospinal fluid pressure at the skull rises by 20 mmHg. What change would a lumbar spinal needle in the same continuous fluid space register?
o: No change, because the needle is far from the skull
Distance doesn't weaken a pressure change in a connected liquid.
An increase of 20 mmHg
Correct: by Pascal's principle, the change is passed along at full strength everywhere.
An increase much smaller than 20 mmHg
A pressure change doesn't fade on its way through a closed liquid.
An increase much larger than 20 mmHg
Pascal's principle passes pressure along; it doesn't multiply it.
questions.x: Pascal's principle says that if you change the pressure anywhere in a closed, connected liquid, that same change shows up everywhere in the liquid, without getting smaller. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF, the clear liquid around the brain and spinal cord) fills one connected space from the skull down to the lower back. So a 20 mmHg rise at the skull also shows up as a 20 mmHg rise at the lumbar needle. Distance doesn't weaken it. That's why the pressure measured in a lumbar puncture can tell doctors about the pressure inside the skull.

questions.q: An object weighs 30 N in air and 20 N when fully submerged in water. What is its density?
o: 1500 kg/m³
This divides by 20 N (30 ÷ 20) instead of the 10 N buoyant force.
2000 kg/m³
This divides the underwater reading by the buoyant force (20 ÷ 10).
3000 kg/m³
Correct: F_b = 10 N gives V = 10⁻³ m³, and 3 kg ÷ 10⁻³ m³ = 3000 kg/m³.
667 kg/m³
This uses 20 ÷ 30. An object that sinks must be denser than water's 1000 kg/m³.
questions.x: Under water, the water pushes up on the object. That push is the buoyant force, and it's how much lighter the object seems: F_b = 30 − 20 = 10 N. The buoyant force equals the weight of water the object pushes aside, so ρ_water × V × g = 10 N, and V = 10 ÷ (1000 × 10) = 10 ÷ 10⁴ = 10⁻³ m³. Mass: m = weight ÷ g = 30 ÷ 10 = 3 kg. Density: ρ = m ÷ V = 3 ÷ 10⁻³. Dividing by 10⁻³ is multiplying by 10³, so ρ = 3 × 10³ = 3000 kg/m³. The trap is using the 20 N reading as the buoyant force.

questions.q: An ice cube floats in a glass of fresh water filled to the brim. When the ice melts completely, the water level:
o: Rises, then falls back as it cools
No temperature effect is needed, and it isn't the reason.
Stays the same
Correct: the ice displaces its own weight of water, and that's exactly what its meltwater fills.
Rises and overflows
The part above the surface is just the extra room ice takes up for being less dense.
Falls
The meltwater fills exactly the space the ice was pushing aside, no less.
questions.x: A floating object pushes aside (displaces) an amount of water that weighs exactly as much as the object. That's Archimedes' principle for floating things. So the ice is pushing aside water equal to its own weight. When it melts, its mass doesn't change; it just becomes that same weight of liquid water. That water fills exactly the 'hole' the ice was making in the water. Nothing extra is added, so the level stays the same. The bit of ice poking above the surface is just the extra room ice takes up because it's less dense than water.

questions.q: A boat floating in a closed pool carries a large rock. The rock is dropped overboard and sinks. The pool's water level:
o: Falls
Correct: in the boat it displaced its weight of water; on the bottom, only its smaller volume.
Rises
A sunken dense rock pushes aside less water than it did while riding in the boat.
Rises, then returns to the original level
There's no temporary rise. The level ends up lower and stays lower.
Stays the same
That would be true only if the rock were exactly as dense as water.
questions.x: Two rules: a floating object pushes aside its WEIGHT of water; a sunken object pushes aside only its own VOLUME of water. In the boat, the rock is floating along with it, so it pushes aside water that weighs as much as the rock. A rock is much denser than water, so that's a lot of water, far more than the rock's own volume. Once it sinks, it pushes aside only its own small volume. Less water pushed aside means the level falls.

questions.q: A 0.001 m³ block of wood (density 600 kg/m³) is held fully under water by a string tied to the bottom of the tank. What is the tension in the string?
o: 4 N
Correct: buoyant force 10 N minus weight 6 N leaves 4 N for the string.
This adds weight and buoyancy, but they push in opposite directions.
That's the buoyant force alone. The weight also pulls down, so the string needs less.
6 N
That's the block's weight, not the string's pull.
questions.x: The block is still, so the forces balance. Up: the buoyant force (the water's upward push). Down: the block's weight and the string's pull. So F_b = W + T, and T = F_b − W. Values: V = 0.001 m³, ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, ρ_wood = 600 kg/m³, g = 10 m/s². Buoyant force: F_b = ρ_water × V × g = 1000 × 0.001 × 10 = 1 × 10 = 10 N. Weight: W = 600 × 0.001 × 10 = 0.6 × 10 = 6 N. Tension: T = 10 − 6 = 4 N. The string pulls down, because the wood would float up if you cut it.

questions.q: Blood leaves the aorta (area 4 cm²) at 25 cm/s. The total cross-sectional area of all systemic capillaries is about 2500 cm². What is the average speed of blood in the capillaries?
o: 625 cm/s
This multiplies by the area ratio. Bigger total area means slower blood, so you divide.
25 cm/s
Speed stays the same only if the total area stays the same. Here it grows 625 times.
Correct: flow = 4 × 25 = 100 cm³/s, then 100 ÷ 2500 = 0.04 cm/s.
0.4 cm/s
Off by a factor of 10: 100 ÷ 2500 is 0.04, not 0.4.
questions.x: Blood can't be squeezed, so the same volume has to pass every level of the circulation each second. That's the continuity rule: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. In the aorta, A₁ = 4 cm² and v₁ = 25 cm/s, so the flow is 4 × 25 = 100 cm³ every second. In the capillaries that same 100 cm³/s spreads over A₂ = 2500 cm², so v₂ = 100 ÷ 2500 = 0.04 cm/s. Each capillary is tiny, but there are so many of them that their total area is huge, and that's why blood slows way down there.

questions.q: An artery divides into 4 identical branches, each with half the parent's radius. Compared with the parent, the average flow speed in each branch is:
o: Four times larger
This looks at one branch only. The flow is shared among four branches.
Twice as large
This uses the radius instead of the area. Area goes with radius squared.
Half as large
This acts as if the total area doubled. It stayed the same.
The same
Correct: total branch area = 4 × (1/2)² = 1 times the parent's, so the speed is the same.
questions.x: Blood can't be squeezed, so the flow in equals the flow out: A_parent × v_parent = A_total × v_branch, where A_total is the combined area of all four branches. Area of a circle is πr², so it goes with the radius squared. Each branch has half the radius, so its area is (1/2)² = 1/4 of the parent's. Four branches: 4 × 1/4 = 1 times the parent's area. The total area hasn't changed, so the average speed doesn't change either. Looking at one branch alone, or using radius instead of area, gives a false change.

questions.q: During a storm, strong wind blowing horizontally across a flat roof lifts the roof off a house. This is best explained by:
o: Lower pressure in the fast-moving air above the roof
Correct: faster air above has lower pressure, so the still air inside pushes the roof up.
Buoyancy of the roof in the surrounding air
Air's buoyant force on a roof is tiny, and wind speed doesn't change it.
Wind pushing directly upward on the roof surface
A sideways wind pushes sideways. It can't push straight up on a flat roof.
Higher pressure in the fast-moving air above the roof
This flips Bernoulli's principle. Faster air has lower pressure, not higher.
questions.note: Faster flow means lower static pressure.
questions.x: Bernoulli's principle says that in a moving fluid, faster flow means lower pressure. Wind racing across the roof makes the air above it fast, so the pressure above the roof drops. The air inside the house is still, so it stays at normal pressure. Now the inside pushes up on the roof harder than the outside pushes down, and that difference in pressure, spread over the whole roof's area, can be enough to lift it. A sideways wind can't push a flat roof straight up, and air's buoyancy is tiny.

questions.q: Which is an assumption of Poiseuille's law?
o: Turbulent flow through a flexible tube
Turbulence and stretchy walls both break the law's assumptions.
Flow of a fluid with zero viscosity
The law is all about viscosity; η is in the formula.
Compressible gas flow at high speed
The law assumes a fluid that can't be squeezed, flowing slowly and smoothly.
Laminar flow of a Newtonian fluid through a rigid cylindrical tube
Correct: the law needs steady laminar flow, constant viscosity and a rigid round tube.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law gives the flow through a tube: Q = πr⁴ΔP ÷ (8ηL), where r is the radius, ΔP the pressure difference, η the viscosity (how thick the fluid is) and L the length. It was worked out for a specific, tidy situation: smooth, layered (laminar) flow that stays steady; a fluid that can't be squeezed and is Newtonian, meaning its viscosity stays constant; and a long, rigid, round tube. Turbulence, stretchy walls, compressible gas or zero viscosity all break those assumptions. Blood vessels only roughly fit.

questions.q: Two vessel segments of equal length are in series; the second has half the radius of the first. Approximately what fraction of the total pressure drop occurs across the narrow segment?
o: Equal drops would need equal resistances, and the radii differ.
This treats resistance as 1/r (2 times), giving 2/3.
This treats resistance as 1/r² (4 times), giving 4/5.
Correct: R goes as 1/r⁴, so the narrow part has 16 times the resistance and takes 16/17 ≈ 94%.
questions.x: In series, the same flow Q goes through both segments, so each one's pressure drop is ΔP = QR: bigger resistance, bigger drop. Poiseuille's law says resistance goes as 1/r⁴. Halving the radius multiplies the resistance by 2⁴ = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16. So if the wide segment has resistance 1, the narrow one has 16, and the total is 1 + 16 = 17. The narrow segment's share is 16/17. 1/17 ≈ 0.06, so 16/17 ≈ 1 − 0.06 = 0.94, or about 94%. That's why most of the pressure drop in the body happens at the narrowest vessels, the arterioles.

questions.q: Unlike liquids, the viscosity of a gas increases with temperature. The best explanation is that, at higher temperature, gas molecules:
o: Become more densely packed
Heating a gas at constant pressure spreads it out, making it less dense.
Form temporary hydrogen-bonded clusters
Heat breaks clusters apart rather than forming them, and gases barely attract anyway.
Move faster and transfer more momentum between layers
Correct: faster molecules carry more momentum between layers, so the drag rises.
Attract each other more strongly
Attractions don't grow with temperature, and they hardly matter in a gas.
questions.x: Viscosity is how much a fluid resists its layers sliding past each other. Liquids and gases get it in different ways. In a liquid, molecules stick to their neighbors, and heat loosens that grip, so viscosity drops. In a gas, molecules are far apart and barely attract each other. Instead, molecules keep zipping from one layer into the next, carrying their momentum (mass × velocity) with them and tugging the other layer along. Heat makes them move faster, so they carry more momentum across, and the drag between layers goes up.

questions.q: While a blood pressure cuff is deflated between systolic and diastolic pressure, Korotkoff sounds are heard. These sounds arise because flow through the partly compressed artery is:
o: Turbulent
Correct: blood spurting fast through the squeezed artery turns turbulent, and turbulence makes noise.
Flowing backward
Blood still moves forward; it's just forced through a narrow gap.
Completely stopped
No flow means no sound. That's above systolic pressure, before the sounds start.
Laminar
Laminar flow is silent. It comes back below diastolic, when the sounds stop.
questions.x: Smooth, layered flow (laminar flow) is silent. Chaotic, swirling flow (turbulent flow) makes noise. When the cuff pressure is between systolic (the top number, the peak pressure) and diastolic (the bottom number, the lowest pressure), the cuff squeezes the artery partly shut. With each heartbeat, blood spurts through the narrow gap at high speed, and fast flow through a narrow opening turns turbulent. That turbulence is the tapping you hear: Korotkoff sounds. Above systolic, no blood gets through, so it's silent. Below diastolic, the artery stays open, flow is smooth again, and the sounds stop.

questions.q: Blood is a shear-thinning (non-Newtonian) fluid. As the shear rate increases, for example during fast flow, blood's apparent viscosity:
o: Increases, as red cells collide more often
Getting thicker with faster flow describes a shear-thickening fluid. Blood is the opposite.
Decreases, as red cells disaggregate and align with flow
Correct: shear-thinning fluids get runnier at higher shear as red cells break apart and line up.
Is unchanged, as with water
Constant viscosity is what water (a Newtonian fluid) does. Blood isn't Newtonian.
Drops to zero
Blood's viscosity drops with shear but never reaches zero.
questions.x: Viscosity is how thick a fluid acts, how much it resists flowing. Shear rate is how fast its layers slide past each other; fast flow means high shear. Water is a Newtonian fluid: its viscosity stays the same at any shear. Blood is non-Newtonian and shear-thinning, meaning it gets runnier the faster it flows. At low shear, red blood cells stack up like coins (called rouleaux) and resist flow. At high shear, the stacks break apart and the cells stretch and line up with the flow, so the blood acts less viscous.

questions.q: At very high pressure, a real gas often occupies a larger volume than the ideal gas law predicts. The main reason is that:
o: Gas molecules have a finite volume of their own
Correct: molecules take up space, and that matters a lot when the gas is squeezed tight.
Collisions with the walls become elastic
The ideal gas law already assumes elastic collisions, so this can't explain a difference.
Intermolecular attractions pull molecules together
Attractions pull molecules together and make the volume smaller, not larger.
Molecules move faster at high pressure
Molecular speed depends on temperature, not pressure.
questions.x: The ideal gas law, PV = nRT, assumes two things that aren't quite true: that molecules take up no space, and that they don't attract each other. At very high pressure, the molecules are squeezed so close that their own size becomes a big part of the container. That space is 'taken', so the gas can't be compressed as much as the ideal law predicts, and the real volume comes out larger. (In the van der Waals equation, that's the b term.) Attractions do the opposite: they pull molecules together and make the volume smaller.

questions.q: A diver fills her lungs to 2 L at 20 m depth (about 3 atm absolute), then holds her breath and ascends to the surface. Her lung gas would expand to about:
o: 4 L
This uses gauge pressure (2 atm). Boyle's law needs absolute pressure (3 atm).
2 L
Gas volume changes when the pressure changes.
6 L
Correct: 3 atm × 2 L = 1 atm × V, so V = 6 L.
That's 2 ÷ 3, as if the gas were squeezed. Rising lowers pressure, so it expands.
questions.x: Boyle's law: at the same temperature, a gas's pressure × volume stays the same, P₁V₁ = P₂V₂. It needs absolute pressure (total pressure, including the air above the water). Values: at 20 m, P₁ ≈ 3 atm (1 atm of air plus about 1 atm for every 10 m of water: 1 + 2 = 3); V₁ = 2 L; at the surface, P₂ = 1 atm. Plug in: 3 × 2 = 1 × V₂, so V₂ = 6 ÷ 1 = 6 L. That's enough to over-stretch and tear lungs, which is why divers must breathe out as they rise.

questions.q: Air (21% O₂) is inhaled at sea level (760 mmHg) and fully humidified at body temperature, where water vapor pressure is 47 mmHg. The PO₂ of the humidified air is about:
o: 100 mmHg
That's alveolar PO₂, lower because O₂ is absorbed and CO₂ is added.
160 mmHg
That's 0.21 × 760, which ignores the water vapor.
150 mmHg
113 mmHg
This subtracts all 47 mmHg from O₂ alone (160 − 47). Water takes it from the total.
questions.x: Dalton's law: in a gas mix, each gas's partial pressure (its share of the total pressure) is its fraction of the mix times the pressure. But when air is warmed and humidified in your airways, water vapor takes 47 mmHg of the total first. Formula: PO₂ = FO₂ × (P_atm − P_H₂O). Values: FO₂ = 0.21, P_atm = 760 mmHg, P_H₂O = 47 mmHg. Plug in: 760 − 47 = 713 mmHg left for the dry gases, and 0.21 × 713 ≈ 150 mmHg. Skip the water and you get 160 mmHg, which is too high.

questions.q: Helium is pumped into a rigid, sealed container of air at constant temperature, doubling the total pressure. The partial pressure of O₂ in the container:
o: Halves
O₂'s share of the mix halves, but the total pressure doubles, so P(O₂) stays the same.
Falls to zero
Helium doesn't react with O₂ or remove it.
Doubles
Only the total doubled. The amount of O₂ didn't change, so its pressure didn't either.
Is unchanged
Correct: O₂'s moles, the volume and the temperature didn't change, so neither did P(O₂).
questions.x: Each gas in a mix acts as if it had the container to itself. Its partial pressure (its own share of the pressure) depends only on its own amount, the volume and the temperature: P = nRT ÷ V. Pumping in helium doesn't change the amount of O₂ (n), the rigid container's volume (V) or the temperature (T). So P(O₂) stays the same. Helium just adds its own pressure on top, which is why the total doubles. O₂'s fraction of the mix does drop by half, but the total doubles, and the two cancel.

questions.q: Across the alveolar membrane, the PO₂ gradient is about 60 mmHg while the PCO₂ gradient is only about 6 mmHg, yet CO₂ exchange is not limited. The best explanation is that CO₂:
o: Is far more soluble in water and tissue than O₂
Correct: CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂, which makes up for its small gradient.
Is actively transported across the membrane
Gas exchange in the lungs is passive diffusion. No pumps are involved.
Has a lower molar mass than O₂
CO₂ (44 g/mol) is heavier than O₂ (32 g/mol), not lighter.
Has a higher partial pressure in air than O₂
Air has far less CO₂ than O₂, so its partial pressure is much lower.
questions.x: Gases cross the alveolar membrane by diffusion: they drift from high partial pressure to low, with no energy spent. Fick's law says the rate depends on the pressure gradient (the difference across the membrane) times the gas's solubility (how easily it dissolves in the watery membrane), along with other factors. CO₂ dissolves about 20 times better than O₂. So its small 6 mmHg gradient does a lot of work: 6 × 20 = 120, compared with O₂'s 60 × 1 = 60. CO₂ is actually heavier than O₂, so molar mass doesn't explain it.

questions.q: Raising a patient's PaO₂ from 100 to 600 mmHg increases arterial O₂ content only modestly. Why?
o: Extra O₂ lowers plasma solubility
Solubility is fixed for a given gas, liquid and temperature. It doesn't drop as pressure rises.
Henry's law stops applying above 100 mmHg
Henry's law keeps working. Dissolved O₂ rises in a straight line with PO₂.
Hemoglobin is already nearly saturated, and dissolved O₂ rises only by a small amount
Correct: Hb is nearly full already, and dissolved O₂ rises only a little (about 1.5 mL/dL).
High PO₂ causes hemoglobin to release O₂
High PO₂ pushes O₂ onto hemoglobin, not off it.
questions.x: Blood carries O₂ two ways: most of it stuck to hemoglobin (Hb, the oxygen-carrying protein in red cells) and a tiny bit dissolved in plasma. At a PaO₂ (arterial O₂ pressure) of 100 mmHg, Hb is already about 98% full, so raising the pressure can't load much more onto it. The dissolved part does keep rising, in a straight line, as Henry's law says: 0.003 mL/dL for every mmHg. From 100 to 600 mmHg, that's 0.003 × 100 = 0.3 rising to 0.003 × 600 = 1.8 mL/dL, a gain of only 1.8 − 0.3 = 1.5 mL/dL. Normal blood holds about 20 mL/dL, so it's a modest bump.

questions.q: Plasma equilibrates with alveolar gas at PO₂ = 100 mmHg and PCO₂ = 40 mmHg. Comparing dissolved gases, the plasma contains:
o: More dissolved CO₂ than O₂, despite CO₂'s lower partial pressure
Correct: CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble, so 20 × 40 = 800 beats 1 × 100 = 100.
Equal concentrations of both gases
Equal amounts would need equal solubility × pressure. These come to 800 and 100.
No dissolved CO₂, since it is all converted to bicarbonate
Lots of CO₂ becomes bicarbonate, but some always stays dissolved as CO₂.
More dissolved O₂ than CO₂, because PO₂ is higher
Higher pressure alone doesn't decide it. Solubility matters too, and CO₂'s is much higher.
questions.x: Henry's law says the amount of a gas dissolved in a liquid is its solubility (how well it dissolves) times its partial pressure. So you need both numbers, not just the pressure. CO₂ is about 20 times more soluble than O₂. In relative units: O₂ is 1 × 100 = 100, and CO₂ is 20 × 40 = 800. So even with less than half the partial pressure, CO₂ ends up about 8 times more concentrated in plasma than dissolved O₂.

questions.q: An experimenter measures flow through a rigid tube at several pressure differences. Flow doubles when ΔP doubles at low ΔP, but at high ΔP, doubling ΔP raises flow by only about 40%. The best interpretation is that:
o: The fluid's viscosity fell at high ΔP
Lower viscosity would make flow rise more, not less.
The tube's radius increased at high ΔP
The tube is rigid, and a wider tube would raise flow anyway.
Poiseuille's law holds at all pressures
Poiseuille's law predicts doubling, and the high-pressure data didn't double.
Flow became turbulent at high ΔP
Correct: turbulent flow goes roughly as √ΔP, and √2 ≈ 1.4, a 40% rise.
questions.x: Poiseuille's law describes smooth, layered (laminar) flow, where flow Q is proportional to the pressure difference ΔP: double ΔP, double Q. That matches the low-pressure data. At high pressure, flow rose only about 40%. That's the sign of turbulent flow, where swirling eddies waste energy and Q goes roughly as √ΔP. Doubling ΔP then multiplies Q by √2 ≈ 1.41, a rise of about 40%. A rigid tube can't widen, and lower viscosity would make the flow rise more, not less.

questions.q: A positively charged rod is held near a neutral metal sphere. The sphere is briefly grounded, the ground is removed, and then the rod is taken away. What is the sphere's final charge?
o: Negative
Correct: the rod pulls electrons up from the ground, and cutting the ground traps them on the sphere.
Positive
Induction leaves the opposite sign of the rod. Positive would need a negative rod.
Neutral
Grounding while the rod is near lets extra electrons flow on, so it's no longer neutral.
Positive near the rod, net neutral
That's polarization with no grounding. Here grounding added real extra charge.
questions.note: Charging by induction leaves the opposite sign of the inducing charge.
questions.x: This is charging by induction, which means charging something without touching it. The positive rod pulls the sphere's free electrons toward it. Grounding means connecting the sphere to the earth, which is a giant supply of electrons, so while the rod is close, extra electrons flow up from the ground onto the sphere. Then the ground wire is removed first, so those extra electrons have no way back. Taking the rod away last just lets them spread out over the sphere. The sphere ends up with more electrons than protons, so it's negative: the opposite sign of the rod.

questions.q: A charge +q sits at x = 0 and a charge +4q sits at x = 3 m. At what position would a small test charge feel zero net electrostatic force?
o: The midpoint only works when the two charges are equal.
x = 2 m
This is closer to +4q, where its push wins. The zero point must be closer to the smaller charge.
x = 1 m
Correct: q/x² = 4q/(3 − x)² gives 3 − x = 2x, so x = 1 m.
x = −1 m, left of +q
Left of +q, both charges push the test charge left, so the forces add and can't cancel.
questions.x: Both charges are positive, so they both push a test charge away. Between them the pushes point opposite ways and can cancel. Let x be the distance from +q, so the distance to +4q is 3 − x. The forces are equal when kq/x² = k(4q)/(3 − x)². Cancel k and q: 1/x² = 4/(3 − x)². Take the square root of both sides: 1/x = 2/(3 − x). Cross-multiply: 3 − x = 2x, so 3 = 3x and x = 1 m. That makes sense: the zero point sits closer to the weaker charge.

questions.q: The ratio of electric force to gravitational force between two protons is about 10³⁶. How does this ratio change if the protons are moved twice as far apart?
o: It decreases by a factor of 4
Each force does drop by 4, but they drop together, so the ratio doesn't change.
It increases by a factor of 4
Neither force gets stronger with distance, and neither fades more slowly than the other.
It decreases by a factor of 2
Neither force goes as 1/r, and since both fall the same way the ratio holds anyway.
It stays the same
Correct: both forces go as 1/r², so r cancels out of the ratio.
questions.x: Both forces follow the same distance rule. The electric force is F = kq²/r² and gravity is F = Gm²/r², where r is the distance between the protons. Each one has r² on the bottom. Double r and r² becomes 4 times bigger, so each force drops to one quarter. When you divide one force by the other, the r² on top and bottom cancels, leaving kq²/(Gm²). That has no r in it at all, so the ratio stays about 10³⁶ no matter how far apart the protons are.

questions.q: Charges +q and −q are a distance d apart. What is the electric field at the midpoint?
o: Zero
Zero is the potential at the midpoint. The two fields point the same way, so they add.
4kq/d², pointing toward +q
That's only one charge's field, and it points the wrong way. Both fields point toward −q.
8kq/d², pointing toward −q
Correct: each is kq/(d/2)² = 4kq/d², and both point toward −q, so 8kq/d².
2kq/d², pointing toward −q
This uses d instead of d/2 for the distance to each charge.
questions.note: Trap: V = 0 at a dipole's midpoint, but E is not.
questions.x: Fields point away from positive charges and toward negative ones. At the midpoint, the field from +q points away from +q, toward −q. The field from −q points toward −q too. Both point the same way, so they add. Use E = kq/r² for each, with r = d/2. Squaring d/2 gives d²/4, and 1 ÷ (d²/4) = 4/d², so each field is 4kq/d². Add them: 4kq/d² + 4kq/d² = 8kq/d², pointing toward −q. It isn't zero: the potential cancels here, but the field doesn't.

questions.q: A proton and an electron are released from rest in the same uniform electric field. Which statement is true?
o: The proton feels a larger force because it is heavier
F = qE depends on charge, not mass, and the two charges are the same size.
The forces have equal magnitude, but the electron accelerates far more
Correct: the charges are equal in size, so the forces are too, and a = F/m is much bigger for the light electron.
Both have the same acceleration in opposite directions
Equal forces on very different masses give very different accelerations.
The electron feels a larger force because it is smaller
Size doesn't appear in F = qE, and the two charges are the same size.
questions.x: The force from a field is F = qE, where q is the charge and E is the field strength. A proton and an electron have charges of the same size, e, just opposite signs. So in the same field they feel forces of the same size, pointing in opposite directions. How fast each speeds up comes from a = F/m, where m is the mass. The electron's mass is about 1/1800 of the proton's, so the same force gives it about 1800 times more acceleration.

questions.q: A hollow metal box is placed in a strong external electric field. Once charges settle, what is the field inside the box's empty interior?
o: Equal to the external field
A metal box blocks the field instead of letting it pass straight through.
Twice the external field
The moved charges cancel the outside field. They don't add to it.
Equal and opposite to the external field
The moved charges' field is opposite, but adding it to the outside field gives zero, not a reversal.
Zero
Correct: surface charges rearrange until they cancel the field inside the conductor.
questions.note: This is the Faraday cage effect.
questions.x: A conductor, like metal, has electrons that can move freely. Put a hollow metal box in an outside field and those electrons slide around the surface until the field they make exactly cancels the outside field inside the metal. Once things settle, the field inside an empty hollow conductor is zero. That's how a Faraday cage works: it shields whatever is inside. The field isn't reversed or doubled. The outside field and the field from the moved charges add up to exactly nothing.

questions.q: An oil drop of mass 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ kg hangs motionless in an upward electric field of 1 × 10⁵ N/C. What is its charge? (g = 10 m/s²)
o: −1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (one extra electron)
A negative charge is pushed opposite the field, so it would be pushed down, not held up.
+3.2 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (two electrons missing)
Twice too big. The weight, 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N, only needs 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C to balance it.
+1.6 × 10⁻²⁰ C (one-tenth of e)
Exponent slip: −14 − 5 = −19, not −20.
+1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C (one electron missing)
Correct: q = mg ÷ E = (1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴) ÷ 10⁵ = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, and it must be positive.
questions.x: The drop isn't moving, so the forces on it must cancel: the electric push up equals the weight pulling down, qE = mg. Weight first: mg = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ × 10. Multiplying powers of 10 means adding the exponents (−15 + 1 = −14), so mg = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ N. Now divide by E: q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁴ ÷ 10⁵. Dividing powers of 10 means subtracting the exponents (−14 − 5 = −19), so q = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The push has to point up, the same way as the field, and only a positive charge gets pushed along the field. So the drop is +1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C: it's missing one electron.

questions.q: In a mass spectrometer, two ions with equal charge and equal speed enter the same magnetic field. Ion 2 has twice the mass of ion 1. Compared with ion 1, ion 2's path radius is:
o: Twice as large
Correct: r = mv/(qB), so with q, v and B fixed, doubling m doubles r.
Half as large
Heavier ions are harder to turn, so they curve less and make a wider circle.
Four times as large
r goes with m, not m², so doubling m doubles r instead of making it 4 times bigger.
The same
Mass is right there in r = mv/(qB), so it does change the radius.
questions.x: A magnetic field pushes a moving charge sideways, so the ion curves in a circle. The magnetic force, qvB, is what holds it on that circle, so it equals the centripetal force, mv²/r (the inward force any circle needs). Set them equal, qvB = mv²/r, and solve for the radius: r = mv/(qB). Here q, v and B are the same for both ions, so r goes up in step with m. Ion 2 has twice the mass, so its circle is twice as wide.

questions.q: Which 0.1 M aqueous solution conducts electricity best?
o: NaCl
NaCl splits fully, but into only 2 ions, fewer than CaCl₂'s 3.
Acetic acid
Acetic acid is a weak acid, so only a small fraction of it forms ions.
CaCl₂
Correct: it splits into 3 ions, Ca²⁺ and 2 Cl⁻, the most charge carriers here.
Glucose
Glucose dissolves as whole molecules and makes no ions.
questions.note: Solution conductivity tracks the concentration of mobile ions.
questions.x: Water conducts electricity only when it has ions (charged particles) floating around to carry the charge. A substance that makes ions in water is called an electrolyte. All four solutions are 0.1 M, so the winner is the one that makes the most ions. CaCl₂ splits completely into 3 ions, one Ca²⁺ and two Cl⁻, and Ca²⁺ carries a double charge. NaCl splits into only 2 ions. Acetic acid is a weak acid, so only a small fraction of it splits apart. Glucose doesn't make any ions at all.

questions.q: Wires A and B are made of the same metal and carry the same current, but B has half the cross-sectional area of A. How does the electron drift speed in B compare with A?
o: Half as fast
This flips it. A narrower wire needs faster electrons to carry the same current.
Twice as fast
Correct: I = nqAv, so with I, n and q fixed, halving A doubles v.
Four times as fast
v goes as 1/A, not 1/A², so halving A doubles v instead of making it 4 times bigger.
The same
At the same speed, a thinner wire would carry less current. Speed must rise.
questions.x: Current is linked to how fast electrons drift by I = nqAv. I is the current, n is how many free electrons are packed into each bit of metal, q is each electron's charge, A is the wire's cross-sectional area, and v is the drift speed. Same metal means the same n and q, and the current is the same too. Solve for speed: v = I/(nqA). So v goes up when A goes down. Wire B has half the area, and dividing by ½ is the same as multiplying by 2, so the electrons drift twice as fast.

questions.q: A 24 V battery is connected to a 4 Ω resistor in series with a parallel pair of 6 Ω and 12 Ω resistors. What is the current through the 12 Ω resistor?
o: 3 A
That's the total current. It splits between the two branches.
2 A
That's the current in the 6 Ω branch: 12 V ÷ 6 Ω = 2 A.
This splits 3 A evenly. Parallel branches share voltage, not current.
1 A
Correct: pair = 4 Ω, total 8 Ω, so 3 A flows; the pair gets 12 V, and 12 ÷ 12 = 1 A.
questions.x: First combine the parallel pair: R = (R₁ × R₂)/(R₁ + R₂) = (6 × 12)/(6 + 12) = 72/18 = 4 Ω. Add the 4 Ω series resistor: 4 + 4 = 8 Ω total. Ohm's law gives the total current: I = V/R = 24/8 = 3 A. That 3 A goes through the series resistor, which uses up V = IR = 3 × 4 = 12 V. That leaves 24 − 12 = 12 V across the parallel pair. Branches in parallel share the same voltage, so the 12 Ω branch carries I = 12/12 = 1 A.

questions.q: A battery with an emf of 9 V and an internal resistance of 1 Ω is connected to a 2 Ω external resistor. What is the terminal voltage?
o: 9 V
Terminal voltage equals the emf only when no current is flowing.
6 V
3 V
That's the voltage lost inside the battery, Ir = 3 × 1 = 3 V.
This uses I = 9/2 and leaves the internal resistance out of the current.
questions.note: V_terminal = emf − Ir.
questions.x: A real battery has a little resistance inside it, called internal resistance, r. The emf is the voltage the battery creates; the terminal voltage is what's left at its ends. The internal and outside resistors are in series, so first find the current: I = emf/(R + r) = 9/(2 + 1) = 9/3 = 3 A. Some voltage is used up inside the battery: Ir = 3 × 1 = 3 V. So the terminal voltage is V = emf − Ir = 9 − 3 = 6 V. Check: across the 2 Ω resistor, IR = 3 × 2 = 6 V.

questions.q: A 2 Ω resistor and an 8 Ω resistor are wired in parallel across a battery. How does the power dissipated by the 2 Ω resistor compare with the 8 Ω resistor?
o: One-fourth as much
That's the series answer, where the current is shared and P = I²R.
The same
Same voltage doesn't mean same power when the resistances differ.
Twice as much
The resistances differ by a factor of 4, so the powers do too, not 2.
4 times as much
Correct: same V in parallel, and P = V²/R is 4 times bigger for the 2 Ω resistor.
questions.note: Parallel: smaller R gets more power. Series: larger R gets more power.
questions.x: Resistors in parallel all have the same voltage across them. When the voltage is the same, the handy power formula is P = V²/R, where P is power (how fast electrical energy turns into heat), V is voltage and R is resistance. R is on the bottom, so smaller resistance means more power. Compare: P(2 Ω) ÷ P(8 Ω) = (V²/2) ÷ (V²/8). The V² cancels, leaving 8/2 = 4. The 2 Ω resistor uses 4 times as much power.

questions.q: A power line delivers the same power to a town, but the transmission voltage is doubled. How does the power lost as heat in the line change?
o: It halves
The loss goes with I², not I, so halving the current cuts the loss to a quarter.
It quadruples
This puts the full line voltage into V²/R. That isn't the voltage across the wire.
It falls to one-fourth
Correct: at fixed P = IV the current halves, and the loss I²R falls to (½)² = ¼.
It does not change
The current drops, and lower current means less heat in the wire.
questions.note: High-voltage transmission cuts current and I²R losses.
questions.x: The town needs the same power, P = IV, where I is the current and V is the voltage. If V doubles and P stays the same, the current has to halve: I(new) = P/(2V) = I/2. The wires have a small resistance R, and the heat they waste is P(loss) = I²R. The current is squared, so halving it gives (½)² = ¼. The heat lost falls to one quarter. Don't plug the full line voltage into V²/R: that voltage isn't the voltage across the wire itself.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor stays connected to a battery while its plates are pulled to twice their separation. What happens to the stored charge?
o: It halves
Correct: the battery holds V fixed, C halves, so Q = CV halves.
It stays the same
Charge stays fixed only when the capacitor is cut off from the battery.
It doubles
A bigger gap lowers C, so at the same V the charge goes down, not up.
It quarters
C goes as 1/d, so doubling d halves Q. It doesn't cut it to a quarter.
questions.note: Connected to a battery: V constant. Isolated: Q constant.
questions.x: A capacitor stores charge on two plates. Its capacitance, C, is how much charge it holds per volt, and Q = CV. For flat plates, C = ε₀A/d, where A is plate area, d is the gap and ε₀ is a constant. Because the battery stays connected, it keeps V the same. Doubling d puts 2d on the bottom, so C becomes C/2. Then Q(new) = (C/2) × V = Q/2. The charge halves, and the extra charge flows back into the battery.

questions.q: A charged parallel-plate capacitor is disconnected from its battery, and then its plate separation is doubled. What happens to the stored energy?
o: It halves
Halving happens when V is held fixed, but here the battery is gone, so Q is fixed.
It stays the same
You do work pulling apart plates that attract, so the stored energy goes up.
It doubles
Correct: Q is fixed and C halves, so U = Q²/(2C) doubles.
It quadruples
U goes as 1/C, and C only halves, so U doubles, not quadruples.
questions.x: With the battery disconnected, the charge Q on the plates is trapped, so Q stays fixed. Use the energy formula that has Q in it: U = Q²/(2C), where U is stored energy and C is capacitance. For flat plates C = ε₀A/d, so doubling the gap d halves C. Plug in C/2: U(new) = Q²/(2 × C/2) = Q²/C. That's 2 × Q²/(2C) = 2U, so the energy doubles. Where does the extra come from? The plates attract each other, so you do work pulling them apart.

questions.q: A dielectric of constant κ is slid between the plates of a charged capacitor that has been disconnected from its battery. What happens to the stored energy?
o: It increases by a factor of κ
Rising by κ happens with the battery connected, when V is fixed.
It stays the same
C goes up by κ while Q stays fixed, so U must change.
It increases by a factor of κ squared
U goes as 1/C, and C changes by κ, not κ².
It decreases by a factor of κ
Correct: Q is fixed and C rises by κ, so U = Q²/(2C) falls by κ.
questions.x: A dielectric is an insulating material slid between the plates. It multiplies the capacitance by its dielectric constant κ (kappa), which is bigger than 1, so C becomes κC. The capacitor is disconnected, so its charge Q is trapped and stays fixed. Use the energy formula with Q in it: U = Q²/(2C). Plug in κC: U(new) = Q²/(2κC) = U/κ. The stored energy goes down by a factor of κ. The missing energy went into pulling the dielectric into the gap.

questions.q: How does inserting a dielectric between a capacitor's plates allow it to store more charge at a given voltage?
o: It conducts charge between the plates
A dielectric is an insulator. If it conducted, it would short out the capacitor.
Its molecules polarize, creating a field that partly cancels the plates' field
Correct: the lined-up molecules weaken the field, so V is lower for the same Q, and C = Q/V rises.
It adds free electrons to the negative plate
A dielectric doesn't add any free charge to the plates.
It increases the area of the plates
The plate area stays the same. The dielectric works by polarizing.
questions.x: A dielectric is an insulator, so charge can't flow through it. Instead, its molecules polarize: each one stretches or turns so its slightly positive end faces the negative plate and its slightly negative end faces the positive plate. All those lined-up molecules make a small field pointing against the plates' field. That shrinks the total field in the gap, so the same charge now gives a smaller voltage. Since capacitance is C = Q/V, a smaller V for the same Q means a bigger C, by a factor of κ.

questions.q: What is the sign of the anode in an electrolytic cell?
o: Negative
The anode is negative in a galvanic cell. In an electrolytic cell the signs flip.
Neutral
The power source gives each electrode a definite charge, so neither is neutral.
Positive
Correct: the power source pulls electrons out of the anode, leaving it positive.
Positive or negative, depending on the metal
The sign doesn't depend on the metal. In an electrolytic cell the anode is always positive.
questions.note: Anode sign: galvanic −, electrolytic +.
questions.x: An electrolytic cell uses an outside power source, like a battery or charger, to force a reaction that wouldn't happen on its own. The anode is still where oxidation (losing electrons) happens, and the cathode is still where reduction (gaining electrons) happens. But the power source is doing the work: it pulls electrons out of the anode and pushes them into the cathode. Losing electrons leaves the anode positive, and the cathode becomes negative. That's the reverse of a galvanic cell, where the anode is negative.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell's salt bridge, which way do anions migrate?
o: Toward the cathode compartment
That's where cations go. Anions head the other way.
Toward the anode compartment
Correct: anions balance the positive ions piling up as the anode metal is oxidized.
