They do not move; only cations migrate
Both kinds of ions in the bridge move to keep each side neutral.
Into the external wire
Ions can't travel through a metal wire. Only electrons move there.
questions.x: A salt bridge is a tube of salt solution that connects the two halves of a galvanic cell. Its job is to keep each side electrically neutral. As the cell runs, the anode metal is oxidized into positive ions, so the anode side keeps gaining positive charge. Anions (negative ions) from the bridge move toward the anode side to balance it. Meanwhile, positive ions are used up at the cathode, so cations (positive ions) from the bridge move toward the cathode side. Ions never travel through the wire; only electrons do.

questions.q: A concentrated aqueous NaCl solution is electrolyzed. What forms at the cathode?
o: Hydrogen gas
Correct: water is much easier to reduce than Na⁺, so H₂ gas forms.
Sodium metal
Na⁺ is very hard to reduce, so water gets reduced first. Na metal needs molten NaCl.
Chlorine gas
Chlorine forms by oxidation, which happens at the anode.
Oxygen gas
Oxygen would come from oxidizing water, which happens at the anode.
questions.note: In water, highly active metal ions are not reduced; water is.
questions.x: Electrolysis means using electricity to force a reaction. At the cathode, reduction (gaining electrons) happens, and whatever is easiest to reduce gets reduced first. Na⁺ is very hard to reduce: its reduction potential is −2.71 V, a big negative number. Water is much easier, so water is reduced instead: 2H₂O + 2e⁻ → H₂ + 2OH⁻. Hydrogen gas bubbles off at the cathode. Sodium metal only forms if you electrolyze molten NaCl, where there's no water to compete.

questions.q: In a galvanic cell's salt bridge containing KNO₃, which way do K⁺ ions move?
o: Toward the cathode compartment
Correct: K⁺ replaces the positive ions used up as they're reduced at the cathode.
Toward the anode compartment
That's the way NO₃⁻ goes. Cations like K⁺ go the other way.
Through the wire to the anode
Ions can't travel through a metal wire. Only electrons do.
They stay put while only NO₃⁻ moves
Both ions move. K⁺ and NO₃⁻ each keep one side neutral.
questions.x: In a galvanic cell, positive ions at the cathode, like Cu²⁺, grab electrons and come out of the solution as metal. That leaves the cathode side short of positive charge. K⁺ ions from the salt bridge move into the cathode side to make up for it. At the same time, NO₃⁻ ions move toward the anode side, where new positive ions are being made. Both kinds of ions move, and they move only through the solution and bridge, never through the wire.

questions.q: Al³⁺/Al has E°red = −1.66 V and Ni²⁺/Ni has E°red = −0.25 V. What is E°cell for a galvanic cell made from them?
o: This adds 1.66 and 0.25. Cell voltage is a difference, not a sum.
This divides by 3 for aluminum's electrons. E° doesn't change with electron count.
This doubles the value for balancing. E° is never multiplied by coefficients.
questions.x: E°red, the standard reduction potential, tells you how badly something wants to gain electrons. The one with the higher E°red gets reduced at the cathode. −0.25 V is higher than −1.66 V, so Ni²⁺/Ni is the cathode and aluminum is oxidized at the anode. Formula: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. Plug in: E°cell = −0.25 − (−1.66). Subtracting a negative is adding: −0.25 + 1.66 = 1.41. So E°cell = +1.41 V. Don't multiply by the electron counts: E° stays the same no matter how much reaction you run.

questions.q: A student pairs an unknown metal M with a standard hydrogen electrode. M acts as the anode, and the cell reads +0.44 V. What is E°red for M²⁺/M?
o: +0.44 V (above hydrogen)
If M were easier to reduce than H⁺, M would be the cathode, not the anode.
This divides by 2 for the electrons. E° doesn't change with electron count.
−0.44 V (below hydrogen)
This doubles for 2 electrons. E° is never multiplied by the electron count.
questions.x: The standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is the reference electrode, set at exactly 0 V. M is the anode, so the SHE must be the cathode. Formula: E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode. Values: E°cell = +0.44 V, E°cathode = 0 V, E°anode = E°(M). Plug in: 0.44 = 0 − E°(M). So E°(M) = −0.44 V. That fits: a metal that gets oxidized when paired with hydrogen must sit below hydrogen on the reduction table, so its E°red has to be negative.

questions.q: Two hydrogen electrodes (1 atm H₂) are in solutions at pH 1 and pH 4. What is the voltage of this concentration cell at 25 °C? (Use 0.06/n per decade.)
o: About 0.09 V
This uses n = 2 but forgets that [H⁺] is squared in Q, which cuts the answer in half.
About 0.18 V
Correct: [H⁺] differs by 10³, and 0.06 V × 3 = 0.18 V.
About 0.30 V
This adds the pH values (1 + 4 = 5). You need their difference, 4 − 1 = 3.
0 V
0 V is E° for a concentration cell. Different [H⁺] on each side still makes a voltage.
questions.x: Both electrodes are the same, so the only thing making voltage is the difference in [H⁺]. pH 1 means [H⁺] = 10⁻¹ M and pH 4 means [H⁺] = 10⁻⁴ M. Dividing them, 10⁻¹ ÷ 10⁻⁴, means subtracting exponents: −1 − (−4) = 3, so one side has 10³ (1000 times) more H⁺. For a hydrogen cell, each 10-fold step in [H⁺] is worth 0.06 V, because the 2 electrons and the squared [H⁺] cancel out in the Nernst equation. Three 10-fold steps give 0.06 × 3 = 0.18 V.

questions.q: Two identical 1.5 V cells are connected in parallel to a load. Compared with one cell, what does this arrangement provide?
o: 3.0 V with the same run time
Adding the voltages to 3.0 V is what series does, not parallel.
0.75 V with a longer run time
Identical cells in parallel don't split the voltage. Each still gives 1.5 V.
The same 1.5 V but a longer run time
Correct: the voltage stays 1.5 V, the current is shared, so the pair lasts longer.
3.0 V with a longer run time
Parallel doesn't add voltage. Only series does.
questions.x: Cells in parallel are hooked up side by side: both positive ends are joined and both negative ends are joined. So the load sees the same 1.5 V as from one cell; parallel doesn't add voltage. What changes is the current. The load's current is split between the two cells, so each one only supplies half as much. That means each drains half as fast, and the pair lasts about twice as long. If you wanted 3.0 V, you'd connect them in series, end to end, which adds the voltages but not the run time.

questions.q: How does a hydrogen–oxygen fuel cell differ from an ordinary battery?
o: It oxidizes O₂ at the anode
O₂ is reduced at the cathode. H₂ is the one oxidized at the anode.
It needs an external power source to run
A fuel cell is galvanic: its reaction runs on its own and makes electricity.
Its reactants are supplied continuously from outside
Correct: H₂ and O₂ are fed in from outside, so it runs as long as fuel flows.
Its electrons flow from cathode to anode
Electrons go anode to cathode in every galvanic cell, so this isn't a difference.
questions.x: A fuel cell is a type of galvanic cell, meaning a spontaneous reaction inside it makes electricity, just like a battery. H₂ is oxidized (loses electrons) at the anode, O₂ is reduced (gains electrons) at the cathode, and the product is water. Electrons flow through the wire from anode to cathode, the same as in any battery. The real difference is the fuel supply. A normal battery has a fixed amount of chemicals sealed inside and dies when they're used up. A fuel cell has H₂ and O₂ piped in from outside, so it keeps running as long as fuel flows.

questions.q: A species contains 26 protons, 30 neutrons and 23 electrons. Which symbol represents it?
o: ⁵⁶Fe³⁻
Fewer electrons than protons makes it positive, not negative.
⁵⁶Mn³⁺
26 protons makes it iron. Manganese has 25.
⁴⁹Fe³⁺
Mass number is protons plus neutrons (56), not protons plus electrons (49).
⁵⁶Fe³⁺
Correct: 26 protons is Fe, 26 + 30 = 56, and 26 − 23 = +3.
questions.x: Read the three numbers one at a time. Protons decide which element it is: 26 protons is iron, Fe. The mass number, written top left, is protons plus neutrons: A = 26 + 30 = 56. The charge, written top right, is protons minus electrons: 26 − 23 = +3. It has fewer electrons than protons, so it's positive, a cation. Put it together: ⁵⁶Fe³⁺. Losing or gaining electrons never changes the element, so it can't be manganese.

questions.q: Boron has an average atomic mass of 10.8 u and consists of ¹⁰B and ¹¹B. What is the approximate percent abundance of ¹¹B?
o: That's the abundance of ¹⁰B, the lighter isotope, not ¹¹B.
A 50:50 mix would average 10.5 u, not 10.8 u.
Correct: 11x + 10(1 − x) = 10.8 gives x = 0.8, so ¹¹B is 80%.
Too high: 92% ¹¹B would average about 10.92 u.
questions.x: The average atomic mass is a weighted average: each isotope's mass times how common it is, added up. Let x be the fraction of ¹¹B, so ¹⁰B is 1 − x. Formula: average = 11x + 10(1 − x). Values: average = 10.8. Plug in: 10.8 = 11x + 10 − 10x = 10 + x. Subtract 10 from both sides: x = 0.8. As a percent, 0.8 × 100 = 80%. Quick check: 10.8 sits 80% of the way from 10 to 11, so the heavier isotope makes up most of it.

questions.q: In Rutherford's gold foil experiment, most α particles passed straight through while a few bounced back. What did this show?
o: Electrons occupy quantized orbits
Fixed electron orbits came from Bohr's work on hydrogen's light spectrum, not this experiment.
Positive charge is spread evenly throughout the whole atom
That's the plum pudding model, which predicted no big bounces back.
The nucleus contains neutral neutrons
Neutrons were discovered later, by Chadwick.
Mass and positive charge sit in a tiny dense nucleus
Correct: mostly empty space explains the pass-throughs, and a tiny dense core explains the rare bounces.
questions.x: Rutherford fired α (α) particles, which are small and positive, at a very thin sheet of gold. Most went straight through, which means the atom is mostly empty space. A few bounced sharply back. Something tiny, heavy and positive must have pushed them away. That's the nucleus: almost all the atom's mass and all its positive charge packed into a very small center. The older 'plum pudding' model, with positive charge spread evenly, couldn't explain those bounces, because a spread-out charge would only nudge the particles slightly.

questions.q: Bromine is about 50% ⁷⁹Br and 50% ⁸¹Br. In a mass spectrum of Br₂, what intensity ratio is expected for peaks at m/z 158, 160 and 162?
o: This forgets the mixed pair can form two ways: 79 then 81, or 81 then 79.
Correct: the chances are ¼, ½ and ¼, which is 1 : 2 : 1.
This overcounts the mixed pair. With two atoms there are only 2 mixed orders.
This flips the pattern. The mixed pair is the most likely, not the least.
questions.x: Each Br atom is a 50:50 pick between ⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br, like a coin flip. Br₂ has two atoms, so there are four equally likely combinations: 79+79 = 158, 79+81 = 160, 81+79 = 160, and 81+81 = 162. Each has a chance of ½ × ½ = ¼. Mass 158 happens one way (¼), mass 160 happens two ways (¼ + ¼ = ½) and mass 162 happens one way (¼). Multiply each by 4 to get whole numbers: 1 : 2 : 1. The middle peak is twice as tall.

questions.q: A nuclide lies above the band of stability, with too many neutrons for its number of protons. Which decay mode is most likely?
o: Positron emission
Positron emission turns a proton into a neutron, making the neutron excess worse.
Electron capture
Electron capture also turns a proton into a neutron, the wrong direction here.
β-minus emission
Correct: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino lowers the neutron-to-proton ratio.
Gamma emission
Gamma emission only releases energy. It doesn't change the numbers of neutrons or protons.
questions.x: Stable nuclei have a certain balance of neutrons (N) to protons (Z), and on a chart they form a strip called the band of stability. Above the band means too many neutrons for the protons. To fix that, the nucleus needs to turn a neutron into a proton. That's exactly what β-minus decay does: n → p + e⁻ + antineutrino. The electron shoots out as the β particle, and the nucleus ends up with one fewer neutron and one more proton. Positron emission and electron capture do the opposite, and γ emission changes neither number.

questions.q: A beam of radiation passes between charged plates. One part bends slightly toward the negative plate, one bends sharply toward the positive plate, and one is undeflected. What is the sharply bent part?
o: Alpha particles
Alphas are positive and heavy, so they bend slightly toward the negative plate.
β-minus particles
Correct: β-minus particles are light, negative electrons, so they bend sharply toward the positive plate.
Gamma rays
Gamma rays have no charge, so they're the part that goes straight.
Neutrons
Neutrons have no charge and wouldn't bend at all.
questions.x: Charged particles bend toward the plate with the opposite charge, and lighter particles bend more for the same push. The part bending sharply toward the positive plate must be negative and light. That's β-minus radiation, which is just fast electrons. An electron is thousands of times lighter than an α particle, so it gets bent much more. Alpha particles are positive and heavy, so they're the part bending slightly toward the negative plate. Gamma rays have no charge, so they're the part going straight through.

questions.q: Electrons emitted in β-minus decay of a given nuclide have a continuous range of energies rather than one value. What explains this?
o: The nucleus recoils by a random amount
The heavy nucleus recoils only a little, and in a two-body split that recoil is fixed.
Electrons lose varying energy leaving the electron cloud
The spread is there the moment the electron is made. It isn't lost on the way out.
Each nucleus has a different decay energy
Every nucleus of the same type releases the same total energy.
An antineutrino shares the decay energy
Correct: the energy is shared among three particles, so the electron's share varies.
questions.note: This puzzle led Pauli to propose the neutrino.
questions.x: Every nucleus of the same type releases exactly the same total energy when it decays. If β-minus decay made only two things, the electron and the new nucleus, that fixed energy would have to split the same way every time, and every electron would come out with the same energy. Instead, the electrons show a whole range. That means a third particle is sharing the energy: the antineutrino, a tiny, uncharged particle that's very hard to detect. Sometimes the electron gets most of the energy, sometimes the antineutrino does.

questions.q: After a nucleus decays by electron capture, which emission commonly follows from the atom?
o: X-rays
Correct: an outer electron drops into the empty inner spot and gives off an X-ray.
Alpha particles
Electron capture doesn't throw out any protons or neutrons.
A positron
Positron emission is a different way to turn a proton into a neutron, not a follow-up.
A β-minus particle
Electron capture lowers Z by 1, and β-minus would raise it right back.
questions.x: In electron capture, the nucleus pulls in one of the atom's own innermost electrons. That electron joins a proton to make a neutron, so the atomic number drops by 1. But now there's an empty spot in the lowest electron shell. An electron from a higher shell drops down to fill it, and it gives off the energy difference as a photon. Gaps between inner shells are big, so that photon is an X-ray. So the X-ray comes from the electron cloud, not the nucleus.

questions.q: In PET imaging, a positron meets an electron and both are annihilated. What is produced?
o: One photon of 511 keV
One photon always has momentum, but the pair started with almost none.
Two 511 keV photons traveling in opposite directions
Correct: each photon carries one particle's rest energy, 511 keV, and they fly apart back to back.
A neutron and a neutrino
Annihilation turns mass into light, not into new particles like neutrons.
Two 1.02 MeV photons in the same direction
This doubles each photon's energy, and photons going the same way break momentum conservation.
questions.x: A positron is the antimatter twin of an electron: same mass, opposite charge. When they meet, both disappear and all their mass becomes light. Each one's mass is worth E = mc² = 511 keV of energy, so the total is 511 + 511 = 1022 keV. They meet almost at rest, so the total momentum is about zero. A single photon always carries momentum, so it can't do the job. Instead, two photons fly off in exactly opposite directions, each with 511 keV. PET scanners detect those back-to-back pairs to find where the tracer is.

questions.q: A radioactive sample is heated from 25 °C to 500 °C. How does its half-life change?
o: It decreases because decay speeds up when hot
This treats decay like a chemical reaction. Heat speeds reactions, not nuclear decay.
It increases because nuclei become more stable
Heat is far too weak to make a nucleus more or less stable.
It doubles for every 10 °C rise
That rough rule is for some chemical reactions, not nuclear decay.
It does not change
Correct: nuclear decay rates don't depend on temperature or pressure.
questions.x: Radioactive decay happens inside the nucleus, and the energies involved there are measured in millions of electron volts (MeV). Heating something to 500 °C gives each particle less than 0.1 eV of extra energy, which is millions of times too small to make any difference to a nucleus. So the half-life, the time it takes for half of the sample to decay, stays exactly the same. Heat speeds up chemical reactions, which involve electrons and bonds, but not nuclear decay.

questions.q: A rock contains a parent isotope (t½ = 500 million years) and its stable daughter in a daughter-to-parent ratio of 7:1. If all daughter came from the parent, how old is the rock?
o: 500 million years
One half-life leaves a 1 : 1 ratio, not 7 : 1.
1.0 billion years
Two half-lives leaves a 3 : 1 ratio.
3.5 billion years
This multiplies 7 by 500 million. The ratio isn't the number of half-lives.
1.5 billion years
Correct: the parent is 1/8 of the original, which is 3 half-lives: 3 × 500 million = 1.5 billion years.
questions.note: Convert D:P to the fraction of parent remaining: P/(P + D).
questions.x: Every daughter atom used to be a parent atom. So the rock started with parent + daughter = 1 + 7 = 8 parts of parent, and 1 part is left. Fraction left = 1/8. Each half-life cuts the parent in half: 1 → ½ → ¼ → ⅛. That's 3 halvings, so (½)³ = ⅛, and 3 half-lives have passed. Formula: age = number of half-lives × half-life. Plug in: age = 3 × 500 million years = 1500 million years = 1.5 billion years.

questions.q: A hospital needs a tracer for diagnostic imaging that is detected outside the body. Which isotope property is most suitable?
o: An alpha emitter with a half-life of about 10 years
Alphas can't get out of the body, and 10 years would keep exposing the patient.
Beta emitter with a half-life of 2 seconds
Betas mostly get absorbed in tissue, and 2 seconds is too short to use.
Gamma emitter with a half-life of several hours
Correct: γ rays get out of the body, and hours is long enough to scan but fades quickly.
Stable isotope with no emission
A stable isotope gives off nothing, so there's no signal to detect.
questions.x: For imaging, the radiation has to get out of the body to reach a detector outside. Alpha and β particles are stopped by skin and tissue within a short distance, so they can't do that. Gamma rays are high-energy light that passes right through the body, so the tracer should be a γ emitter. The half-life matters too. It has to be long enough to make the tracer, inject it and take the scan, which takes hours. But it should be short enough that the radiation fades soon after.

questions.q: Why does excited hydrogen gas produce a line spectrum instead of a continuous rainbow?
o: Electron energy levels are quantized
Correct: only certain level gaps exist, so only certain photon energies come out.
Hydrogen absorbs all visible light
Absorbing every color would make it look dark, not give bright lines.
The nucleus emits light at fixed frequencies
Visible lines come from electrons changing levels, not from the nucleus.
Photons of other colors are too fast to detect
All photons travel at the same speed, the speed of light.
questions.x: Electrons in an atom can only have certain set energies, called energy levels. Scientists call this 'quantized'. When an excited electron drops from a higher level to a lower one, it gives off a photon (a particle of light) with energy equal to the gap between the two levels. Only certain gaps exist, so only certain photon energies, and so only certain colors, come out. Each one shows up as a bright line. A rainbow-like continuous spectrum comes from hot, dense things like a glowing solid, not a thin gas.

questions.q: White light passes through cool sodium vapor and then a prism. What does the spectrum look like?
o: Bright lines on a dark background
That's an emission spectrum, from looking straight at hot, glowing gas.
A continuous spectrum with no features
Sodium absorbs certain colors, so the rainbow has gaps in it.
A continuous spectrum with dark lines at sodium's emission wavelengths
Correct: the gas absorbs exactly the photon energies that match its level gaps.
Dark lines at wavelengths different from sodium's emission lines
Absorbing and emitting use the same level gaps, so the lines are at the same spots.
questions.x: White light contains every color. Sodium atoms can only absorb photons (bits of light) whose energy exactly matches a gap between their electron energy levels. So as the white light passes through the cool sodium gas, those few colors get soaked up and everything else passes through. Spread out by the prism, you see a full rainbow with thin dark lines where the missing colors should be. This is an absorption spectrum. The dark lines sit at exactly the same spots as the bright lines hot sodium gives off, because both use the same level gaps.

questions.q: Sodium salts give a yellow color in a flame. What produces the light?
o: Sodium nuclei undergoing γ decay
Sodium-23 is stable, and γ rays aren't visible light.
Combustion of the anion
Many different sodium salts all give yellow, so the color comes from sodium.
Excited electrons emitting photons as they drop to lower levels
Correct: heat lifts the outer electron, and it gives off yellow light (about 589 nm) as it drops back.
Electrons being removed to form Na⁺
Pulling off an electron takes in energy. It doesn't give off a set color.
questions.x: The heat of the flame gives energy to sodium's outermost electron and bumps it up from its usual level (3s) to a higher one (3p). This is called being excited. The electron doesn't stay there. It drops back down and gives off the energy difference as a photon. For sodium, that gap gives light with a wavelength of about 589 nm, which looks yellow. Every element has its own level gaps, so each gives its own flame color. That's how a flame test identifies a metal.

questions.q: An atom absorbs a 500 nm photon, then relaxes in two steps. One emitted photon has a wavelength of 1000 nm. What is the wavelength of the other?
o: 500 nm
This subtracts the wavelengths (1000 − 500). Only energies add up, not wavelengths.
This adds the wavelengths (500 + 1000). Energies add, wavelengths don't.
333 nm
This adds the two energies instead of subtracting the emitted one from the absorbed one.
questions.note: Energy (∝ 1/λ) is conserved, not wavelength.
questions.x: Energy is conserved: the energy absorbed equals the energy of the two photons given off. A photon's energy is E = hc/λ, where h and c are constants and λ is the wavelength, so energy goes as 1/λ. So 1/500 = 1/1000 + 1/λ. Rewrite 1/500 as 2/1000 (multiply top and bottom by 2). Then 2/1000 − 1/1000 = 1/1000, so 1/λ = 1/1000 and λ = 1000 nm. The absorbed energy just splits into two equal halves. Wavelengths themselves never add or subtract; energies do.

questions.q: What is the ground-state electron configuration of Cu⁺?
o: [Ar]4s²3d⁸
This ignores copper's exception and also takes the electron from 3d instead of 4s.
[Ar]3d¹⁰
Correct: Cu is [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰, and the 4s electron leaves first.
[Ar]4s¹3d⁹
This takes the electron from 3d. The 4s electrons always leave first.
[Ar]4s²3d⁹
That's what the simple filling order predicts for neutral Cu, with no electron removed.
questions.x: Copper has 29 electrons. The simple filling order predicts [Ar]4s²3d⁹, but copper is an exception: it's really [Ar]4s¹3d¹⁰, because a completely full d subshell is extra stable. Now make the +1 ion by removing one electron. For transition metals, electrons come out of the 4s subshell before the 3d, because 4s is the outermost shell. Copper's single 4s electron goes, leaving Cu⁺ = [Ar]3d¹⁰. The 4s fills first, but it also empties first.

questions.q: How many unpaired electrons does a ground-state Mn²⁺ ion have?
o: This removes the 2 electrons from 3d (leaving 3d³) instead of from 4s.
This pairs up the d electrons, which breaks Hund's rule.
Correct: Mn²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵, with one electron in each of the five d orbitals.
That's all 7 outer electrons of neutral Mn, not the unpaired count in the ion.
questions.x: Neutral manganese has 25 electrons: [Ar]4s²3d⁵. To make Mn²⁺, remove 2 electrons, and for transition metals they come out of 4s first. That leaves [Ar]3d⁵. Now place those 5 d electrons into the five d orbitals. Hund's rule says electrons spread out one per orbital, all spinning the same way, before any of them pair up. Five electrons, five orbitals: one each, none paired. So Mn²⁺ has 5 unpaired electrons, the most a d subshell can have.

questions.q: In a hydrogen atom, the 2s and 2p orbitals have equal energy, but in lithium the 2s is lower. Why?
o: Lithium has more neutrons
Neutrons have no charge, so they don't change orbital energies.
The 2p orbitals in lithium hold more electrons
In ground-state lithium, the 2p orbitals are empty.
Lithium's nucleus is smaller
Lithium's nucleus isn't smaller, and nuclear size isn't what splits the energies.
2s penetrates the core, so it is shielded less than 2p
Correct: 2s gets close to the nucleus, so it's shielded less and feels a stronger pull.
questions.x: Hydrogen has just one electron, so nothing gets in the way of the nucleus's pull. Every orbital in the same shell (same n) has the same energy. Lithium has three electrons, and the two inner 1s electrons partly block the nucleus from the outer ones. That blocking is called shielding. A 2s electron spends a little of its time very close to the nucleus, inside the 1s electrons. This is called penetration. There it feels more of the nucleus's pull, called a higher effective nuclear charge, so 2s ends up lower in energy than 2p.

questions.q: The photoelectron spectrum of a neutral sodium atom shows how many peaks?
o: Correct: one peak for each occupied subshell: 1s, 2s, 2p and 3s.
This counts shells. 2s and 2p have different energies, so they make separate peaks.
Peaks match subshells, not individual electrons.
PES knocks out inner electrons too, not just the outermost one.
questions.note: Peak height is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.
questions.x: Photoelectron spectroscopy (PES) blasts atoms with high-energy light and measures how much energy it takes to knock each electron out, called the binding energy. Electrons in the same subshell have the same binding energy, so each occupied subshell gives one peak. Sodium has 11 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. That's four occupied subshells (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s), so the spectrum shows 4 peaks. Peak height tracks how many electrons are in each subshell, giving heights of 2 : 2 : 6 : 1.

questions.q: Iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺. Why is Fe³⁺ often especially stable?
o: It has a noble gas configuration
Fe³⁺ is [Ar]3d⁵. A noble gas setup would be plain [Ar].
It retains both 4s electrons
Both 4s electrons leave first, in Fe²⁺ and in Fe³⁺.
It has a half-filled 3d subshell
Correct: [Ar]3d⁵ has one electron in each d orbital, which is extra stable.
It has a filled 3d subshell
A full 3d subshell would be 3d¹⁰. Fe³⁺ has only 5 d electrons.
questions.x: Iron has 26 electrons: [Ar]4s²3d⁶. Transition metal ions lose their 4s electrons first, so Fe²⁺ is [Ar]3d⁶. Taking away one more electron, from 3d, gives Fe³⁺ = [Ar]3d⁵. A d subshell has 5 orbitals, so 3d⁵ means exactly one electron in each, which is half full. That arrangement is extra stable: no two electrons have to squeeze into the same orbital, and electrons spinning the same way get a small energy bonus. It's not a noble gas setup, which would be plain [Ar].

questions.q: Which element releases the most energy when a gaseous atom gains an electron?
o: F
Fluorine is so small that the extra electron is crowded, so it releases a bit less than Cl.
Br
Br is bigger than Cl, so the new electron sits farther out and is held less tightly.
O
Oxygen releases less for its first extra electron than the halogens do.
Cl
Correct: Cl has the most negative electron affinity of any element.
questions.note: Trap: fluorine is the most electronegative but not the highest EA.
questions.x: Electron affinity is the energy change when a gas atom picks up an extra electron. The more energy released, the more negative the electron affinity. Halogens, the column with F, Cl and Br, release the most, because one more electron fills their outer shell. You'd guess fluorine wins, but chlorine does. Fluorine is so small that its outer electrons are crammed close together, and the new electron gets pushed on by them. Chlorine is a bit bigger and has more room. Bromine is bigger still and holds the new electron less tightly.

questions.q: Zirconium (period 5) and hafnium (period 6) have almost the same atomic radius. What explains this?
o: Lanthanide contraction from poorly shielding 4f electrons
Correct: 14 extra protons, poorly shielded by 4f electrons, cancel the size added by the new shell.
Hafnium has fewer protons than zirconium
Hafnium (Z = 72) has far more protons than zirconium (Z = 40).
Both lack d electrons
Both are d-block metals and both have d electrons.
Relativistic expansion of hafnium's 6s orbital
Relativity slightly shrinks heavy s orbitals, not expands them, and isn't the main cause.
questions.x: Going down a column usually makes atoms bigger, because each row adds a new shell of electrons. But between zirconium (row 5) and hafnium (row 6), the 14 lanthanide elements fill the 4f subshell. That adds 14 protons and 14 electrons in f orbitals. f electrons are bad at shielding, meaning they don't block much of the nucleus's pull from the outer electrons. So the extra 14 protons pull the outer electrons in more tightly. That shrinking, called the lanthanide contraction, cancels out the size gained from the new shell.

questions.q: Which species in the isoelectronic set Ne, Na⁺, F⁻, O²⁻ has the highest first ionization energy?
o: Ne
Ne has 10 protons, one fewer than Na⁺, for the same 10 electrons.
F⁻
F⁻ has only 9 protons for 10 electrons, so its hold is loose.
Na⁺
Correct: Na⁺ has the most protons (11) pulling on the same 10 electrons.
O²⁻
O²⁻ has the fewest protons (8), so it has the lowest ionization energy.
questions.x: All four have 10 electrons, the same setup as neon. That's what 'isoelectronic' means. Ionization energy is the energy needed to pull one electron off. With the same electrons, the deciding factor is the number of protons pulling on them. Na⁺ has 11 protons, Ne has 10, F⁻ has 9 and O²⁻ has 8. Na⁺ pulls hardest on its 10 electrons, so it's the hardest to take one from. It's also already positive, which makes removing another electron even harder.

questions.q: Which aqueous ion is most likely to give a colorless solution?
o: Cu²⁺
Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, with room for d electrons to jump, so it's blue.
Ni²⁺
Ni²⁺ is 3d⁸, so d–d jumps can happen and it's green.
Zn²⁺
Correct: Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰, so there's no room for a d electron to jump.
Fe³⁺
Fe³⁺ is 3d⁵, with partly filled d orbitals, so it's yellow to brown.
questions.x: Most transition metal ions get their color from d–d transitions. In water, the d orbitals split into two groups with slightly different energies. A d electron can absorb a bit of visible light and jump to the higher group, and the color we see is the light left over. But a jump needs somewhere to go. Zn²⁺ is 3d¹⁰: every d orbital is completely full, so no electron can jump, no visible light is absorbed, and the solution is colorless. Cu²⁺ (3d⁹), Ni²⁺ (3d⁸) and Fe³⁺ (3d⁵) all have room, so they're colored.

questions.q: In sodium hydride (NaH), what is the oxidation state of hydrogen?
o: Hydrogen is +1 next to atoms that pull harder on electrons, like O or Cl, not Na.
Correct: H pulls harder on electrons than Na, so it becomes hydride, H⁻.
0 is for pure H₂. Here hydrogen is bonded to sodium.
Hydrogen has only one electron, so it can't lose two.
questions.x: An oxidation state is the charge an atom would have if every shared electron went to the atom that pulls harder on electrons (the more electronegative one). Hydrogen is usually +1, because it's normally bonded to atoms that pull harder, like oxygen or chlorine. But sodium is a metal and pulls on electrons less than hydrogen does. So in NaH, hydrogen takes the electron and becomes hydride, H⁻. Check: sodium is always +1, and the compound is neutral, so +1 + (−1) = 0.

questions.q: Xenon forms compounds such as XeF₄, but neon forms none. What best explains the difference?
o: Xenon's valence electrons are farther out and have a lower ionization energy
Correct: Xe's outer electrons are far out and easier to share with a strong puller like F.
Xenon has unpaired electrons in its ground state
Ground-state xenon has all its electrons paired.
Neon is radioactive
Neon's common forms aren't radioactive.
Neon has a higher electron affinity
Noble gases don't want extra electrons, and Xe bonds to F by sharing, not gaining.
questions.x: Noble gases have full outer shells, so they rarely react. But going down the column, the outer electrons sit farther from the nucleus and more inner electrons shield them. Neon's outer electrons are in shell 2, close to the nucleus and held very tightly. Xenon's are in shell 5, far out and well shielded, so its ionization energy (the energy to pull an electron away) is much lower. That's low enough for fluorine, the hardest-pulling element, to draw xenon's electrons into bonds, as in XeF₄. Neon's electrons are held too tightly for that.

questions.q: Transition metals often show several oxidation states, unlike alkali metals. Why?
o: They have more protons
Proton count alone doesn't create several oxidation states.
Their ns and (n−1)d electrons are close in energy
Correct: the s and d electrons are close in energy, so different numbers can be removed.
They have filled p subshells
Lots of main-group elements have filled p subshells and only one common state.
They are always paramagnetic
Some transition metal ions aren't magnetic, and magnetism isn't the reason anyway.
questions.x: To lose electrons, an atom gives up the ones that are easiest to remove. In transition metals, the outer s electrons (like 4s) and the d electrons just below them (like 3d) have almost the same energy. So it costs about the same to remove just the s electrons, or the s electrons plus one or more d electrons. That's why iron can be Fe²⁺ or Fe³⁺. An alkali metal like sodium has a single outer electron sitting above a full, noble-gas core. Removing a second electron means breaking into that core, which costs far too much, so it's only ever +1.

questions.q: An unknown solid is shiny, conducts electricity, reacts with water to release H₂, and has a first IE far below its second. Which element fits best?
o: Mg
Mg has 2 outer electrons, so its big jump comes after the second, not the first.
Al
Al has 3 outer electrons, so its big jump comes after the third.
Sr
Sr is in group 2, so its big jump comes after the second electron.
Na
Correct: with one outer electron, the big jump comes right after the first.
questions.x: Being shiny and conducting electricity only tells you it's a metal, and all four choices are metals. The key clue is the ionization energies. Ionization energy (IE) is the energy needed to pull off an electron: IE₁ is the first one, IE₂ the second. If IE₂ is far bigger than IE₁, the atom has just one outer (valence) electron, and the second has to come out of a full inner core. That's a group 1 metal, like sodium. Sodium also reacts with water to give H₂ gas, which fits.

questions.q: In a coordinate covalent bond, such as the N–B bond in H₃N–BF₃, the shared electron pair:
o: Is transferred completely to the more electronegative atom
A complete handover of electrons is an ionic bond. Here the pair is still shared between N and B.
Comes entirely from one atom, here the nitrogen lone pair
Correct: nitrogen's lone pair supplies both electrons to boron's empty orbital.
Comes one electron from each atom, as in any covalent bond
One electron from each atom is an ordinary covalent bond, not a coordinate one.
Is delocalized over all the fluorine atoms
The pair sits between N and B. The fluorines aren't the donor and don't share it.
questions.note: Coordinate (dative) bond = Lewis base donates both electrons to a Lewis acid.
questions.x: A normal covalent bond is a shared pair of electrons where each atom chips in one electron. A coordinate (or dative) bond is still a shared pair, but both electrons come from the same atom. In H₃N–BF₃, nitrogen has a spare lone pair, and boron in BF₃ has only six electrons and an empty orbital. Nitrogen hands over its whole pair, so nitrogen is the Lewis base (the pair donor) and boron is the Lewis acid (the pair acceptor). Once it forms, the bond acts like any other covalent bond. The only difference is where the electrons came from.

questions.q: As two isolated hydrogen atoms approach and form an H₂ molecule, how does the potential energy of the system change?
o: It rises steadily until the bond forms, then stays constant
Forming a bond releases energy, so the energy falls as the atoms approach. It doesn't rise.
It stays constant because no electrons are gained or lost
Sharing electrons lowers the energy, even though no electrons are gained or lost.
It decreases continuously the closer the nuclei get
Too close and the two positive nuclei repel, so the energy climbs steeply.
It falls to a minimum at the bond length, then rises sharply if the nuclei get closer
Correct: the energy bottoms out at the bond length, then rises sharply as the nuclei crowd.
questions.note: The well depth of the energy curve equals the bond dissociation energy.
questions.x: Potential energy is stored energy that depends on position. Two hydrogen atoms far apart don't affect each other, so call their energy zero. As they come closer, each electron gets pulled by both nuclei, and the energy drops. It hits a lowest point at the bond length, about 74 pm for H₂. Push the nuclei any closer and their two positive charges repel hard, so the energy shoots back up. The curve looks like a well, and how deep the well is equals the bond energy.

questions.q: Which of these molecules does NOT exist because its central atom cannot expand its octet?
o: PCl₅
Phosphorus is in period 3, so it can hold 10 electrons. PCl₅ is real.
SF₄
Sulfur is in period 3, so it can hold 10 electrons. SF₄ is real.
NCl₅
Correct: nitrogen is in period 2 and can't hold the 10 electrons five bonds need.
XeF₂
Xenon is in period 5, so it can hold 10 electrons: two bonds plus three lone pairs.
questions.note: Only period 3 and lower atoms can have expanded octets.
questions.x: An expanded octet means an atom holds more than eight electrons around it. Only atoms in period 3 or lower can do that, because they're bigger and have empty d orbitals in their outer shell. Nitrogen is in period 2, with only 2s and 2p orbitals, so eight electrons is its limit. Five N–Cl bonds would need 10 electrons, so NCl₅ doesn't exist. Phosphorus is right below nitrogen in period 3, which is why PCl₅ does exist. Sulfur (SF₄) and xenon (XeF₂) are also big enough to expand.

questions.q: Using bond energies H–H = 440, Cl–Cl = 240 and H–Cl = 430 kJ/mol, what is ΔH for H₂ + Cl₂ → 2 HCl?
o: Right size, wrong sign: this is formed minus broken. Use broken minus formed.
This counts only one H–Cl bond formed: 680 − 430 = 250. The equation makes two.
This counts only the bonds formed and forgets the 680 kJ spent breaking H–H and Cl–Cl.
questions.note: ΔH ≈ Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed).
questions.x: Use ΔH = (bonds broken) − (bonds formed). Breaking bonds costs energy and forming bonds releases it. Broken: one H–H at 440 kJ and one Cl–Cl at 240 kJ, so 440 + 240 = 680 kJ. Formed: two H–Cl at 430 kJ each, so 2 × 430 = 860 kJ. Plug in: ΔH = 680 − 860 = −180 kJ. The sign is negative, so the reaction gives off heat (it's exothermic). If you subtract the other way around, you get +180 kJ with the wrong sign.

questions.q: Which Lewis structure contributes most to the cyanate ion, OCN⁻ (C central)?
o: O=C=N with −1 on nitrogen
A decent drawing, but it puts the −1 on nitrogen, which holds negative charge worse than oxygen.
O≡C–N with +1 on O and −2 on N
+1 and −2 are big, separated charges, so this is a minor contributor.
O=C=N with no formal charges
The ion has an overall −1 charge, so some atom has to carry it.
O–C≡N with −1 on oxygen
Correct: small formal charges, with the −1 on oxygen, the most electronegative atom.
questions.note: Best structure: minimal formal charges, negative charge on the most electronegative atom.
questions.x: To pick the best resonance structure, check three things in order. First, every atom should have a full octet. Second, formal charges (the charge an atom would have if every bond were shared equally) should be as small as possible. Third, any negative charge should sit on the most electronegative atom, the one that pulls electrons hardest. Two drawings of OCN⁻ pass the first two tests: one with −1 on N and one with −1 on O. Oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen, so it holds the negative charge better, and O–C≡N with −1 on oxygen wins.

questions.q: Why do many textbooks draw SO₄²⁻ with two S=O bonds rather than four S–O single bonds?
o: It gives sulfur a complete octet, which the single-bond structure lacks
Four single bonds already give sulfur eight electrons. The double bonds push it past eight.
It reduces the formal charge on sulfur from +2 to 0
Correct: four single bonds give S a +2; two S=O bonds bring it to 0.
It makes the four S–O bonds unequal, as measured experimentally
Experiments show all four S–O bonds are the same length.
It reduces the total number of valence electrons to 30
The electron count is fixed at 6 + 4 × 6 + 2 = 32, however you draw it.
questions.note: Formal-charge minimization is the MCAT rationale for expanded octets.
questions.x: Formal charge = V − (L + B), where V is the atom's valence electrons, L is its lone-pair electrons, and B is its number of bonds. Sulfur has V = 6 and no lone pairs here, so L = 0. With four S–O single bonds, B = 4: 6 − (0 + 4) = +2, and each oxygen ends up −1. Make two of them S=O double bonds and B = 6: 6 − (0 + 6) = 0. Sulfur is in period 3, so it can hold more than eight electrons. Drawing the double bonds isn't about finishing an octet; it brings the charges closer to zero.

questions.q: How does the bookkeeping for formal charge differ from that for oxidation state?
o: Formal charge gives all bonding electrons to the more electronegative partner atom
Handing all bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom is the oxidation-state rule.
Formal charge treats bonding electrons as shared equally between the two atoms
Correct: formal charge gives each atom half of every bonding pair, ignoring electronegativity.
Formal charge ignores lone pairs
Lone pairs count in full toward the atom that holds them.
Formal charge applies only to ions
Neutral molecules like CO and O₃ have atoms with nonzero formal charges too.
questions.x: Formal charge and oxidation state are two ways of counting electrons on an atom, and they split bonds differently. Formal charge pretends every bond is shared perfectly evenly: each atom keeps its own lone-pair electrons plus exactly half of every bonding pair, whatever the electronegativity. Oxidation state pretends every bond is fully ionic: the more electronegative atom takes all the bonding electrons. That's why nitrogen in NO₃⁻ has a formal charge of +1 but an oxidation state of +5.

questions.q: Which species has the longest N–O bonds?
o: NO₂⁺
O=N=O has two double bonds, bond order 2, so its bonds are short.
NO₂⁻
Nitrite has resonance, but its bond order is 1.5, higher than nitrate's 1⅓.
NO₃⁻
Correct: one double bond spread over three N–O links gives 4 ÷ 3 = 1⅓, the lowest.
NO
NO's bond order is about 2.5, the highest here, so its bond is the shortest.
questions.note: Lower average bond order → longer bond.
questions.x: Bond order is the average number of bonds between two atoms, and a lower bond order means a longer bond. Work it out for each: NO is about 2.5. NO₂⁺ is O=N=O, so 2. Nitrite, NO₂⁻, has one double and one single bond shared over two N–O links: 3 ÷ 2 = 1.5. Nitrate, NO₃⁻, has one double and two single bonds over three links: 4 ÷ 3 = 1⅓. Nitrate has the lowest bond order, so it has the longest N–O bonds.

questions.q: Acetic acid (pKₐ ≈ 4.8) is far more acidic than ethanol (pKₐ ≈ 16). Which factor best explains this?
o: Acetate's negative charge is delocalized over two oxygens by resonance
Correct: resonance spreads acetate's charge over two oxygens, so the base is stable and the acid is strong.
The O–H bond in acetic acid is a stronger bond
A stronger O–H bond would make the H⁺ harder to remove, so the acid would be weaker.
Ethanol has more hydrogen atoms to lose
Only one acidic H leaves. Acidity depends on how stable the leftover base is, not on H count.
Ethoxide is stabilized by resonance with the neighboring methyl group
Ethoxide has no resonance. Its negative charge sits on one oxygen.
questions.note: More stable conjugate base → stronger acid.
questions.x: An acid is strong when the piece left behind after it loses H⁺, its conjugate base, is stable. When acetic acid loses H⁺, it becomes acetate, and acetate's negative charge is shared between two oxygens by resonance (the electrons spread across more than one atom). Spreading a charge out makes it much more stable. When ethanol loses H⁺, it becomes ethoxide, and that charge is stuck on a single oxygen. So acetic acid gives up H⁺ far more easily. A stronger O–H bond would do the opposite and make an acid weaker.

questions.q: The C–N bond in an amide is shorter than a typical C–N single bond, and rotation about it is restricted. What is the best explanation?
o: The nitrogen lone pair is delocalized into the carbonyl, giving the C–N bond partial double-bond character
Correct: resonance gives the C–N bond partial double-bond character, so it's short and won't twist.
Nitrogen is sp³ hybridized, which holds substituents rigidly
An sp³ nitrogen would let the bond spin freely. Amide nitrogen behaves as sp².
Hydrogen bonding between N–H and C=O locks the bond
Amides with no N–H at all still can't rotate, so hydrogen bonding isn't the cause.
The carbonyl oxygen sterically blocks rotation
Crowding can't make a bond shorter. Only extra bonding does that.
questions.note: This planarity underlies the rigid peptide bond.
questions.x: In an amide, nitrogen's lone pair can slide toward the carbonyl carbon and push the C=O π electrons (the electrons in the second part of the double bond) onto oxygen. That gives a second resonance drawing with a C=N double bond and a negative oxygen. The real amide is a blend of both drawings, so the C–N bond is part single, part double. Partial double-bond character makes the bond shorter and makes it hard to twist. Hydrogen bonding can't be the cause, because amides with no N–H at all are just as rigid.

questions.q: For protonated acetone, which resonance contributor is more important: (CH₃)₂C=OH⁺ or (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH?
o: (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH, because the positive charge rests on the less electronegative carbon
Carbon handles a + charge better, but here it has only six electrons. Full octets matter more.
Both contribute equally because they have the same charge
Same overall charge doesn't mean equal stability. The drawings are ranked by octets first.
(CH₃)₂C=OH⁺, because every atom has a full octet
Correct: every atom has a full octet, and that outranks where the charge sits.
Neither, because protonated acetone has no resonance
Moving the π pair onto oxygen gives a valid second drawing, so resonance exists.
questions.note: Priority: full octets first, then minimal formal charge, then charge on the right atom.
questions.x: When you rank resonance drawings, full octets come first. In (CH₃)₂C=OH⁺, every atom has eight electrons around it, and the +1 sits on oxygen. In (CH₃)₂C⁺–OH, the positive charge sits on carbon, which is less electronegative and handles a + charge better. But that carbon has only six electrons. A missing octet is a bigger problem than where the charge sits, so the C=OH⁺ form is the major contributor. The carbocation drawing still matters: it shows why that carbon attracts electron-rich molecules.

questions.q: The H–O–H angle in water is about 104.5°, smaller than the ideal tetrahedral 109.5°. Why?
o: Hydrogen atoms attract each other
The hydrogens are slightly positive and repel a little, which would widen the angle, not shrink it.
Lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle
Correct: the bulky lone pairs push the two O–H bonds closer together.
Oxygen is sp² hybridized
Water's oxygen has four electron groups, so it's treated as sp³, not sp².
Hydrogen bonding between molecules bends each molecule
The angle is the same in a lone gas-phase molecule, so hydrogen bonding isn't the cause.
questions.note: Repulsion: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair.
questions.x: Water's oxygen has four electron groups around it: two O–H bonds and two lone pairs (pairs of electrons not in a bond). Four groups spread out into a tetrahedron, with ideal angles of 109.5°. But a lone pair is held by only one nucleus, so it puffs out and takes up more room near the oxygen than a bonding pair does. The two lone pairs push the O–H bonds closer together, squeezing the angle to about 104.5°. Hydrogen bonding isn't the reason, since a single water molecule in the gas has the same angle.

questions.q: What is the molecular geometry of XeF₂?
o: Bent
Bent shapes come from three or four electron groups. Xenon here has five.
Linear
Correct: the three lone pairs fill the middle ring, leaving the two F atoms 180° apart.
Trigonal planar
Trigonal planar needs three bonded atoms and no lone pairs. XeF₂ has two bonded atoms.
T-shaped
T-shaped needs three bonded atoms. XeF₂ has only two.
questions.note: Three equatorial lone pairs on a trigonal bipyramid → linear.
questions.x: Xenon in XeF₂ has five electron groups: two bonds to F and three lone pairs. Five groups arrange as a trigonal bipyramid, with three spots around the middle (equatorial, 120° apart) and two at the top and bottom (axial). Lone pairs go in the middle spots, because there they have fewer close neighbors to bump into. All three lone pairs fill the middle ring, so the two F atoms end up at the top and bottom, directly opposite each other. That makes a straight line: F–Xe–F at 180°. Lone pairs don't always make a molecule bent.

questions.q: Which ranking of bond angles is correct?
o: H₂O > NH₃ > CH₄
Reversed. Water has the most lone pairs, so it has the smallest angle.
CH₄ > NH₃ > H₂O
Correct: 109.5° > about 107° > about 104.5°, as lone pairs go from 0 to 1 to 2.
NH₃ > CH₄ > H₂O
Methane has no lone pairs, so it has the largest angle, not ammonia.
All three are 109.5°
Only CH₄ keeps 109.5°. Lone pairs squeeze the angles in NH₃ and H₂O.
questions.x: CH₄, NH₃ and H₂O all have four electron groups around the central atom, so each starts from the tetrahedral angle of 109.5°. What changes is the number of lone pairs, which push harder than bonds. Methane has 0 lone pairs and keeps 109.5°. Ammonia has 1 lone pair, which squeezes its angles to about 107°. Water has 2 lone pairs, which squeeze its angle to about 104.5°. So the order is CH₄ > NH₃ > H₂O. The same electron arrangement doesn't mean the same bond angle.

questions.q: In SF₄, the lone pair on sulfur occupies an equatorial rather than an axial position. Why?
o: Equatorial positions are closer to the nucleus
The distance to the nucleus barely differs. What matters is how many 90° neighbors each spot has.
Axial positions are reserved for the most electronegative atoms only, like fluorine
Electronegative atoms tend to go axial, but nothing reserves those spots. 90° crowding decides.
An equatorial lone pair is perpendicular to the π system
SF₄'s shape comes from electron-group repulsion (VSEPR), not from any π system.
An equatorial site has only two 90° neighbors versus three for an axial site
Correct: an equatorial spot has two 90° neighbors, an axial spot three, so the lone pair goes equatorial.
questions.x: SF₄ has five electron groups arranged as a trigonal bipyramid: three equatorial spots around the middle and two axial spots at the top and bottom. Neighbors at 90° repel each other much more than neighbors at 120°. An axial spot has three neighbors at 90° (the three equatorial groups). An equatorial spot has only two at 90° (the two axial groups). A lone pair is bulky and pushes hardest, so it goes where it bumps into the fewest 90° neighbors: equatorial. That gives SF₄ its seesaw shape.

questions.q: In pyridine, nitrogen is part of the aromatic ring. What is the hybridization of N, and where is its lone pair?
o: sp³; in an orbital above the ring
Atoms in an aromatic ring are sp², so the ring stays flat with overlapping p orbitals.
sp²; in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring
Correct: sp² nitrogen with its lone pair in the ring plane, free to pick up H⁺.
sp²; in the p orbital as part of the aromatic π system
That's pyrrole. Pyridine's nitrogen already gives one p electron to the ring.
sp; along the C–N axis
Nitrogen has three electron groups here, so it's sp², not sp.
questions.note: Pyridine's lone pair is available for protonation; pyrrole's is not.
questions.x: Pyridine's nitrogen has three electron groups: two bonds in the ring and one lone pair. Three groups means sp² hybridization. Its leftover p orbital holds one electron, which helps make the six π electrons the ring needs to be aromatic (an extra-stable flat ring of shared electrons). The lone pair isn't needed for that, so it sits in an sp² orbital in the plane of the ring, pointing outward. It's free to grab an H⁺, which is why pyridine is a base. In pyrrole it's the other way: the lone pair is part of the ring's π system.

questions.q: In allene, H₂C=C=CH₂, what is the hybridization of the central carbon, and how are the two CH₂ planes oriented?
o: sp²; the two CH₂ groups are coplanar
The central carbon has only two electron groups, so it's sp, not sp². The ends aren't flat together.
sp; the two CH₂ groups are coplanar
sp is right, but the two π bonds use p orbitals at right angles, which twists the ends.
sp²; the two CH₂ groups are perpendicular
sp² would need three electron groups. The central carbon has only two.
sp; the two CH₂ groups are perpendicular
Correct: an sp carbon's two p orbitals are at 90°, so the two CH₂ planes are at 90°.
questions.x: To find hybridization, count the electron groups around the atom. The central carbon of allene has two double bonds and no lone pairs, so it has just two groups, which makes it sp and linear. That leaves it two p orbitals, and they point at right angles to each other. One p orbital makes a π bond (the side-by-side second half of a double bond) with the left carbon, and the other makes a π bond with the right carbon. Each CH₂ group has to lie flat at a right angle to its own π bond, so the two CH₂ planes end up twisted 90° from each other.

questions.q: How many σ and π bonds are in benzene, C₆H₆?
o: Correct: 6 C–C + 6 C–H = 12 σ, and 6 π electrons ÷ 2 = 3 π bonds.
9 σ, 3 π
Only 9 σ misses three. Each of the six C–C links has a σ bond, plus six C–H bonds.
6 σ, 6 π
This skips the six C–H σ bonds and counts each π electron as a whole π bond.
12 σ is right, but 6 π electrons make 3 π bonds, not 6.
questions.note: Count π bonds as pairs of π electrons.
questions.x: Every connection between two atoms has exactly one σ bond (the head-on part of a bond). Benzene has 6 C–C links around the ring and 6 C–H bonds, so σ = 6 + 6 = 12. π bonds are the extra, side-by-side bonds in double bonds, and each π bond holds 2 electrons. Benzene has 6 π electrons, so π bonds = 6 ÷ 2 = 3. They're spread around the whole ring rather than fixed in place, but there are still three of them. So benzene has 12 σ and 3 π bonds.

questions.q: NH₃ has a dipole moment of about 1.5 D, but NF₃ has only about 0.2 D, even though N–F bonds are more polar than N–H bonds. Why?
o: In NF₃ the N–F bond dipoles point away from N and oppose the lone-pair dipole
Correct: the N–F arrows point away from N and fight the lone pair, so they mostly cancel.
NF₃ is trigonal planar, so its dipoles cancel
NF₃ has a lone pair on N, so it's a pyramid like NH₃, not flat.
Fluorine is less electronegative than nitrogen
Fluorine is the most electronegative element, more than nitrogen.
NF₃ has no lone pair on nitrogen
Nitrogen in NF₃ still has one lone pair.
questions.note: Net dipole = vector sum of bond dipoles and lone-pair contributions.
questions.x: A molecule's dipole (its overall lopsidedness of charge) is the sum of arrows: one for each polar bond, plus one for the lone pair. Bond arrows point toward the more electronegative atom, the one that pulls electrons harder. In NH₃, nitrogen beats hydrogen, so the N–H arrows point toward N, the same way as the lone pair's arrow, and they add up to 1.5 D. In NF₃, fluorine beats nitrogen, so the N–F arrows point away from N, against the lone pair, and they nearly cancel, leaving about 0.2 D. Both molecules are pyramid-shaped.

questions.q: A charged rod is held near thin falling streams of four liquids. Which stream is deflected most strongly toward the rod?
o: Hexane
Hexane is a nonpolar hydrocarbon with no net dipole to turn toward the rod.
Carbon disulfide
S=C=S is a straight line, so its two bond dipoles cancel.
Dichloromethane
Correct: CH₂Cl₂ has a net dipole, so it turns and gets pulled toward the rod.
Benzene
Benzene is flat and symmetric, so it has no net dipole.
questions.note: Polar molecules align in an electric field; nonpolar ones barely respond.
questions.x: A charged rod pulls on polar molecules, ones with a slightly positive end and a slightly negative end. They turn so their oppositely charged end faces the rod, and then they get drawn toward it. Dichloromethane, CH₂Cl₂, is a tetrahedron with two Cl atoms and two H atoms, so its bond dipoles don't cancel, and it has a net dipole. Hexane, carbon disulfide and benzene are all nonpolar overall: hexane's C–H bonds are barely polar, and CS₂ and benzene are symmetric, so their bond dipoles cancel. Polar bonds alone don't make a polar molecule; shape decides.

questions.q: For molecules of comparable size, which ranking of interaction strengths is typical, from strongest to weakest?
o: Hydrogen bond > ion–dipole > dipole–dipole > London dispersion
Ion–dipole involves a full charge, so it beats hydrogen bonds.
Ion–dipole > hydrogen bond > dipole–dipole > London dispersion
Correct: full charges beat partial ones, and H-bonds are the strongest dipole–dipole forces.
Dipole–dipole > hydrogen bond > ion–dipole > London dispersion
Ordinary dipole–dipole is weaker than both hydrogen bonds and ion–dipole forces.
London dispersion > dipole–dipole > hydrogen bond > ion–dipole
This is upside down. For similar-sized molecules, dispersion is the weakest.
questions.note: Caveat: dispersion can dominate for very large molecules.
questions.x: Forces between particles get stronger as the charges involved get bigger. Ion–dipole forces involve a full charge on an ion (like Na⁺) pulling on the partial charge of a polar molecule, so they're the strongest here. Hydrogen bonds come next: they're an extra-strong kind of dipole–dipole force that forms when H is bonded to N, O or F, which leaves that H very positive. Ordinary dipole–dipole forces, between partial charges, come third. London dispersion, the brief attraction from electrons sloshing around, is the weakest for molecules of similar size.

questions.q: Which hydrogen halide has the lowest boiling point?
o: HF
HF forms hydrogen bonds, so it has the highest boiling point of the four.
HCl
Correct: no hydrogen bonds and the fewest electrons of HCl, HBr and HI.
HBr
HBr has more electrons than HCl, so stronger dispersion forces.
HI
HI has the biggest electron cloud, so the strongest dispersion of HCl, HBr and HI.
questions.note: HF is the anomaly; otherwise boiling point rises down the group.
questions.x: Boiling point depends on how hard the molecules hold onto each other. HCl, HBr and HI are held by dipole–dipole forces and London dispersion (brief attractions from electrons bunching up). Dispersion gets stronger as the electron cloud gets bigger, so boiling points rise from HCl (−85 °C) to HBr (−67 °C) to HI (−35 °C). HF breaks the pattern: H bonded to F forms hydrogen bonds, so HF boils near 20 °C even though it's the smallest. That leaves HCl with the lowest boiling point.

questions.q: o-Nitrophenol boils at a much lower temperature than p-nitrophenol. What is the best explanation?
o: The ortho isomer has a lower molar mass
The two isomers have the same formula, so the same molar mass.
The ortho isomer forms an intramolecular H-bond, leaving fewer intermolecular H-bonds
Correct: OH and NO₂ bond inside one molecule, leaving fewer H-bonds between molecules.
The para isomer is nonpolar
The para isomer is very polar and hydrogen bonds with its neighbors.
The ortho isomer cannot hydrogen bond at all
The ortho isomer does hydrogen bond, just inside its own molecule.
questions.note: Intramolecular H-bonds lower boiling points relative to isomers.
questions.x: A hydrogen bond can form inside one molecule (intramolecular) or between two molecules (intermolecular). Only the ones between molecules hold the liquid together. In o-nitrophenol, the OH and NO₂ groups sit right next to each other on the ring, so the OH's hydrogen bonds to a nitro oxygen in the same molecule, closing a small ring. With that H already busy, the molecule makes few hydrogen bonds to its neighbors, so it escapes into the gas more easily and boils lower. In p-nitrophenol the groups are on opposite sides, so the OH bonds to other molecules instead. Both isomers have the same mass.

questions.q: Propane (C₃H₈), acetaldehyde (CH₃CHO) and ethanol (C₂H₅OH) have similar molar masses (44–46 g/mol). Which order lists them by increasing boiling point?
o: Ethanol < acetaldehyde < propane
Reversed. Stronger forces between molecules mean a higher boiling point.
Acetaldehyde < propane < ethanol
Propane has only weak dispersion forces, so it boils below polar acetaldehyde.
Propane < acetaldehyde < ethanol
Correct: dispersion only < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding.
Propane < ethanol < acetaldehyde
Acetaldehyde has no O–H, so it can't donate hydrogen bonds and boils below ethanol.
questions.note: At similar mass, rank by the strongest IMF available.
questions.x: All three have about the same mass, so their London dispersion forces are similar. The difference comes from the strongest extra force each one has. Propane has only dispersion, so it boils lowest, near −42 °C. Acetaldehyde has a polar C=O, which adds dipole–dipole attraction, and boils near 20 °C. Ethanol has an O–H, so it can form hydrogen bonds, and it boils at 78 °C. Acetaldehyde has an oxygen, but no H attached to it, so it can't donate a hydrogen bond. The order is propane < acetaldehyde < ethanol.

questions.q: In ethane, H₃C–CH₃, each C–H σ bond forms from the overlap of which orbitals?
o: A carbon 2p orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
Plain p orbitals are 90° apart and can't make four equal bonds at 109.5°.
A carbon sp² orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
An sp² carbon has three electron groups. Each ethane carbon has four σ bonds.
A carbon sp³ orbital and a hydrogen 1s orbital
Correct: a carbon sp³ orbital overlaps hydrogen's 1s orbital, its only one.
A carbon sp³ orbital and a hydrogen sp³ orbital
Hydrogen has only a 1s orbital, so it can't hybridize.
questions.x: Each carbon in ethane makes four σ bonds (single bonds formed by head-on overlap): three to H and one to the other C. Four electron groups means carbon mixes its one 2s and three 2p orbitals into four matching sp³ orbitals, which point to the corners of a tetrahedron, 109.5° apart. Hydrogen has only one orbital to offer, its 1s, so it never hybridizes. So each C–H bond is a carbon sp³ orbital overlapping a hydrogen 1s orbital. Plain p orbitals sit at 90° to each other and couldn't give the 109.5° angles we see.

questions.q: At 25 °C, which liquid has the highest vapor pressure?
o: Water
Water's strong hydrogen bonding keeps its molecules in the liquid.
Diethyl ether
Correct: no O–H, so only weak forces hold it and molecules escape easily.
Ethanol
Ethanol has an O–H and hydrogen bonds, which lowers its vapor pressure.
Glycerol
Glycerol's three O–H groups give it very strong hydrogen bonding and the lowest vapor pressure.
questions.note: Weaker IMFs → higher vapor pressure → lower boiling point.
questions.x: Vapor pressure is the push of gas molecules that have escaped from the surface of a liquid. The weaker the forces holding the liquid together, the more molecules escape, and the higher the vapor pressure. Diethyl ether has no O–H, so it can't hydrogen bond with itself. Only weak dipole–dipole and dispersion forces hold it, so it evaporates very easily and boils at just 35 °C. Water, ethanol and glycerol all have O–H groups and hydrogen bond, which keeps their molecules in the liquid. Glycerol, with three O–H groups, has the lowest vapor pressure.

questions.q: Acetic acid (60 g/mol, bp 118 °C) boils higher than 1-propanol (60 g/mol, bp 97 °C). What is the best explanation?
o: Acetic acid has more electrons, so stronger dispersion forces
The molar masses are equal, so the electron counts and dispersion forces are about the same.
1-Propanol cannot hydrogen bond
1-Propanol has an O–H and does hydrogen bond.
Acetic acid ionizes completely in the pure liquid
Acetic acid is a weak acid, so the pure liquid is barely ionized.
Acetic acid pairs form two hydrogen bonds each (dimers) and the C=O adds strong polarity
Correct: two acid molecules lock together with two hydrogen bonds, and the C=O adds polarity.
questions.note: Carboxylic acids boil higher than alcohols of similar mass.
questions.x: Both compounds weigh 60 g/mol and both can hydrogen bond, so the difference is in how they hydrogen bond. Acetic acid's carboxyl group (COOH) has an O–H that donates a hydrogen bond and a C=O right next to it that accepts one. Two acid molecules can face each other and form two hydrogen bonds at once, making a paired unit called a dimer. Its polar C=O adds extra pull too. That's stronger than the single O–H in 1-propanol, so acetic acid boils about 20 °C higher (118 °C vs 97 °C). Pure acetic acid barely ionizes.

questions.q: SiO₂ melts above 1600 °C, but CO₂ sublimes at −78 °C. What explains this difference?
o: SiO₂ is ionic and CO₂ is covalent
SiO₂ is held by covalent bonds, not ions.
Si–O bonds are polar and C=O bonds are not
Both Si–O and C=O bonds are polar.
CO₂ is linear, so it has no intermolecular forces at all
CO₂ still has weak dispersion forces between its molecules.
SiO₂ is a network solid whose melting breaks covalent bonds; CO₂ is held only by weak intermolecular forces
Correct: melting quartz breaks Si–O covalent bonds; CO₂ only needs to overcome weak forces.
questions.note: Network covalent solids (diamond, quartz) have the highest melting points.
questions.x: SiO₂ and CO₂ have similar formulas but very different structures. Silicon doesn't form good double bonds with oxygen, so instead each Si bonds to four O atoms with single bonds, and each O bridges two Si atoms. That builds one giant 3-D network, called a network solid. To melt quartz, you have to break strong Si–O covalent bonds, so it takes over 1600 °C. CO₂ is made of small, separate O=C=O molecules held to each other only by weak dispersion forces, so it turns to gas at −78 °C. Both have polar covalent bonds.

questions.q: Sodium stearate (a soap) forms micelles in water. How are the molecules arranged?
o: Nonpolar tails point inward and charged heads face the water
Correct: the tails hide in the middle, and the charged heads face the water.
Charged heads point inward and the nonpolar tails face the water
Heads in and tails out is a reverse micelle, which forms in nonpolar solvents.
Molecules stack in a flat bilayer sheet
Flat bilayers are typical of two-tailed lipids. One-tailed soaps form round micelles.
Molecules dissolve individually with no organization
Above a certain concentration, soap molecules group together.
questions.note: The hydrophobic effect drives micelle formation.
questions.x: Soap molecules are amphipathic, which means each one has a water-loving part and a water-avoiding part. In sodium stearate, the long hydrocarbon tail is nonpolar and avoids water, and the charged carboxylate head (COO⁻) loves water. In water, the molecules gather into a ball called a micelle: the tails tuck into the middle, away from the water, and the charged heads cover the outside, where they're attracted to water molecules. Grease dissolves in the oily center, which is how soap washes it away. The reverse arrangement only forms in a nonpolar solvent like oil.

questions.q: Which compound has the greater lattice energy, and why: NaF or NaI?
o: NaI, because iodide has more electrons
More electrons make I⁻ bigger, and a bigger ion weakens the attraction.
NaI, because I⁻ is more polarizable
Polarizability affects dispersion forces, not the charge-and-distance attraction here.
NaF, because the smaller F⁻ lets the ions get closer
Correct: smaller F⁻ means a shorter distance between ions and a stronger pull.
They are equal, because both ions have the same charges
Same charges, but different sizes change the distance between the ions.
questions.x: Lattice energy is the energy released when separate ions come together into a solid crystal. It follows Coulomb's law: attraction ∝ (q₁ × q₂) ÷ r, where q is each ion's charge and r is the distance between their centers. NaF and NaI both have a +1 ion and a −1 ion, so the top of the fraction is the same. That leaves r. F⁻ is much smaller than I⁻, so Na⁺ and F⁻ sit closer together. A smaller r means a bigger attraction, so NaF has the greater lattice energy and a higher melting point.

questions.q: Why are ionic crystals brittle, shattering when struck?
o: Their covalent bonds are weak
Ionic crystals are held together by ionic attractions, not covalent bonds.
Electrons flow away from the impact site
Ionic solids have no electrons free to move.
Ions are only weakly attracted to each other
Ionic attractions are strong, which is why ionic solids melt at high temperatures.
Shifting a layer puts like charges side by side
Correct: shifting a layer lines up like charges, which repel and split the crystal.
questions.note: Contrast: metals deform because their electron sea moves with the ions.
questions.x: In an ionic crystal, positive and negative ions alternate like a checkerboard, so every ion is surrounded by opposite charges. That's stable and strong. But hit the crystal hard enough to slide one layer over by half a step, and suddenly positive ions sit next to positive ions and negative next to negative. Like charges repel strongly, so the crystal splits apart along that plane. The attractions themselves are strong, which is why ionic solids have high melting points. The brittleness comes from that sudden repulsion, not from weak bonds.

questions.q: Which bond has the greatest ionic character?
o: Cs–F
Correct: the least electronegative metal with the most electronegative element gives the biggest gap.
Li–I
Li is more electronegative than Cs and I less than F, so the gap is smaller.
Na–Cl
Ionic, but its electronegativity gap is smaller than Cs–F's.
Be–Cl
Small Be²⁺ pulls on chloride's electrons, so Be–Cl is mostly covalent.
questions.x: Electronegativity is how strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons. The bigger the difference between two atoms, the more one atom hogs the electrons, and the more ionic the bond. Fluorine is the most electronegative element (about 4.0), and cesium is one of the least (about 0.8). Their difference is about 4.0 − 0.8 = 3.2, the biggest here. Na–Cl is ionic too, but its difference is smaller, about 2.2. Small cations like Li⁺ and Be²⁺ pull on the anion's electron cloud, which gives Li–I and Be–Cl a lot of covalent character.

questions.q: Butane and 2-methylpropane (isobutane), both C₄H₁₀, are best described as:
o: Enantiomers
Enantiomers are mirror images with the same connections. These two connect differently.
Diastereomers
Diastereomers are stereoisomers, so they share the same connections. These don't.
Conformers
Conformers just rotate around single bonds. These would need bonds broken.
Constitutional (structural) isomers
Correct: same formula, but the atoms are connected in a different order.
questions.x: Isomers are molecules with the same formula. Butane is four carbons in a straight chain. Isobutane is three carbons in a row with a fourth carbon branching off the middle one. Both are C₄H₁₀, but their atoms are connected in a different order, so they're constitutional (structural) isomers. Stereoisomers, which include enantiomers and diastereomers, keep the same connections and differ only in 3-D arrangement. Conformers are just one molecule twisted around a single bond. To turn butane into isobutane you'd have to break and remake bonds.

questions.q: Which method can separate a racemic mixture into its two enantiomers?
o: Simple distillation
Enantiomers have the same boiling point, so distillation can't split them.
Extraction with water
Enantiomers dissolve the same way in a non-chiral solvent like water.
Reaction with a single enantiomer of a chiral acid, then crystallization
Correct: this makes diastereomeric salts, which have different solubilities.
Standard silica gel chromatography
Plain silica isn't chiral, so it treats both enantiomers the same.
questions.note: Resolution converts enantiomers into separable diastereomers.
questions.x: A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of two enantiomers, mirror-image molecules. In an ordinary, non-chiral setting, enantiomers have the same boiling point, solubility and everything else, so distillation, extraction and regular chromatography can't tell them apart. The trick is to react the mixture with one pure enantiomer of a chiral acid (or base). The two products are now diastereomers: stereoisomers that aren't mirror images. Diastereomers do have different properties, like solubility, so one crystallizes out first. Then you remove the added acid to get each enantiomer back.

questions.q: A pure enantiomer has specific rotation +20°. A mixture of it and its enantiomer has specific rotation +6°. What percentage of the mixture is the (+) enantiomer?
o: 30% is the enantiomeric excess, not the total share of (+).
70% is the racemic (50:50) part of the mixture.
35% is the share of the (−) enantiomer.
questions.note: ee = observed ÷ pure rotation; major = ee + (100 − ee)/2.
questions.x: Enantiomeric excess (ee) is how much extra of one enantiomer there is beyond a 50:50 mix. The formula is ee = observed rotation ÷ rotation of the pure enantiomer. Here, observed = +6° and pure = +20°, so ee = 6 ÷ 20 = 0.30 = 30%. That 30% is all (+). The other 100% − 30% = 70% is a 50:50 mix, so it splits into 70 ÷ 2 = 35% (+) and 35% (−). Total (+) = 30% + 35% = 65%. Stopping at 30% gives the excess, not the actual share of (+).

questions.q: Diethyl ether (density 0.71 g/mL) is shaken with water in a separatory funnel. Where is the ether layer?
o: On top, because it is less dense than water
Correct: layers stack by density, and ether (0.71 g/mL) is lighter than water (1.00 g/mL).
On the bottom, because organic layers always sink
Organic layers sink only if they're denser than water, like dichloromethane. Ether is lighter.
On top, because it is more polar than water
Density decides the layer, not polarity. And ether is less polar than water, not more.
Mixed evenly through the water as one phase
Ether and water barely mix, so they form two separate layers.
questions.x: A separatory funnel holds two liquids that don't mix (they're immiscible), so they form two layers. Which one ends up on top depends only on density, the mass in each mL. The less dense liquid floats. Diethyl ether is 0.71 g/mL and water is 1.00 g/mL, so ether is lighter and sits on top. Polarity decides whether two liquids mix, not which one floats. Plenty of organic solvents float on water (ether, hexane, ethyl acetate), but chlorine-containing ones like dichloromethane sink.

questions.q: A product is extracted from water into dichloromethane (density 1.33 g/mL). Which layer should be drained and kept?
o: The top layer, which is the organic phase
Dichloromethane (1.33 g/mL) is denser than water, so the organic layer is on the bottom, not the top.
The bottom layer, which is the aqueous phase
Water (1.00 g/mL) is lighter than dichloromethane, so the water layer is on top, not the bottom.
Either layer, since the product splits evenly
A neutral organic product moves mostly into the organic layer, not half and half.
The bottom layer, which is the organic phase
Correct: dichloromethane is denser than water, so the organic layer with the product is on the bottom.
questions.note: Trap: halogenated solvents like CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃ sink below water.
questions.x: In an extraction, a neutral organic product moves into the organic solvent, so you want to keep the organic layer. Now find where it is. The layers stack by density, and dichloromethane is 1.33 g/mL while water is 1.00 g/mL. Dichloromethane is denser, so the organic layer is on the bottom, and you drain it out through the tap. The common mistake is assuming organic layers always float. That's only true for solvents lighter than water, like ether. Solvents with chlorine in them, like CH₂Cl₂ and CHCl₃, sink.

questions.q: An ether solution contains p-cresol (a phenol, pKₐ ≈ 10) and naphthalene. Which aqueous wash moves p-cresol into the water layer?
o: Saturated NaHCO₃
Bicarbonate's conjugate acid has pKₐ ≈ 6.4, below the phenol's 10, so it's too weak a base.
1 M NaOH
Correct: hydroxide pulls off the phenol's H⁺, making a charged phenoxide that dissolves in water.
1 M HCl
Acid keeps the phenol neutral, so it stays in the ether.
Saturated NaCl
Brine pulls water out of the organic layer. It doesn't react with the phenol.
questions.note: NaHCO₃ removes carboxylic acids only; NaOH removes carboxylic acids and phenols.
questions.x: Neutral molecules stay in the ether, and charged ones (ions) dissolve in water. To move p-cresol into water, you need a base strong enough to pull off its H⁺ and turn it into a charged ion. The rule: the base works if its conjugate acid (the base after it picks up H⁺) has a higher pKₐ than the acid you're removing. Hydroxide's conjugate acid is water, pKₐ about 15.7, which is higher than the phenol's 10, so NaOH works. Bicarbonate's conjugate acid has a pKₐ of about 6.4, lower than 10, so it's too weak.
