questions.q: In the sequence NaHCO₃ wash then NaOH wash of an ether solution of benzoic acid, 2-naphthol and naphthalene, what is in the NaOH extract?
o: Benzoic acid as sodium benzoate
The earlier bicarbonate wash already removed the benzoic acid.
Naphthalene
Naphthalene has no acidic H, so it stays in the ether.
2-Naphthol as its sodium salt
Correct: bicarbonate already took the carboxylic acid, so NaOH takes only the phenol.
Both benzoate and naphthoxide
Both would come out together only if NaOH were used first.
questions.note: Use the weaker base first to separate a carboxylic acid from a phenol.
questions.x: Washing with bases in order of strength sorts acids by pKₐ. The first wash, NaHCO₃, is a weak base. It's strong enough to remove a carboxylic acid (pKₐ about 4 to 5) but not a phenol (pKₐ about 10). So it pulls out only the benzoic acid, as sodium benzoate. The second wash, NaOH, is a strong base, and the only acid left is 2-naphthol, a phenol. NaOH turns it into sodium naphthoxide, which goes into the water. Naphthalene has no acidic H, so it stays in the ether the whole time.

questions.q: For a fixed total volume of extracting solvent, which approach recovers the most solute from water?
o: One extraction with the whole volume
One big extraction leaves more solute behind than several small ones.
Either approach, since total solvent volume is equal
Same total volume doesn't mean the same recovery. Splitting it pulls out more.
One extraction followed by heating the funnel
Heating a closed funnel of volatile solvent is dangerous and doesn't help.
Several extractions with smaller portions
Correct: each fresh portion removes a fraction of what's left, so repeating it wins.
questions.x: Each time you shake water with fresh solvent, the same fraction of whatever solute is still in the water moves over. With several small portions, that happens again and again, and the leftover keeps shrinking by that fraction each time. One big portion only gets one try. So for the same total volume, several smaller extractions pull out more. It's like a sale that takes a third off, then a third off the new price: the price keeps dropping with every round. Recovery gets closer and closer to 100% but never quite reaches it.

questions.q: A solute has a partition coefficient K = [organic]/[water] = 4. A solution of 1.0 g of it in 100 mL of water is extracted twice with 50 mL organic portions. About how much is extracted in total?
o: This is only the first 50 mL pass: 1 − 1/3 = 2/3 ≈ 0.67 g.
This is one 100 mL pass. Two 50 mL passes pull out more.
Correct: each pass leaves 1/3, so 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9 stays and 8/9 ≈ 0.89 g comes out.
Some solute always stays behind after a limited number of extractions.
questions.x: Use the formula for the fraction left in the water after one extraction: fraction left = Vaq ÷ (Vaq + K × Vorg). The values are Vaq = 100 mL of water, K = 4, and Vorg = 50 mL of solvent per pass. Plug in: 100 ÷ (100 + 4 × 50) = 100 ÷ (100 + 200) = 100 ÷ 300 = 1/3. Two passes leave 1/3 × 1/3 = 1/9 of the solute behind. So the amount extracted is 1 − 1/9 = 8/9 of 1.0 g, about 0.89 g. That beats the 0.80 g from one 100 mL pass.

questions.q: How does a fractionating column improve separation compared with simple distillation?
o: It raises the boiling point of the less volatile component further
A column can't change a compound's boiling point.
It cools the vapor so it condenses faster
Cooling the vapor into liquid is the condenser's job, not the column's.
It filters nonvolatile impurities from the vapor
Nonvolatile impurities never boil off, so there's nothing for the column to filter.
It provides many successive vaporization–condensation cycles
Correct: each boil-and-condense cycle makes the vapor richer in the lower-boiling liquid.
questions.x: In simple distillation, the liquid boils once and the vapor condenses once. A fractionating column is a tube packed with beads or metal that sits between the flask and the condenser. Rising vapor condenses on that packing, then boils again, over and over on its way up. Each cycle works like another small distillation, called a theoretical plate, and each one makes the vapor a little richer in the lower-boiling liquid. The column doesn't change anyone's boiling point; it just repeats the separation many times.

questions.q: A compound boils at 280 °C at 1 atm but decomposes near 250 °C. Why is vacuum distillation used to purify it?
o: The vacuum raises its vapor pressure at every temperature
At a given temperature, vapor pressure belongs to the liquid. A vacuum doesn't change it.
The vacuum removes oxygen, which is the only cause of decomposition
Heat alone can break a compound down, even without oxygen. The real fix is a lower temperature.
Lowering the pressure lowers its boiling point below the decomposition temperature
Correct: less outside pressure means the liquid boils at a lower temperature, below 250 °C.
Reduced pressure increases the difference between boiling points
The goal is a lower boiling temperature, not a bigger gap between boiling points.
questions.x: A liquid boils when its vapor pressure, its push to escape as gas, equals the pressure of the air around it. At 1 atm, this compound doesn't reach that point until 280 °C, but it falls apart near 250 °C. A vacuum lowers the outside pressure, so the compound's vapor pressure matches it at a lower temperature. That lets it boil, and be distilled, below 250 °C, before it decomposes. The vacuum doesn't change the compound's vapor pressure at any given temperature; it lowers the pressure the vapor has to match.

questions.q: Fractional distillation of dilute aqueous ethanol stops enriching at about 95.6% ethanol no matter how efficient the column. Why?
o: Ethanol and water have identical boiling points
Ethanol boils at 78 °C and water at 100 °C, so they're different.
The mixture forms an azeotrope whose vapor and liquid have the same composition
Correct: at the azeotrope, the vapor matches the liquid, so distilling can't enrich it further.
The column runs out of theoretical plates
Even unlimited plates can't get past an azeotrope.
Water reacts with ethanol at its boiling point
Ethanol and water don't react. The limit comes from how the mixture boils.
questions.x: Ethanol and water form an azeotrope at about 95.6% ethanol. An azeotrope is a mixture whose vapor has exactly the same makeup as the liquid it boiled from. Distillation only works because the vapor is usually richer in one liquid than the boiling mixture is. At the azeotrope, the vapor matches the liquid, so boiling and condensing again changes nothing. That's why even a perfect column stalls at 95.6%. Getting past it takes a different trick, like a drying agent or adding a third substance.

questions.q: An ideal 50:50 (mole) liquid mixture has P°A = 300 torr and P°B = 100 torr. What is the mole fraction of A in the vapor?
o: 0.50 is the liquid. The vapor has more of A, the liquid that evaporates more easily.
This uses 300 ÷ (300 + 150). Use the partial pressures: 150 ÷ (150 + 50).
Too high. Raoult's law gives 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75, not 0.90.
questions.note: Raoult's law: Pᵢ = xᵢP°ᵢ, then yᵢ = Pᵢ/P(total).
questions.x: Use Raoult's law for each liquid: P = x × P°, where x is its mole fraction in the liquid and P° is its vapor pressure when pure. The values are x = 0.5 for each, P°A = 300 torr and P°B = 100 torr. So PA = 0.5 × 300 = 150 torr and PB = 0.5 × 100 = 50 torr. The total is 150 + 50 = 200 torr. A's share of the vapor is yA = PA ÷ Ptotal = 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75. The vapor is richer in A than the 50:50 liquid because A evaporates more easily.

questions.q: During fractional distillation of a two-liquid mixture, the head temperature holds steady, then rises sharply before leveling off again. What does the sharp rise indicate?
o: The column has flooded and must be emptied
Flooding messes up the flow. It doesn't cause a clean jump from one steady level to another.
An azeotrope has formed in the pot
An azeotrope boils at one steady temperature. It wouldn't cause a jump.
The higher-boiling component is decomposing
A clean rise to a new steady level isn't a sign of something breaking down.
The lower-boiling component has largely distilled over
Correct: once the lower-boiling liquid runs out, the temperature climbs to the next boiling point.
questions.note: Change receivers during the temperature jump to keep fractions pure.
questions.x: The thermometer at the top of the column (the head) reads the temperature of the vapor that's distilling. While one liquid is distilling, the reading holds steady at that liquid's boiling point; that flat stretch is called a plateau. When the lower-boiling liquid is mostly used up, nothing is left to hold the temperature there, so it climbs until the higher-boiling liquid starts to distill, and then it levels off again. That jump is normal. It's the moment to switch to a fresh collection flask so each fraction stays pure.

questions.q: A hot recrystallization solution contains insoluble dust particles. What should be done next?
o: Cool the solution in ice first, then vacuum-filter the cold mixture
Cooling first means the dust gets collected along with the crystals.
Add more solvent until the dust dissolves
Dust won't dissolve, and extra solvent just lowers how many crystals you get back.
Gravity-filter the solution while hot, then cool the filtrate
Correct: filter the hot solution to catch the dust while the product stays dissolved.
Add activated charcoal to dissolve the dust
Charcoal soaks up colored impurities. It doesn't dissolve dust.
questions.x: In recrystallization, you dissolve a solid in hot solvent and then cool it so pure crystals form. Dust doesn't dissolve, so you have to get it out while the solution is still hot and your product is still dissolved. Pour it through fluted (pleated) filter paper using gravity. The dust stays on the paper and the product passes through. Then cool the liquid that came through so the crystals form. Vacuum filtration isn't used at this step, because suction cools the solution and crystals would form early inside the funnel.

questions.q: Compound X dissolves to 20 g/100 mL at 80 °C and 2 g/100 mL at 0 °C. If 10 g of X is dissolved in 50 mL of hot solvent and cooled to 0 °C, what is the maximum recovery?
o: 8 g
This subtracts 2 g. At 2 g per 100 mL, 50 mL holds only 1 g.
9 g
Correct: 50 mL holds 2 × 50 ÷ 100 = 1 g cold, so 10 − 1 = 9 g crystallizes.
Some X always stays dissolved in the cold solvent.
5 g
This just halves the mass and ignores the solubility numbers.
questions.x: Whatever stays dissolved in the cold solvent is lost, so: recovered = mass used − mass that stays dissolved cold. Values: 10 g of X, 50 mL of solvent, and cold solubility of 2 g per 100 mL. The cold solubility is given per 100 mL, but you have 50 mL, which is half as much, so it holds 2 × 50 ÷ 100 = 1 g. Plug in: recovered = 10 − 1 = 9 g. First check it all dissolves hot: at 20 g per 100 mL, 50 mL holds 20 × 50 ÷ 100 = 10 g, so yes.

questions.q: Purified crystals are usually collected after recrystallization by:
o: Simple distillation
Distillation separates liquids by how easily they boil. It doesn't collect solids.
Vacuum filtration with a Büchner funnel
Correct: suction quickly pulls off the leftover liquid and partly dries the crystals.
Gravity filtration through fluted paper
Gravity filtration is slow. It's used for hot solutions or when the liquid is what you want.
Liquid–liquid extraction
Extraction moves dissolved substances between two liquids. It doesn't collect solids.
questions.x: When the crystals are your product, you collect them by vacuum filtration through a Büchner funnel. Suction pulls the leftover liquid, called the mother liquor, through the filter fast and leaves the crystals behind. It also pulls air through the crystals, which helps dry them. Then you rinse them with a little ice-cold solvent. Gravity filtration is slower, and it's used when you want the liquid, or when the solution has to stay hot, like when removing dust before crystallizing.

questions.q: An alcohol (Rf 0.25 on silica) is oxidized to a ketone. After 1 hour, the reaction lane shows spots at Rf 0.25 and 0.55. What is the best interpretation?
o: The reaction is complete, and the ketone is the lower spot
The lower spot matches the starting alcohol, not the ketone.
The reaction is incomplete, and the less polar ketone is the upper spot
Correct: the ketone has no O–H and runs higher; leftover alcohol stays at 0.25.
The ketone is more polar than the alcohol and runs at 0.25
Losing the O–H makes the ketone less polar, so it runs higher, not lower.
Two side products formed and no starting material remains
The spot at 0.25 matches the starting alcohol, so some is still there.
questions.x: On TLC (thin-layer chromatography), Rf is how far a spot travels compared with the solvent. Silica, the plate coating, is polar, so polar compounds stick to it and travel less, giving a lower Rf. An alcohol has an O–H that hydrogen bonds to the silica. The ketone product has a C=O but no O–H, so it sticks less and travels farther: it's the new spot at 0.55. The spot still at 0.25 sits exactly where the starting alcohol ran, so some alcohol hasn't reacted yet. The reaction isn't finished.

questions.q: An unknown and an authentic sample give identical Rf values in one solvent system. What is the best additional evidence that they are the same compound?
o: Rerunning both in the same eluent again gives the same Rf value
Repeating the same conditions just repeats the same match. It can't rule out a coincidence.
Both spots appear under UV light
Lots of different compounds show up under UV light.
Both spots have the same size
Spot size depends on how much you put on, not what the compound is.
A co-spot gives a single spot in a second, different eluent
Correct: one spot in a co-spot, in a second solvent, rules out a chance match.
questions.x: Two different compounds can land on the same Rf in one solvent just by chance, so one match isn't strong proof. A co-spot means putting the unknown and the known sample on top of each other in the same lane. If they're different compounds, you usually see two spots or one stretched-out spot. If they still give one clean spot, and they do so again in a second, different solvent (eluent), a coincidence becomes very unlikely. Repeating the same test, checking UV, or comparing spot size can't rule out a chance match.

questions.q: On silica TLC, a target compound has Rf 0.00 in pure hexane and 0.95 in pure ethyl acetate. What is the best eluent for column purification?
o: Pure hexane
At Rf 0 the compound would never leave the column.
Pure ethyl acetate
At Rf 0.95 it would race through with the solvent and barely separate.
A hexane/ethyl acetate mixture giving the target Rf ≈ 0.3
Correct: a mix tuned to Rf ≈ 0.3 holds the compound enough to separate it, but still lets it out.
Water
Water isn't used on silica columns and would ruin the silica's grip.
questions.x: The eluent is the solvent you pour through a column to carry compounds down it. You pick it with TLC first, and a good choice gives your compound an Rf of about 0.2 to 0.4. At Rf 0 in pure hexane, the compound would stick at the top of the column and never come out. At Rf 0.95 in pure ethyl acetate, it would rush through with the solvent and come out mixed with everything else. A blend of the two gives an in-between push, so you can tune it to an Rf near 0.3.

questions.q: A carboxylic acid (pKₐ 4.5) is analyzed by reverse-phase HPLC. The mobile phase pH is lowered from 7 to 2.5. What happens to its retention time?
o: It decreases, because the acid becomes ionized
At pH 2.5 the acid is mostly neutral, not ionized. It was ionized at pH 7.
It increases, because the neutral acid binds the C18 phase more strongly
Correct: below its pKₐ the acid is mostly neutral and oilier, so it clings to C18 longer.
It is unchanged, because pH does not affect reverse phase
pH changes the acid's charge, and charge strongly affects how long it's held.
It decreases, because the C18 phase becomes charged
C18 chains are just carbon and hydrogen, so they can't pick up a charge.
questions.note: Neutral forms are retained longer in reverse phase than ionized forms.
questions.x: In reverse-phase HPLC, the column is coated with C18, long oily carbon chains, and the liquid flowing through is polar. Oily, neutral molecules cling to the C18 and come out late. Charged molecules prefer the polar liquid and come out early. Use Henderson–Hasselbalch: [A⁻]/[HA] = 10 raised to the power of (pH − pKₐ). At pH 2.5, pH − pKₐ = 2.5 − 4.5 = −2, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 10⁻² = 1/100. About 99% of the acid is neutral RCOOH. At pH 7 it was mostly charged RCOO⁻. Now it clings longer, so its retention time goes up.

questions.q: A protein runs as a single 50 kDa band on SDS-PAGE but elutes from a calibrated gel filtration column at about 200 kDa. What is the best interpretation?
o: The protein is degraded during gel filtration
Breaking down would make it look smaller, not bigger.
SDS adds 150 kDa of mass to the protein
SDS adds charge, not 150 kDa of mass. And gel filtration is run without SDS.
The native protein is a tetramer of identical subunits
Correct: SDS-PAGE shows one subunit and gel filtration shows the whole complex, 200 ÷ 50 = 4.
The protein is a monomer held together by four disulfide bonds
Disulfide bonds inside one chain can't make it four times heavier.
questions.x: The two methods measure different things. SDS-PAGE uses a detergent (SDS) that unfolds the protein and pulls apart any subunits that are only stuck together, not bonded, so it shows the mass of one chain: 50 kDa. Gel filtration keeps the protein folded and intact, so it measures the whole working protein: about 200 kDa. Divide to find how many chains are in the complex: number of subunits = 200 ÷ 50 = 4. So the native protein is a tetramer, four identical 50 kDa subunits.

questions.q: Proteins with pI 4.5, 6.5 and 9.0 are loaded onto a DEAE (anion-exchange) column at pH 7.5. Which protein flows through without binding?
o: The protein with pI 9.0
Correct: pH 7.5 is below its pI, so it's positive and the positive DEAE beads push it away.
The protein with pI 4.5
pH 7.5 is well above its pI, so it's strongly negative and sticks tightly.
The protein with pI 6.5
pH 7.5 is above its pI, so it's a little negative and sticks.
None of them binds the column
Proteins with a pI below 7.5 are negative at this pH, so they stick to DEAE.
questions.x: The pI is the pH at which a protein has no overall charge. If the buffer pH is above a protein's pI, the protein is negative. If it's below, the protein is positive. DEAE is an anion exchanger: its beads carry positive charges, so they grab negative proteins. At pH 7.5, the proteins with pI 4.5 and 6.5 are below the buffer pH, so they're negative and stick. The protein with pI 9.0 is above the buffer pH, so it's positive. The positive beads push it away, and it flows straight through.

questions.q: Proteins with pI 4.5 and 6.5 are bound to DEAE at pH 7.5 and eluted with an increasing NaCl gradient. Which elutes last?
o: The protein with pI 6.5
It's less negative at pH 7.5, so it lets go with less salt and comes out first.
Both elute together
Different overall charges mean different grip, so they come off at different salt levels.
The protein with pI 4.5
Correct: it's more negative at pH 7.5, so it grips tighter and needs the most salt.
Neither elutes with salt
Salt competes for the charged spots on the beads, so it does push bound proteins off.
questions.x: On an anion exchanger, the positive beads hold negative proteins. To release them, you add more and more salt (NaCl). The chloride ions, Cl⁻, compete with the proteins for the positive spots and push them off. A more negative protein holds on tighter, so it takes more salt to push it off, and it comes out later. At pH 7.5, the protein with pI 4.5 is 7.5 − 4.5 = 3 units above its pI, while the pI 6.5 protein is only 7.5 − 6.5 = 1 unit above. The pI 4.5 protein is more negative, so it comes out last.

questions.q: Uncut plasmid DNA shows three bands: supercoiled, nicked circular and linear forms of the same length. Which form typically migrates fastest?
o: Supercoiled
Correct: its tightly twisted, compact shape slips through the gel most easily.
Nicked (relaxed) circular
The open, floppy loop drags the most and is usually slowest.
Linear
Linear DNA usually runs between the supercoiled and nicked forms.
All migrate equally, since they have equal mass
Same mass doesn't mean same speed. Shape changes how easily DNA moves through the gel.
questions.x: In gel electrophoresis, DNA is negative and gets pulled through a gel toward the positive end. The gel is a mesh, so compact molecules slip through more easily. All three plasmid forms are the same length, so they have the same mass and charge, and only their shape differs. Supercoiled DNA is twisted tightly on itself into a compact bundle, so it usually moves fastest. Nicked circular DNA has a cut in one strand, which lets it relax into a big, floppy loop that drags the most and moves slowest. Linear DNA usually runs in between.

questions.q: On an agarose gel, a 1000 bp marker runs 4 cm and a 100 bp marker runs 8 cm. Migration distance is linear in log(size). About how large is a fragment that runs 6 cm?
o: 550 bp
This averages the sizes, (100 + 1000) ÷ 2 = 550. Distance follows log(size), not size.
300 bp
Correct: halfway in log terms is log(size) = 2.5, and 10 to the power of 2.5 ≈ 316, about 300 bp.
200 bp
Too small. The log halfway point between 100 and 1000 is about 316.
750 bp
Too close to 1000. The fragment sits halfway, which on a log scale is about 316.
questions.note: Use log(size) vs distance for gel standards.
questions.x: On a gel, distance moved goes in a straight line with log(size), not with size. Values: 1000 bp at 4 cm, and log(1000) = 3 because 1000 = 10³. 100 bp at 8 cm, and log(100) = 2. The fragment at 6 cm is exactly halfway between 4 and 8 cm, so its log(size) is halfway between 3 and 2: (3 + 2) ÷ 2 = 2.5. So the size is 10 to the power of 2.5, which is 10² × √10. √10 is about 3.16, so the size is about 100 × 3.16 ≈ 316, about 300 bp. Averaging the sizes instead gives 550 bp, which is wrong.

questions.q: An antibody runs at about 150 kDa on nonreducing SDS-PAGE but gives bands at about 50 and 25 kDa when β-mercaptoethanol is added. What explains this?
o: SDS breaks peptide bonds under reducing conditions
Neither SDS nor β-mercaptoethanol breaks peptide bonds.
The chains are held by noncovalent forces only
If only weak forces held the chains, SDS alone would have split them.
β-Mercaptoethanol removes the carbohydrate chains from the antibody
β-Mercaptoethanol breaks disulfide bonds. It doesn't remove sugars.
Heavy and light chains are held together by disulfide bonds
Correct: the reducing agent breaks the S–S links, freeing 50 kDa heavy and 25 kDa light chains.
questions.x: SDS breaks apart proteins held together by weak, non-covalent forces, but it can't break covalent bonds. A disulfide bond (an S–S link between two cysteines) is covalent, so it survives SDS. β-Mercaptoethanol is a reducing agent: it breaks disulfide bonds. An IgG antibody is two heavy chains and two light chains linked by disulfides. Without β-mercaptoethanol, it stays whole at about 150 kDa. With it, the links break and you see heavy chains (about 50 kDa) and light chains (about 25 kDa). Check: 2 × 50 + 2 × 25 = 100 + 50 = 150 kDa.

questions.q: Two globular proteins of 60 kDa have pI values of 5.0 and 6.5. They are run on native PAGE at pH 8.8 toward the anode. Which migrates farther?
o: The protein with pI 6.5
It's only 2.3 units above its pI, so it's less negative and moves slower.
The protein with pI 5.0
Correct: it's 3.8 units above its pI, so it's more negative and moves faster.
Both migrate equally, since they have equal mass
In native PAGE, charge and shape matter, not just mass.
Neither enters the gel
Both are negative at pH 8.8, so both move into the gel toward the anode.
questions.x: Native PAGE runs proteins without SDS, so they keep their folded shape and their own natural charge. Their speed depends on that charge plus their size and shape. A protein is negative when the buffer pH is above its pI, and the farther above, the more negative it is. At pH 8.8, the pI 5.0 protein is 8.8 − 5.0 = 3.8 units above its pI, and the pI 6.5 protein is 8.8 − 6.5 = 2.3 units above. Both are negative and head for the positive end (the anode), but the pI 5.0 protein carries more charge, so with the same mass it moves farther.

questions.q: Two forms of a protein differ only by a single phosphate group. In 2D gel electrophoresis (IEF then SDS-PAGE), how are they best distinguished?
o: By a shift in the IEF dimension toward lower pI
Correct: the negative phosphate lowers the pI, while the tiny mass change is too small to see.
By a large shift in the SDS-PAGE (mass) dimension
A phosphate adds only about 80 Da, far too little to shift a protein on SDS-PAGE.
By a shift toward higher pI
A negative group lowers the pI, not raises it.
They cannot be separated in 2D gels
IEF separates forms that differ in charge, including phosphorylated ones.
questions.x: A 2D gel separates proteins two ways. First, isoelectric focusing (IEF) sorts them by pI, the pH at which a protein has no overall charge. Then SDS-PAGE sorts them by mass. A phosphate group carries negative charge, so adding one lowers the protein's pI, and the phosphorylated form settles at a slightly more acidic spot in the IEF direction. But a phosphate adds only about 80 Da, which is tiny next to a protein's tens of thousands of daltons, so SDS-PAGE can't see the difference. The two forms show up side by side, at the same height but shifted in pI.

questions.q: Glycine (pI ≈ 6.0) is placed in an electric field in a buffer at pH 3. Which way does it migrate?
o: Toward the anode
Glycine goes to the anode only above its pI, where it's negative.
It does not move
It stays still only when the pH equals its pI, 6.0.
It splits evenly toward both electrodes
H⁺ hops on and off so fast that every molecule carries the same average charge, so they all move together.
Toward the cathode
Correct: below its pI, glycine is positive on average, so it moves to the negative electrode.
questions.x: The pI is the pH at which an amino acid has no overall charge. Below its pI, there are extra H⁺ around, so the amino acid holds onto more of them and ends up positive. At pH 3, glycine's amino group is NH₃⁺, and some of its carboxyl groups still have their H (COOH), so the average charge is positive. In an electric field, a positive molecule moves toward the negative electrode, the cathode. Glycine would move toward the anode only above pH 6.0, and stay still at exactly pH 6.0.

questions.q: A mixture of aspartate (pI 2.8), glycine (pI 6.0) and lysine (pI 9.7) undergoes electrophoresis at pH 6.0. What happens?
o: All three move to the anode
At pH 6.0, lysine is positive and glycine has no overall charge.
Aspartate moves to the anode, glycine stays, lysine moves to the cathode
Correct: aspartate is negative, glycine is neutral, and lysine is positive at pH 6.0.
Lysine moves to the anode and aspartate to the cathode
This flips the charges. Lysine is positive and aspartate is negative here.
None move, since all are zwitterions
Only glycine has zero overall charge at pH 6.0.
questions.x: Compare the buffer pH with each pI. If the pH is above a molecule's pI, it's negative and moves to the anode (the positive electrode). If the pH is below its pI, it's positive and moves to the cathode (the negative electrode). If they're equal, it has no overall charge and stays put. At pH 6.0: aspartate (pI 2.8) is below the pH, so it's negative and goes to the anode. Glycine (pI 6.0) matches, so it stays. Lysine (pI 9.7) is above the pH, so it's positive and goes to the cathode.

questions.q: In rate-zonal centrifugation through a sucrose gradient, particles separate according to sedimentation rate. Why is the run stopped before completion?
o: Sucrose crystallizes if the run continues
Sucrose stays dissolved the whole time.
Particles would reverse direction at equilibrium
Particles denser than the gradient keep sinking. They don't turn around.
Longer runs denature all proteins
The time limit keeps the bands apart. It isn't about damaging proteins.
Given enough time, all particles would reach the bottom and the separation would be lost
Correct: if you waited, everything would reach the bottom together and the separation would be lost.
questions.x: In rate-zonal centrifugation, you layer a sample on top of a sucrose gradient (a solution that gets denser toward the bottom) and spin it. Particles sink at different speeds depending on their size and shape, so they spread out into separate bands. But the gradient isn't dense enough to stop them. If you kept spinning, every particle would eventually reach the bottom and pile up together, and the separation would be gone. So you stop the run partway, while the bands are still apart. It's a race you photograph before anyone finishes.

questions.q: How does adding a high concentration of ammonium sulfate precipitate proteins?
o: Sulfate covalently cross-links proteins
Salting out is reversible and doesn't form any covalent bonds.
Salt ions sequester water, reducing protein solvation
Correct: the salt ions grab the water, so proteins lose their water coat and clump.
It denatures proteins by reducing disulfides
Ammonium sulfate doesn't break disulfides and usually keeps proteins folded.
It shifts every protein's pI to the buffer pH
Salt doesn't change a protein's pI.
questions.x: Proteins stay dissolved because water molecules crowd around them. When you add lots of ammonium sulfate, its ions grab huge numbers of water molecules for themselves. That leaves less water to surround the proteins. Without their water coat, proteins stick to each other through their oily patches, clump together, and fall out of solution. This is called salting out. Different proteins fall out at different salt levels, so it can be used to separate them. It's gentle and reversible: add water back and the proteins dissolve again, still folded.

questions.q: A crude extract has 200 mg protein and 1000 units of enzyme activity. After a column step, 10 mg protein with 600 units remains. What is the fold purification?
o: This doesn't compare activity per mg. The specific activities are 5 and 60 units/mg.
Correct: specific activity goes from 1000 ÷ 200 = 5 to 600 ÷ 10 = 60 units/mg, and 60 ÷ 5 = 12.
200 ÷ 10 = 20 counts only the protein removed and ignores the lost activity.
600 ÷ 1000 = 0.6 is the yield, the share of activity kept, not the purification.
questions.note: Fold purification = new specific activity / original specific activity.
questions.x: Fold purification compares specific activity before and after a step. Specific activity (SA) = units of enzyme activity ÷ mg of total protein, and fold purification = SA after ÷ SA before. Before: 1000 units and 200 mg, so SA = 1000 ÷ 200 = 5 units/mg. After: 600 units and 10 mg, so SA = 600 ÷ 10 = 60 units/mg. Plug in: fold purification = 60 ÷ 5 = 12. The protein dropped 20-fold, but some enzyme was lost too (only 600 of 1000 units kept), so the enzyme's purity rose 12-fold, not 20.

questions.q: Why is size-exclusion chromatography usually placed late in a protein purification scheme?
o: It accepts only small sample volumes, so it follows steps that concentrate the protein
Correct: it handles only small volumes and dilutes the sample, so it's a final polishing step.
It denatures proteins, so it must come last
Gel filtration is gentle and doesn't unfold proteins.
It removes salt, which must be present for earlier steps
It can remove salt, but that's not why it goes late.
It has the highest capacity of any method
Its capacity is low, not high.
questions.x: Size-exclusion chromatography, also called gel filtration, sorts proteins by size as they pass through a column of porous beads. It has a low capacity: you can only load a small volume, a few percent of the column's volume, and it spreads the protein out, making it more dilute. So it goes late in a purification, after high-capacity steps like ion exchange or affinity columns have removed most of the junk and concentrated the protein. It's gentle and doesn't unfold proteins, so that isn't the reason it comes last.

questions.q: His-tagged protein eluted from Ni²⁺–NTA shows a target band plus a few contaminants of different size. Which next step best removes them while keeping the protein native?
o: SDS-PAGE followed by gel extraction
SDS unfolds the protein, so it wouldn't stay native.
Size-exclusion chromatography
Correct: gel filtration separates by size and keeps the protein folded.
A second identical Ni²⁺–NTA column under the same conditions
Contaminants that stuck to the nickel column once will likely stick again.
Boiling the sample to precipitate contaminants
Boiling would likely unfold and clump the target protein too.
questions.x: The question asks for two things: remove contaminants that differ in size, and keep the protein native, meaning folded and working. Size-exclusion chromatography (gel filtration) does both. It separates proteins by size using a gentle buffer, so the target stays folded while the bigger or smaller contaminants come out at different times. Running the same Ni²⁺–NTA column again won't help, since those contaminants stuck to it once and will stick again. SDS-PAGE and boiling would both unfold the target.

questions.q: A racemic carboxylic acid is resolved by reacting it with an enantiomerically pure amine. Why does this allow separation?
o: It converts one enantiomer into the other
Making a salt doesn't flip any stereocenter.
It forms enantiomeric salts that have different boiling points
The salts aren't enantiomers. If they were, they couldn't be separated this way.
It destroys one enantiomer selectively
Both enantiomers react and form salts. Neither is destroyed.
It forms diastereomeric salts with different physical properties
Correct: the salts are diastereomers, which differ in solubility and can be separated by crystallization.
questions.x: Enantiomers are mirror-image molecules. In an ordinary, non-chiral setting they have the same solubility, melting point and boiling point, so you can't crystallize one away from the other. The trick is to react the racemic (50:50) acid with one pure enantiomer of a chiral amine, say the (R) form. The R-acid makes an (R,R) salt and the S-acid makes an (S,R) salt. Those two salts aren't mirror images of each other, so they're diastereomers, and diastereomers have different solubilities. One crystallizes first, and adding acid afterward gives back each pure enantiomer.

questions.q: A neutral organic product is contaminated with a carboxylic acid and an amine. Which wash sequence removes both impurities from the ether solution?
o: Two separate washes with dilute aqueous HCl
HCl pulls out the amine, but the carboxylic acid stays neutral and remains in the ether.
Two washes with brine
Brine dries the ether layer. It doesn't charge either impurity.
Aqueous NaHCO₃ only
Bicarbonate pulls out the acid, but the amine stays neutral and remains in the ether.
Dilute HCl, then aqueous NaHCO₃
Correct: HCl pulls the amine into water, then bicarbonate pulls the acid into water.
questions.x: Neutral molecules stay in the ether, and charged ones dissolve in water. So the plan is to make each impurity charged, one at a time. Dilute HCl gives the amine an H⁺, turning it into a charged ammonium ion (R–NH₃⁺) that moves into the water. Then NaHCO₃, a weak base, takes the H⁺ off the carboxylic acid, turning it into a charged carboxylate (R–COO⁻) that also moves into the water. The neutral product isn't changed by either wash, so it stays in the ether. Each wash only catches one kind of impurity, so you need both.

questions.q: A protein of interest precipitates between 40% and 60% ammonium sulfate saturation. Which procedure enriches it?
o: Bring to 60%, keep the supernatant
At 60% your protein has fallen out, so it's in the pellet, not the liquid.
Bring to 40%, discard the pellet, then bring the supernatant to 60% and keep the pellet
Correct: the 40% cut removes earlier-falling proteins, and the 60% cut collects yours.
Bring to 40%, keep the pellet
At 40% your protein is still dissolved, so it isn't in that pellet.
Bring to 100% and keep the pellet
At 100% nearly every protein falls out, so there's little enrichment.
questions.x: Salting out with ammonium sulfate makes proteins fall out of solution, and each protein falls out at its own salt level. Your protein falls out between 40% and 60%. So you make two cuts. First, bring the salt to 40%. Proteins that fall out below 40% form a pellet (the solid at the bottom after spinning), and you throw it away; your protein is still dissolved in the liquid on top, the supernatant. Then raise that liquid to 60%. Now your protein falls out, so you keep this second pellet. Going straight to 100% would bring down almost everything.

questions.q: How are (2R,3S)-2,3-dibromobutane and (2S,3R)-2,3-dibromobutane related?
o: They are one meso compound
Correct: the two ends match, so R,S and S,R are one meso molecule numbered from opposite ends.
They are enantiomers
Flipping both centers of a meso compound gives back the very same molecule, not a mirror twin.
They are a racemic pair
A racemic pair needs two chiral molecules. This one is meso, so it isn't chiral.
They are diastereomers
Diastereomers are different compounds. These two names describe one compound.
questions.note: Trap: R,S vs S,R are enantiomers only when the two ends differ.
questions.x: Flipping every stereocenter usually gives you the mirror-image twin (the enantiomer). The exception is a molecule that has a mirror plane running through its own middle. In 2,3-dibromobutane, both stereocenters (carbons with four different groups) carry the same set of groups: H, Br, CH₃ and the other CHBr. So the R,S form is symmetric, top half matching bottom half. A molecule like that is called meso: its mirror image is itself. (2R,3S) and (2S,3R) are the same molecule, just numbered starting from opposite ends.

questions.q: Which dimethylcyclohexane can adopt a chair conformation with both methyl groups equatorial?
o: trans-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane
Correct: trans-1,2 groups sit one up, one down, which matches both equatorial spots on neighboring carbons.
cis-1,2-Dimethylcyclohexane
Cis on neighboring carbons always leaves one group axial and one equatorial.
trans-1,3-Dimethylcyclohexane
At 1,3 the rule flips: cis is the both-equatorial isomer. Trans always keeps one axial.
cis-1,4-Dimethylcyclohexane
At 1,4, trans is the both-equatorial isomer. Cis always keeps one group axial.
questions.note: Di-equatorial: cis-1,3; trans-1,2 and trans-1,4.
questions.x: A chair-shaped ring has two kinds of spots on each carbon. Axial spots point straight up or down; equatorial spots point out to the side, where there's more room. Methyl groups want the roomy equatorial spots. On neighboring carbons, the two equatorial spots point one up and one down. Trans means the groups are on opposite faces of the ring (one up, one down), so trans-1,2 can put both methyls equatorial. The pattern flips at 1,3 (cis works) and flips back at 1,4 (trans works). Cis-1,2, trans-1,3 and cis-1,4 always leave one methyl axial.

questions.q: A racemic carboxylic acid is treated with an enantiopure (R)-amine to form salts. Why can these salts be separated by crystallization?
o: They are enantiomers that happen to have different solubilities
The salts aren't mirror images, so they're not enantiomers. Enantiomers would dissolve exactly the same.
The amine racemizes the acid
The amine doesn't change the acid's configuration. Scrambling it wouldn't help separate anything anyway.
They are diastereomers with different physical properties
Correct: (R,R) and (S,R) salts aren't mirror images, so they're diastereomers with different solubilities.
Only one enantiomer of the acid reacts
Both acids react and form salts. The point is that the two salts differ.
questions.note: Resolution works by turning enantiomers into diastereomers.
questions.x: Enantiomers (mirror-image twins) have the same solubility and melting point, so you can't pull them apart by crystallizing. The trick is to react the 50:50 mix of acids with an amine that is only one hand, here (R). The R acid gives an (R,R) salt and the S acid gives an (S,R) salt. Those two salts aren't mirror images of each other, so they're diastereomers, and diastereomers have different physical properties, including solubility. One salt crystallizes out first. Then you add strong acid to free the pure acid back up.

questions.q: Enantiopure (S)-3-bromo-3-methylhexane is heated in water. What best describes the alcohol formed?
o: An achiral meso alcohol
The alcohol has only one stereocenter. Meso needs at least two.
A nearly racemic mixture
Correct: SN1 goes through a flat carbocation that water attacks from both faces.
Pure (R)-alcohol by inversion
Clean inversion is the SN2 result. A crowded tertiary carbon can't be attacked from the back.
Pure (S)-alcohol by retention
Once the carbocation is flat, the original shape is gone, so retention can't be pure.
questions.x: A tertiary carbon (one bonded to three other carbons) heated in water reacts by SN1. In SN1 the bromide leaves first, leaving behind a carbocation, a carbon with a positive charge. That carbon is flat. Water can attack the flat carbon from the top face or the bottom face about equally, so you get both the R and S alcohols. The original (S) shape is lost and the product is nearly racemic, close to 50:50. Pure inversion would need SN2, and a crowded tertiary carbon blocks the backside attack SN2 needs.

questions.q: In DMSO, a polar aprotic solvent, which halide ion is the strongest nucleophile?
o: I⁻
I⁻ wins in protic solvents like water, where small anions get caged by hydrogen bonds. DMSO doesn't do that.
F⁻
Correct: with no hydrogen bonding, nucleophile strength follows basicity, and F⁻ is the strongest base here.
Cl⁻
Cl⁻ is a weaker base than F⁻, so it's a weaker nucleophile in DMSO.
Br⁻
Br⁻ is a weak base, so it ranks near the bottom once there's no hydrogen bonding.
questions.note: Trap: the halide nucleophilicity order reverses between protic and aprotic solvents.
questions.x: A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that attacks positive centers. In DMSO, a polar aprotic solvent, there's no O–H or N–H bond to hydrogen bond with anions. DMSO hugs the positive ions but leaves the negative ions free. With nothing holding them back, the halides rank by basicity, meaning how much they want to grab a proton: F⁻ > Cl⁻ > Br⁻ > I⁻. So F⁻ wins. The order you may remember with I⁻ on top is for protic solvents like water, where small ions like F⁻ get wrapped up in hydrogen bonds.

questions.q: Which atom of a carbonyl group is attacked by nucleophiles?
o: Neither; carbonyls are unreactive
Carbonyls are some of the most reactive groups in organic chemistry and biochemistry.
The α-carbon
The α-carbon becomes a nucleophile once deprotonated. It isn't the spot nucleophiles attack.
The oxygen, which carries a partial negative charge
The electron-rich oxygen is attacked by electron-poor species like H⁺, not by nucleophiles.
The carbon, which carries a partial positive charge
Correct: oxygen pulls electrons away, leaving the carbon slightly positive and open to attack.
questions.x: A carbonyl is a carbon double-bonded to an oxygen (C=O). Oxygen is more electronegative, which means it pulls shared electrons toward itself harder. That leaves oxygen slightly negative and carbon slightly positive. A nucleophile is an electron-rich species that goes after positive centers, so it attacks the carbon, and the extra electrons from the double bond move onto the oxygen. The oxygen reacts with electron-poor things like H⁺ instead. The α-carbon (the one next door) only becomes reactive toward electrophiles after it loses a proton to form an enolate.

questions.q: 2-Bromo-3-methylbutane is warmed in water. What is the major alcohol product?
o: 3-Methylbutan-2-ol
This skips the hydride shift that turns the secondary cation into a more stable tertiary one.
2-Methylbutan-2-ol
Correct: a hydride hops from C3 to C2, making a tertiary cation that water then attacks.
3-Methylbutan-1-ol
No step ever puts the positive charge, or the OH, on an end carbon.
2,2-Dimethylpropan-1-ol
This needs a different carbon skeleton. No shift here would make it.
questions.note: Carbocations rearrange toward greater substitution.
questions.x: Warming in water sets up SN1, so the bromide leaves first and leaves a positive charge on C2. A carbocation (positively charged carbon) is more stable when more carbons surround it: tertiary beats secondary. C2 is only secondary. Next door, C3 holds a methyl, so a hydrogen with its two electrons (a hydride) can hop from C3 to C2. Now the positive charge sits on C3, which is bonded to two methyls and an ethyl, so it's tertiary. Water attacks there, giving 2-methylbutan-2-ol. 3-Methylbutan-2-ol is the trap: it assumes water grabs the cation before it rearranges.

questions.q: A chemist triples [N₃⁻] in a reaction with 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, and the rate stays the same. What does this indicate?
o: That azide is too weak to react
Product still forms. Azide just isn't part of the slow step, so it's missing from the rate law.
An E2 mechanism
E2 needs the base in its only step, so tripling the base would triple the rate.
An SN1 mechanism with rate-limiting ionization
Correct: no change with [N₃⁻] means the slow step is the chloride ionizing on its own.
An SN2 mechanism with backside attack by azide
SN2 rate = k[RCl][Nu], so tripling the nucleophile would triple the rate.
questions.x: A rate law lists only the things that take part in the slowest step (or the steps before it). Here, tripling the azide (N₃⁻) changes nothing, so azide must come in after the slow step. That fits SN1. The slow step is the tertiary chloride falling apart into a carbocation on its own, so rate = k[RCl]. SN2 and E2 both happen in one step that needs the nucleophile or base, so tripling [N₃⁻] would triple their rates.

questions.q: 1-Bromo-2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentyl bromide) reacts extremely slowly by SN2 even though it is primary. Why?
o: Bulky groups on the adjacent carbon block backside attack
Correct: the three methyls on the next carbon block the nucleophile's path to the back of the C–Br carbon.
It has no hydrogens on the α-carbon
The carbon holding Br is CH₂, so it does have hydrogens. Missing hydrogens isn't the issue.
Its carbocation is too stable
Carbocation stability matters for SN1, not SN2. And this cation would be primary, which is very unstable.
Bromide is a poor leaving group
Bromide is a good leaving group. Other primary bromides react fast by SN2.
questions.x: SN2 is a one-step reaction where the nucleophile has to reach the back of the carbon, directly opposite the bromine. In neopentyl bromide the carbon holding Br is primary (bonded to just one other carbon), which usually means fast SN2. But that one neighbor carbon carries three methyl groups, a bulky tert-butyl group, and they crowd the path to the back. So SN2 crawls. SN1 doesn't help either, because the bromide leaving would create a primary carbocation, which is very unstable.

questions.q: S-Adenosylmethionine (SAM) transfers its methyl group to an amine nucleophile. Why is this methyl carbon a good SN2 electrophile?
o: Sulfur is more electronegative than oxygen
Sulfur is less electronegative than oxygen. The positive charge on sulfur is what matters.
The methyl group is a strong nucleophile
The methyl carbon is being attacked, so it's the electrophile, not the nucleophile.
It forms a stable methyl carbocation
A methyl carbocation is extremely unstable. This transfer is SN2, not SN1.
It is unhindered and bonded to a positively charged sulfonium leaving group
Correct: the methyl is wide open, and the positive sulfur leaves easily as a neutral thioether.
questions.x: SAM is the cell's main methyl (CH₃) donor. Its methyl sits on a sulfur that carries a positive charge, called a sulfonium. When an amine attacks the methyl carbon in an SN2 reaction, the sulfur leaves as a neutral molecule (S-adenosylhomocysteine). Going from charged to neutral is easy and favorable, which makes it an excellent leaving group. On top of that, a methyl carbon has nothing crowding it, so the nucleophile can easily reach its back side. Unhindered carbon plus great leaving group equals a great SN2 target.

questions.q: N,N-Dimethylbenzamide is treated with LiAlH₄, then water. What is the product?
o: Benzaldehyde
LiAlH₄ is too strong to stop at an aldehyde, and amides don't give aldehydes with it.
Benzyl alcohol and dimethylamine
This breaks the C–N bond. With amides, the oxygen leaves and the C–N bond stays.
Benzoic acid
That's hydrolysis, which needs water with acid or base. LiAlH₄ reduces instead.
N,N-Dimethylbenzylamine
Correct: LiAlH₄ turns the amide C=O into CH₂, so you get an amine.
questions.x: LiAlH₄ (lithium aluminum hydride) is a strong reducer that delivers hydride, H⁻, a hydrogen carrying two electrons. With an ester, the OR group leaves and you end up with an alcohol. Amides are different, because nitrogen is a poor leaving group. Instead, the carbonyl oxygen, now stuck to aluminum, gets kicked out. That leaves a C=N⁺ (an iminium ion), and a second hydride adds to it. The net result: the C=O becomes CH₂ and the nitrogen stays put. So N,N-dimethylbenzamide becomes N,N-dimethylbenzylamine, PhCH₂N(CH₃)₂.

questions.q: (R)-Butan-2-ol is converted to its tosylate with TsCl and pyridine, then treated with NaBr in DMSO. What is the final product?
o: (S)-Butan-2-ol
The nucleophile is bromide, not hydroxide, so Br ends up on the carbon.
(S)-2-Bromobutane
Correct: making the tosylate keeps R (C–O untouched), then SN2 flips it to S.
Racemic 2-bromobutane
Racemic needs a carbocation (SN1). Bromide in DMSO on a tosylate goes SN2.
(R)-2-Bromobutane
This assumes the shape is kept in both steps. The SN2 step flips it.
questions.note: Tosylation keeps configuration; the displacement is where inversion happens.
questions.x: Two steps, so track the stereocenter through each. First, TsCl turns the OH into a tosylate (OTs), a great leaving group. This step builds a bond to the oxygen and never breaks the C–O bond, so the carbon keeps its R shape. Second, bromide in DMSO (a polar aprotic solvent that favors SN2) attacks from the back and kicks out OTs. Backside attack flips the carbon like an umbrella in the wind. Br takes the top-priority spot that OTs had, so the flip also flips the label: R becomes S. No carbocation forms, so nothing gets scrambled into a racemic mix.

questions.q: Which hydrogens in pentane-2,4-dione (CH₃COCH₂COCH₃) are the most acidic?
o: All hydrogens are equally acidic
Where a hydrogen sits relative to the carbonyls makes a huge difference.
None; diketones are not acidic
β-Diketones are unusually acidic for compounds that lose a proton from carbon.
The hydrogens on the terminal CH₃ groups
These touch only one carbonyl (pKₐ about 20), so they're less acidic than the middle CH₂.
The CH₂ hydrogens between the carbonyls
Correct: the anion spreads onto both oxygens, so the pKₐ is about 9.
questions.x: An acidic hydrogen is one that comes off easily as H⁺. On a carbon, that only happens if the negative charge left behind has somewhere to spread out. The CH₂ in the middle of pentane-2,4-dione sits between two C=O groups. When it loses a proton, the negative charge can spread by resonance onto both oxygens. More spreading means a more stable anion, so the pKₐ drops to about 9. The end CH₃ hydrogens touch only one carbonyl, so their charge spreads onto one oxygen, and their pKₐ is about 20. Remember, lower pKₐ means more acidic.

questions.q: In a crossed aldol reaction between benzaldehyde and acetone in base, why are few side products formed?
o: Base prevents acetone from self-condensing entirely
Base doesn't stop acetone from reacting with itself. Benzaldehyde just wins as the better target.
Acetone has no α-hydrogens
Acetone has six α-hydrogens. That's exactly why it forms the enolate.
Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens, so it acts only as the electrophile
Correct: benzaldehyde can't form an enolate, so it can only be attacked, and it's the better target.
Benzaldehyde is not electrophilic
Aldehydes are good targets for nucleophiles. Benzaldehyde is the electrophile here.
questions.x: An aldol reaction joins an enolate to a carbonyl. The enolate is the attacker (nucleophile); you make it by pulling an α-hydrogen, one on the carbon next to the C=O, off with base. If both partners can make enolates, you get a messy mix of products. Benzaldehyde has no α-hydrogens (its C=O is attached right to the benzene ring), so it can't make an enolate. It can only be attacked. And as an aldehyde, it's a better target than acetone, so acetone's enolate adds mostly to benzaldehyde instead of to another acetone. One role for each partner keeps side products low.

questions.q: In an α,β-unsaturated ketone, which carbon other than the carbonyl carbon is electrophilic?
o: The α-carbon
Resonance puts positive charge on every other carbon and skips the α-carbon.
The carbonyl oxygen
Oxygen is the electron-rich end. It holds the negative charge.
The β-carbon
Correct: resonance puts a partial positive charge on the β-carbon, where conjugate addition happens.
The γ-carbon only
The γ-carbon is outside the C=C–C=O system, so resonance doesn't reach it.
questions.note: Michael acceptors react at the β-carbon.
questions.x: In an α,β-unsaturated ketone, a C=C sits right next to the C=O, so their electrons are linked (conjugated). Oxygen pulls electrons toward itself. Draw the resonance: electrons from the C=C slide toward the C=O, and the C=O electrons slide onto the oxygen. That leaves a positive charge on the β-carbon, the far end of the C=C. So nucleophiles can attack in two places: the carbonyl carbon or the β-carbon. Attack at β is called conjugate (1,4) addition, as in the Michael reaction. The α-carbon never gets the positive charge.

questions.q: Which compound is most reactive toward nucleophilic acyl substitution?
o: Acetyl chloride
Correct: Cl⁻ leaves very easily and chlorine barely shares electrons with the carbonyl.
Acetamide
Amides are the least reactive. Nitrogen shares its electrons strongly and is a poor leaving group.
Ethyl acetate
Alkoxide (RO⁻) leaves worse than chloride, and the ester oxygen shares electrons with the carbonyl.
Acetic anhydride
Anhydrides are reactive, but carboxylate leaves less easily than chloride, so they come second.
questions.note: Reactivity: acyl halide > anhydride > thioester > ester > amide > carboxylate.
questions.x: In nucleophilic acyl substitution, a nucleophile attacks a carbonyl carbon and a leaving group gets kicked out. Two things make it faster: a more positive carbonyl carbon, and a leaving group that's happy to leave. Chloride wins on both. Cl⁻ is a very weak base, so it leaves easily. And chlorine barely shares its electrons with the carbonyl carbon (its bigger 3p orbital doesn't overlap well with carbon's 2p), so the carbon stays very positive. Anhydrides come second, then esters, then amides. Amides are the slowest because nitrogen shares its electrons strongly and leaves badly.

questions.q: Acetic acid is esterified with ¹⁸O-labeled ethanol under acid catalysis. Where does the ¹⁸O label end up?
o: In the ester's carbonyl oxygen
The ester's C=O oxygen comes from the acid, which isn't labeled.
Distributed equally among all of the product's oxygens
The alcohol's C–O bond never breaks, so the label stays in one spot.
In the water by-product
Water leaves from the acid's OH, so it carries the acid's unlabeled oxygen.
In the ester's alkoxy (C–O–CH₂CH₃) oxygen
Correct: the alcohol oxygen attacks and stays in the ester; the acid's OH leaves as water.
questions.note: Fischer esterification: the acid loses OH, the alcohol loses only H.
questions.x: In Fischer esterification, an acid and an alcohol join to make an ester, with an acid catalyst. The alcohol is the attacker (nucleophile). Its oxygen bonds to the acid's carbonyl carbon and stays attached to its own ethyl group the whole time. Later, the acid's original OH picks up a proton and leaves as water. So the labeled ¹⁸O ends up as the ester oxygen that links to the ethyl group (C–O–CH₂CH₃), and the water carries no label. This experiment is how chemists proved that the acid loses OH and the alcohol loses only H.

questions.q: Why is base-promoted hydrolysis of an ester (saponification) effectively irreversible?
o: Esters cannot be re-formed from acids under any conditions
Fischer esterification re-forms esters from acids under acidic conditions.
The carboxylic acid product is deprotonated to an unreactive carboxylate
Correct: the acid becomes a carboxylate right away, and that stable anion can't be attacked to go back.
The alcohol product evaporates
Whether the alcohol evaporates isn't the reason. The acid-base step drives it.
Hydroxide is a catalyst that is regenerated
Hydroxide gets used up, one full equivalent. It isn't regenerated like a catalyst.
questions.x: Saponification means breaking an ester with hydroxide (OH⁻). Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon, an alkoxide (RO⁻) gets kicked out, and you get a carboxylic acid. But you're in strong base, so that acid loses its proton right away and becomes a carboxylate (RCOO⁻). The carboxylate's negative charge is spread over two oxygens, which makes it very stable, and a negatively charged carbonyl doesn't attract nucleophiles. So the alkoxide can't attack it to go backward. That last acid-base step locks the reaction in, and it uses up a full equivalent of hydroxide.

questions.q: Two equivalents of methylamine are needed to convert one equivalent of acetyl chloride fully into N-methylacetamide. Why?
o: The amide must be protonated to form
Making the amide releases a proton (as HCl). It doesn't need one.
The first equivalent reduces the acid chloride to an aldehyde
Amines act as nucleophiles and bases here. Nothing gets reduced.
Two amines add to each carbonyl
Only one amine ends up in the amide.
The second equivalent neutralizes the HCl by-product
Correct: the second amine soaks up the HCl, which would otherwise protonate the amine and shut it down.
questions.x: Methylamine attacks acetyl chloride, chloride leaves, and you get N-methylacetamide plus one HCl. HCl is a strong acid. It grabs the next methylamine it finds and turns it into CH₃NH₃⁺Cl⁻. A protonated amine has used its lone pair (its unshared electron pair) to hold the proton, so it can't attack anything. That means you need a second equivalent of amine just to soak up the HCl. Another base, like pyridine, can do that job instead.

questions.q: Peptide bond hydrolysis is thermodynamically favorable, yet peptides persist for years in neutral water. Why?
o: Amide resonance raises the activation energy
Correct: the reaction is favorable but extremely slow, because amide resonance makes the energy barrier high.
Water cannot act as a nucleophile
Water can attack carbonyls. It's just very slow with amides.
Peptide bonds are ionic
Peptide bonds are covalent amide bonds, not ionic.
Hydrolysis is endergonic at pH 7 and 25 °C
Hydrolysis has a negative ΔG. The issue is the barrier, not the overall energy.
questions.note: Thermodynamics says if; kinetics says how fast.
questions.x: There are two separate questions here. ΔG (Gibbs free energy change) tells you whether a reaction can go downhill on its own; a negative ΔG means yes. Activation energy tells you how fast it goes. Breaking a peptide bond with water has a negative ΔG, so it's favorable. But the amide's nitrogen shares its lone pair with the C=O (resonance), which strengthens the C–N bond and makes the carbonyl carbon less positive. That creates a very high activation energy, so without help the reaction takes years. Proteases speed it up by lowering the barrier, but they don't change ΔG.

questions.q: Which acid loses CO₂ most readily on gentle heating?
o: Butanoic acid
A plain acid has no carbonyl at the β-carbon, so it needs harsh conditions.
3-Oxobutanoic acid
Correct: as a β-keto acid it loses CO₂ easily through a six-atom ring.
Benzoic acid
Benzoic acid resists losing CO₂ on heating. The ring doesn't help.
4-Oxopentanoic acid
The ketone here is one carbon too far away to form the six-atom ring.
questions.x: Decarboxylation means losing CO₂ from a carboxylic acid (–COOH). It's easy only when there's a C=O on the β-carbon, the carbon two steps away from the COOH carbon. 3-Oxobutanoic acid, CH₃COCH₂COOH, has exactly that, so it's a β-keto acid. On gentle heating, the ketone oxygen grabs the acid's hydrogen while CO₂ breaks off, all through a six-atom ring. That gives an enol (a C=C with an OH), which quickly shifts to a ketone. Here the product is acetone. The other acids don't have a carbonyl in the right spot to form that ring.

questions.q: Which nitrogen atom is the least basic?
o: The nitrogen of triethylamine
Triethylamine's lone pair is free, and alkyl groups push in electrons, so it's strongly basic.
The nitrogen of ethylamine
A typical alkylamine: its conjugate acid has a pKₐ near 10.7, so it's a good base.
The nitrogen of acetamide
Correct: acetamide's lone pair is shared with the C=O, so it's basically not basic.
The nitrogen of pyridine
Pyridine's lone pair is free, so it's weakly basic (pKₐ about 5), still more than an amide.
questions.x: A nitrogen acts as a base by using its lone pair (an unshared pair of electrons) to grab a proton. So the question is: whose lone pair is busy? In acetamide, the nitrogen's lone pair is shared with the C=O next to it through resonance. It isn't free, so amides are basically not basic at all (a protonated amide has a pKₐ near 0). Pyridine's lone pair is free but held tightly in an sp² orbital, so pyridine is weakly basic (pKₐ about 5). The two alkylamines have free lone pairs and are the strongest bases (pKₐ about 10 to 11).

questions.q: Why is pyridine basic while pyrrole is essentially nonbasic?
o: Pyrrole's nitrogen lone pair is part of its aromatic sextet; pyridine's is not
Correct: pyrrole needs its lone pair for aromaticity; pyridine's lone pair is a spare.
Pyrrole has no lone pair on nitrogen
Pyrrole's nitrogen does have a lone pair. It's just being used in the aromatic ring.
Pyridine is not aromatic
Pyridine is aromatic, with 6 π electrons from its three double bonds.
Pyridine's nitrogen is sp³ hybridized
Pyridine's nitrogen is sp², and its lone pair points out in the plane of the ring.
questions.x: Aromatic rings are extra stable, and to be aromatic a flat ring needs 6 π electrons (electrons in the p orbitals above and below the ring). In pyrrole, a five-membered ring, the carbons supply only 4. The nitrogen's lone pair supplies the other 2. If pyrrole grabbed a proton with that lone pair, it would lose aromaticity, which costs a lot of energy, so it doesn't. In pyridine, a six-membered ring, the three C=C and C=N double bonds already supply 6 π electrons. Its nitrogen lone pair sits off to the side in the ring's plane, free to grab a proton.

questions.q: Ammonia is treated with one equivalent of bromoethane. A mixture of ethyl-, diethyl- and triethylamine results. Why?
o: Each alkylated amine is at least as nucleophilic as the starting amine
Correct: each product is at least as good an attacker as ammonia, so it keeps reacting.
The C–N bonds rearrange after formation
C–N bonds don't rearrange. The mixture comes from repeated alkylation.
Bromoethane reacts by SN1
A primary halide like bromoethane reacts by SN2. It doesn't form a carbocation.
Ammonia is not nucleophilic
Ammonia does attack first. The products just compete with it.
questions.x: Ammonia (NH₃) attacks bromoethane by SN2 and becomes ethylamine. Here's the catch: an ethyl group pushes electron density onto nitrogen, so ethylamine is at least as good a nucleophile (attacker) as ammonia. Now ethylamine competes with the leftover ammonia for the remaining bromoethane. It reacts again to give diethylamine, which reacts again to give triethylamine, and so on, even up to a quaternary ammonium salt. This is called overalkylation. It's why chemists use other methods, like the Gabriel synthesis or reductive amination, to make primary amines cleanly.

questions.q: One-electron reduction of ubiquinone produces which species?
o: A carbocation
Adding an electron makes something more negative, so it can't create a cation.
A semiquinone radical
Correct: one electron gives a semiquinone, a radical stabilized by resonance.
Ubiquinol
Ubiquinol needs two electrons and two protons, not one electron.
A hydroquinone dianion
A dianion needs two added electrons, not one.
questions.x: Reduction means adding electrons. Ubiquinone (coenzyme Q) can take its two electrons one at a time. Add just one electron and you get the semiquinone, a radical, meaning a species with one unpaired electron. That lone electron is spread by resonance over the ring and both oxygens, which keeps the radical fairly stable. Add a second electron plus two protons and you reach ubiquinol (QH₂), the fully reduced form. Having this halfway stop lets Q pass electrons between carriers that move two at a time (like NADH) and carriers that move one at a time (like iron-sulfur clusters and cytochromes).

questions.q: Phenol reacts with Br₂ much faster than benzene does, and substitution occurs at which positions?
o: Randomly at all positions
The OH pushes electrons to specific carbons, so the products follow a clear pattern.
At the carbon bearing OH (ipso)
Bromine replaces a ring hydrogen. The OH isn't kicked off.
Ortho and para
Correct: OH pushes electrons into the ring, boosting the ortho and para carbons.
Meta only
Meta is where electron-withdrawing groups send new groups. OH is a donor.
questions.x: A benzene ring is electron-rich, so it attacks electron-poor things like Br⁺. That's called electrophilic aromatic substitution. The OH on phenol has lone pairs (unshared electron pairs) on its oxygen, and it pushes them into the ring by resonance. That makes the ring much more eager to attack, so phenol reacts far faster than benzene. The extra electron density lands on the ortho carbons (right next to OH) and the para carbon (straight across). When Br attacks there, the positive charge in the intermediate can sit right next to the oxygen, which steadies it. So bromine goes ortho and para. Meta direction belongs to electron-withdrawing groups.

questions.q: Fructofuranose forms when which groups in open-chain fructose react?
o: The C1 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
C1 and C2 are neighbors, so bonding them would make a strained three-atom ring.
The C6 hydroxyl and the C1 aldehyde
Fructose has no aldehyde. Its C1 is a CH₂OH group.
The C5 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
Correct: the C5 OH attacks the C2 ketone, giving a five-atom ring (a hemiketal).
The C4 hydroxyl and the C2 ketone
This would make a four-atom ring, which is too strained to form.
questions.x: In water, sugars mostly curl up into rings. A ring forms when one of the sugar's own OH groups attacks its own C=O carbon. Fructose is a ketose: its C=O is a ketone at C2. When the OH on C5 attacks C2, the ring holds C2, C3, C4, C5 and the oxygen from C5. That's 4 carbons + 1 oxygen = 5 atoms, a five-membered ring called a furanose. Because the carbonyl was a ketone, the new group is a hemiketal. (If the C6 OH attacks instead, you get a six-membered ring, fructopyranose.) OH groups closer to C2 would make tiny, strained rings.

questions.q: A fatty acid is described as 18:3 cis-Δ9,12,15. What ω class is it?
o: ω-6 would need the last double bond at C12 (18 − 12 = 6). There's another one at C15.
9 is the first Δ position, counted from the carboxyl end, not the methyl end.
Correct: ω = 18 − 15 = 3.
15 is a Δ number counted from the carboxyl end. You still have to subtract it from 18.
questions.x: Fatty acids have two ends: the carboxyl end (COOH) and the methyl end (CH₃). Δ (delta) numbers count from the carboxyl carbon, which is C1. The ω (ω) class counts from the other end, the methyl end, to the nearest double bond. Formula: ω = N − d, where N is the number of carbons and d is the Δ number of the last double bond. Here N = 18 and the last double bond starts at C15, so d = 15. Plug in: ω = 18 − 15 = 3. This is an ω-3 fatty acid (α-linolenic acid).

questions.q: Phospholipase A₂ hydrolyzes a membrane phospholipid. What are the products?
o: Glycerol and three fatty acids
Phospholipids have only two fatty acids, and PLA₂ removes only one.
Phosphatidic acid and free choline
Phosphatidic acid plus free choline is what phospholipase D makes.
A free fatty acid from the sn-2 position and a lysophospholipid
Correct: PLA₂ cuts the ester at glycerol C2, freeing a fatty acid and leaving a lysophospholipid.
Diacylglycerol and a phosphorylated head group
Diacylglycerol plus a phosphorylated head group is what phospholipase C makes.
questions.x: A phospholipid has a glycerol backbone with two fatty acid tails (on carbons 1 and 2) and a phosphate head group (on carbon 3). Phospholipases are enzymes named by the bond they cut. PLA₂ cuts the ester bond at the sn-2 carbon, the middle carbon of glycerol. That frees one fatty acid, often arachidonic acid, which the body uses to make prostaglandins and other eicosanoids. What's left has just one tail and is called a lysophospholipid. PLC cuts just before the phosphate, and PLD cuts just after it.

questions.q: Soap molecules (one hydrocarbon tail) form micelles in water, but diacyl phospholipids form bilayers. What best explains the difference?
o: Micelles form only from uncharged molecules
Soaps are charged and form micelles easily.
Single-tailed amphiphiles are cone-shaped; two-tailed ones are roughly cylindrical
Correct: one tail makes a cone that packs into a ball; two tails make a cylinder that packs flat.
Soaps lack a polar head group
A soap's carboxylate (COO⁻) is its polar head.
Phospholipids are not amphipathic
Phospholipids have polar heads and nonpolar tails, so they're amphipathic.
questions.x: Both soap and phospholipids are amphipathic: they have a water-loving (polar) head and a water-avoiding (nonpolar) tail. In water, the tails hide together and the heads face out. What decides the final structure is shape. A soap molecule has a big head and one thin tail, so it's shaped like a cone. Cones fit together point-in, forming a ball called a micelle. A phospholipid has two tails, about as wide as its head, so it's shaped like a cylinder. Cylinders stand side by side in flat sheets, forming a bilayer.

questions.q: Most L-amino acids have the S configuration, but L-cysteine is R. Why?
o: L-Cysteine has the opposite spatial arrangement from other L-amino acids
L-cysteine has the same 3D arrangement as other L-amino acids. Only the ranking changes.
Disulfide formation inverts the α-carbon
Disulfide bonds form between side-chain sulfurs. The α-carbon isn't touched.
The sulfur in –CH₂SH gives the side chain higher CIP priority than –COOH
Correct: sulfur (atomic number 16) beats oxygen (8), so CH₂SH outranks COOH and the label flips.
Cysteine's α-carbon is not a stereocenter
The α-carbon has four different groups, so it's a stereocenter.
questions.note: D/L is about geometry; R/S is about priorities.
questions.x: L and D describe the real 3D arrangement, compared with a reference sugar (glyceraldehyde). R and S come from a ranking rule (the CIP rules): rank the four groups on the stereocenter by atomic number, then see which way the ranking turns. In most amino acids the ranking is NH₂ > COOH > side chain > H, which makes L amino acids S. In cysteine, the side chain is CH₂SH. Its first atom is carbon, the same as COOH's, so you look at what's attached: sulfur (atomic number 16) beats oxygen (8). So CH₂SH outranks COOH. The shape is the same, but the ranking swaps two groups, so the label reads R.

questions.q: Lysine has pKₐ values of 2.2 (α-COOH), 9.0 (α-NH₃⁺) and 10.5 (side-chain NH₃⁺). What is its pI?
o: This averages all three pKₐ values. Only the two around the neutral form count.
This averages the carboxyl and side-chain values, which don't border the neutral form.
This averages the α-groups and ignores lysine's basic side chain.
Correct: the neutral form sits between 9.0 and 10.5, and (9.0 + 10.5) ÷ 2 = 9.75.
questions.x: The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH where a molecule has zero net charge. Track lysine's charge as pH rises. Below 2.2, everything has its proton: +2. Past 2.2 the COOH loses its proton: +1. Past 9.0 the α-amino group loses its proton: 0. Past 10.5 the side chain loses its proton: −1. The neutral form lives between 9.0 and 10.5, so average those two: pI = (pKₐ₁ + pKₐ₂) ÷ 2 = (9.0 + 10.5) ÷ 2 = 19.5 ÷ 2 = 9.75. That makes sense: lysine has an extra basic group, so its pI is well above 7.

questions.q: A histidine side chain has pKₐ 6.0. At pH 7.0, approximately what fraction of histidine side chains are protonated?
o: About 9%
Correct: the ratio is 10 neutral to 1 protonated, and 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 9%.
About 1%
1% would need the pH to be two units above the pKₐ (a 100 to 1 ratio).
About 91%
This flips the ratio. Above the pKₐ, most side chains have lost their proton.
About 50%
50% happens only when the pH equals the pKₐ.
questions.x: Use the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation: pH = pKₐ + log([A⁻]/[HA]), where [A⁻] is the deprotonated (neutral) form and [HA] is the protonated form. Values: pH = 7.0, pKₐ = 6.0. Plug in: 7.0 = 6.0 + log([A⁻]/[HA]), so log([A⁻]/[HA]) = 7.0 − 6.0 = 1. Log reads off the exponent of 10, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 10¹ = 10. That's 10 neutral side chains for every 1 protonated one, 11 in all. Protonated fraction = 1 ÷ 11 ≈ 0.09, about 9%.

questions.q: In a Strecker synthesis, an aldehyde reacts with NH₃ and HCN, and the aminonitrile is hydrolyzed. What is the stereochemistry of the amino acid product?
o: Racemic
Correct: cyanide attacks the flat imine from either face equally.
Pure L
Nothing here prefers one face. Only an enzyme or chiral catalyst would favor L.
Meso
An amino acid with one stereocenter can't be meso.
Pure D
Nothing favors D, just as nothing favors L.
questions.x: In the Strecker synthesis, the aldehyde and NH₃ first join to make an imine, a C=N double bond. The imine carbon is flat. Cyanide (CN⁻) then attacks that carbon, which creates the new stereocenter, the carbon that will become the amino acid's α-carbon. Since the carbon is flat, cyanide can come in from the top face or the bottom face, and nothing in the flask prefers one side. The two faces give mirror-image products in equal amounts, so the product is racemic, a 50:50 mix. Getting only the L form would take an enzyme or a chiral catalyst.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of ATP's terminal phosphoanhydride bond is strongly exergonic. Which factor contributes?
o: Release of energy stored in the adenine ring
The adenine base doesn't change during hydrolysis.
Breaking bonds releases energy
Breaking a bond costs energy. The release comes from the products being more stable.
Formation of a new phosphoanhydride bond
Hydrolysis breaks an anhydride bond; it doesn't form one.
Relief of electrostatic repulsion among adjacent negative phosphates
Correct: the negative phosphates stop pushing on each other, and the products are better stabilized.
questions.note: Trap: breaking a bond never releases energy by itself.
questions.x: First, a key rule: breaking a bond always costs energy. So ATP hydrolysis (splitting off a phosphate with water) releases energy only because its products, ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pᵢ), are much more stable than ATP and water. Why? ATP's three phosphates sit in a row and each carries negative charge. Like charges push each other apart, so ATP is strained. Splitting one off relieves that push. The free phosphate also gets more resonance forms (its charge spreads over more oxygens), and both products are better surrounded by water. Together that gives ΔG°′ of about −30.5 kJ/mol.

questions.q: Spontaneous deamination of cytosine produces uracil. How does using thymine in DNA help cells repair this damage?
o: Any uracil in DNA can be recognized as damage and removed
Correct: since DNA uses thymine, any uracil must be damage and can be removed.
Thymine prevents cytosine from deaminating
Thymine doesn't change how cytosine reacts. Cytosine still deaminates.
Thymine cannot be deaminated
True that thymine has no amino group, but that doesn't explain fixing cytosine damage.
Uracil pairs with guanine more strongly than cytosine does
Uracil pairs with adenine, which is exactly why unrepaired U causes mutations.
questions.x: Cytosine sometimes loses its amino group (NH₂) all on its own. That's called deamination, and it turns cytosine into uracil. If DNA normally used uracil, a repair enzyme couldn't tell a 'real' U from a damaged C. DNA uses thymine instead, which is just uracil with a methyl group (5-methyluracil). So any plain uracil found in DNA has to be damage. An enzyme called uracil-DNA glycosylase spots it and cuts it out, and the gap gets filled with C again. If it isn't fixed, U pairs with A, and after copying, a G–C pair becomes an A–T pair, a mutation.

questions.q: A chemist must add CH₃MgBr to an ester in a molecule that also has a free OH group. Why must the OH be protected first?
o: The OH would be reduced to an alkane
Grignard reagents don't reduce alcohols to alkanes.
The OH group makes the ester unreactive
The ester stays reactive. The OH destroys the Grignard instead.
The OH would add to the ester first
The OH attacking the ester isn't the main issue. The acid-base reaction is much faster.
The acidic OH would protonate and destroy the Grignard reagent
Correct: the acidic OH turns the Grignard into methane. A silyl ether removes that proton.
questions.x: A Grignard reagent like CH₃MgBr acts like a carbanion, a carbon carrying a negative charge. That makes it a great nucleophile (attacker) but also an extremely strong base. An alcohol's O–H proton (pKₐ about 16) is acidic enough to react with it instantly: the Grignard grabs the proton and becomes methane gas, CH₄. That uses up the reagent before it ever reaches the ester. The fix is to protect the OH, for example by turning it into a silyl ether (O–SiR₃), which has no acidic proton. After the Grignard does its job, fluoride removes the silyl group and gives the OH back.

questions.q: Which methyl halide's protons appear farthest downfield in ¹H NMR?
o: CH₃Br
Bromine is less electronegative than F or Cl, so it deshields less.
CH₃F
Correct: fluorine is the most electronegative, so it pulls the most electron density away.
CH₃Cl
Chlorine is less electronegative than fluorine.
CH₃I
Iodine is the least electronegative here, so it gives the most upfield signal.
questions.x: In ¹H NMR, the chemical shift (in ppm) tells you where a proton's signal shows up. Electrons around a proton shield it, and shielded protons appear upfield (lower ppm). An electronegative atom nearby pulls those electrons away, which deshields the proton and moves its signal downfield (higher ppm). Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so it pulls hardest. CH₃F shows up farthest downfield, about 4.3 ppm, then CH₃Cl (about 3.1), CH₃Br (about 2.7) and CH₃I (about 2.2). The larger halogens are bigger atoms, but size isn't what controls the shift; electronegativity is.

questions.q: Which type of system can exchange energy, but not matter, with its surroundings?
o: Closed system
