Correct: a closed system lets heat and work cross, but no matter.
Open system
An open system swaps both matter and energy.
Isolated system
An isolated system swaps neither matter nor energy.
Isothermal system
Isothermal means constant temperature. It doesn't describe what crosses the boundary.
questions.x: In thermodynamics, the system is whatever you're studying, and the surroundings are everything else. Systems get sorted by what can cross the boundary between the two. An open system lets both matter and energy through, like a pot of soup with no lid. A closed system lets energy through, as heat or work, but no matter, like a sealed flask you can warm on a hot plate. An isolated system lets nothing through. Isothermal is a tempting pick because it sounds like thermodynamics, but it just means constant temperature. It describes a process, not a boundary.

questions.q: According to the third law of thermodynamics, which of the following has an entropy of exactly zero?
o: Any element in its standard state at 25 °C
Standard-state elements have ΔH°f = 0, not S = 0. Their entropy is positive at 25 °C.
A perfect crystal of a pure substance at 0 K
Correct: a perfect crystal at absolute zero has only one possible arrangement, so S = 0.
An ideal gas at 0 °C
0 °C is 273 K, not absolute zero, and gases have large entropies.
A pure liquid at its freezing point
A liquid at its freezing point is still disordered, so its entropy is well above zero.
questions.note: Trap: zero ΔH°f for elements is a convention; zero S applies only to perfect crystals at 0 K.
questions.x: Entropy (S) measures how many ways the particles in something can be arranged. Each possible arrangement is called a microstate. The third law of thermodynamics says that a perfect crystal of a pure substance at 0 K (absolute zero) has only one possible arrangement. With just one microstate, the entropy is zero: S = k ln 1 = 0, since ln 1 = 0. Anything warmer, or any crystal with flaws, has more than one arrangement and positive entropy. Don't confuse this with the rule that elements in their standard states have ΔH°f = 0. That's about enthalpy, not entropy.

questions.q: An ideal gas expands adiabatically against a constant external pressure. What happens to its temperature?
o: It decreases, because the gas does work with no heat input
Correct: q = 0, so ΔU = w, and w is negative when the gas expands. Lower U means lower T.
It stays constant because no heat is exchanged
No heat flow doesn't mean constant temperature. Work alone can lower the internal energy.
It increases because the gas occupies more volume
Expanding costs the gas energy, so its temperature can't go up.
It cannot be predicted without the heat capacity
Heat capacity sets the size of the drop, but ΔU = w < 0 already fixes its direction.
questions.x: The first law says ΔU = q + w, where ΔU is the change in the gas's internal energy, q is heat added to the gas, and w is work done on the gas. Adiabatic means no heat flows, so q = 0 and ΔU = w. When the gas expands, it pushes on its surroundings, so it does work on them. That means w is negative (the gas loses energy). So ΔU is negative too. For an ideal gas, internal energy depends only on temperature, so a drop in U means a drop in T. The gas cools.

questions.q: According to the second law of thermodynamics, every spontaneous process:
o: Increases the entropy of the system
A system's entropy can fall if the surroundings gain even more.
Decreases the enthalpy of the system
Heat-absorbing processes, like ice melting at room temperature, can be spontaneous.
Increases the entropy of the universe
Correct: the entropy of the universe goes up in every spontaneous process.
Increases the total energy of the universe
The universe's total energy stays constant. That's the first law.
questions.x: The second law says that in every spontaneous process (one that happens on its own), the entropy of the universe goes up. The universe here means the system plus its surroundings. Entropy is a measure of how spread out energy and matter are. The system's own entropy can go down, as long as the surroundings gain more. When water freezes below 0 °C, the water gets more ordered, but it releases heat that raises the surroundings' entropy by even more. Spontaneous processes can also absorb heat, like ice melting at room temperature, so neither the system's entropy nor its enthalpy decides on its own.

questions.q: Which statement about ΔS of the universe for an idealized reversible process is true?
o: It equals zero
Correct: a reversible process creates no new entropy, so the system and surroundings cancel.
It is always positive
A positive total describes real, irreversible processes.
It is always negative
A negative total would break the second law.
It equals ΔH/T of the system
ΔH/T gives the system's ΔS at constant T and P, not the universe's.
questions.x: A reversible process is an ideal one, done so slowly that the system stays at equilibrium the whole way and could be run backward with no trace left behind. Because nothing is wasted along the way, no new entropy is created. Whatever entropy the system gains, the surroundings lose exactly the same amount, or the other way around. So ΔS_universe = 0. Real processes are irreversible and always have ΔS_universe > 0. A negative ΔS_universe never happens; that would break the second law.

questions.q: Hess's law works because enthalpy is:
o: Always negative for real reactions
Many reactions are endothermic. The sign of ΔH has nothing to do with Hess's law.
Equal to the heat at constant volume
Heat at constant volume is ΔU, and that isn't why Hess's law works.
A state function
Correct: ΔH depends only on the starting and ending states, so any path gives the same total.
Independent of the amounts of reactants
ΔH grows with the amount reacting. True, but it isn't the reason.
questions.x: Hess's law says that if you can write a reaction as a series of steps, its ΔH equals the sum of the steps' ΔH values. That works because enthalpy (H) is a state function, meaning its value depends only on where you start and where you finish, not on the path in between. It's like the change in height between the bottom and top of a hill: same no matter which trail you hike. The other choices aren't the reason. ΔH can be positive or negative, and it does grow with the amount reacting.

questions.q: Using ΔH°f (kJ/mol): CH₄(g) −75, CO₂(g) −394, H₂O(l) −286, what is ΔH° for CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l)?
o: This counts only 1 mol of water. The equation makes 2 H₂O.
This does reactants minus products, which flips the sign.
This adds methane's −75 instead of subtracting it.
questions.note: ΔH°rxn = ΣΔH°f(products) − ΣΔH°f(reactants); O₂ contributes zero.
questions.x: Use ΔH°rxn = ΣnΔH°f(products) − ΣnΔH°f(reactants), where n is each coefficient. Values: CO₂ = −394 (n = 1), H₂O = −286 (n = 2), CH₄ = −75 (n = 1), and O₂ = 0 because it's an element in its standard state. Products: −394 + 2 × (−286) = −394 + (−572) = −966 kJ. Reactants: −75 + 0 = −75 kJ. Plug in: ΔH° = −966 − (−75). Subtracting a negative is adding: −966 + 75 = −891 kJ. A big negative number makes sense, since burning methane gives off lots of heat.

questions.q: Why is the molar enthalpy of vaporization of water much larger than its enthalpy of fusion?
o: Vaporization breaks covalent O–H bonds
Phase changes don't break the covalent bonds inside a molecule.
Vaporization occurs at a higher temperature, and ΔH scales directly with T
Phase-change enthalpies reflect how many attractions get overcome, not the temperature.
Liquid water has stronger hydrogen bonds than ice
Ice has the more complete hydrogen-bond network, not liquid water.
Vaporization overcomes nearly all hydrogen bonding, while melting disrupts only part of it
Correct: boiling breaks nearly all hydrogen bonds; melting breaks only some.
questions.x: Melting and boiling don't break the O–H bonds inside a water molecule. They only overcome the attractions between molecules, here mostly hydrogen bonds. Melting just loosens the hydrogen-bond network enough for molecules to slide past each other; most of the attractions are still there in the liquid. Boiling has to pull the molecules almost completely apart, so nearly all of those attractions must be overcome. That's why water's enthalpy of vaporization (about 41 kJ/mol) is roughly seven times its enthalpy of fusion, or melting (about 6 kJ/mol).

questions.q: Why are reaction enthalpies estimated from bond energies less accurate than those from ΔH°f values?
o: Bond energies ignore whether bonds are broken or formed
The method is built on counting bonds broken and bonds formed.
Bond energies apply only to liquids and solids
Bond energies are defined for gas-phase molecules, not liquids and solids.
Bond energies include entropy contributions
Bond energies are enthalpy values only. Entropy isn't in them.
Tabulated bond energies are averages over many different molecules
Correct: each table value is an average, and a real bond's strength depends on its molecule.
questions.x: Bond energy is the energy it takes to break 1 mol of a particular bond, like C–H, in the gas phase. The catch is that the tables give one average number per bond type. A C–H bond in methane isn't exactly as strong as a C–H bond in ethanol, because the neighboring atoms change how tightly it's held. So adding up average bond energies gives you an estimate. Heats of formation (ΔH°f) are measured for each specific compound, so using them with Hess's law gives the actual value for that reaction.

questions.q: 1 mol of ice melts reversibly at 0 °C. If ΔH°fus = 6.0 kJ/mol, what is ΔS for the melting?
o: −22 J/(mol·K)
Melting absorbs heat and makes things more disordered, so ΔS is positive.
+22 J/(mol·K)
Correct: ΔS = 6000 J ÷ 273 K ≈ +22 J/(mol·K).
This leaves ΔH in kJ but reports the answer in J, so it's 1000 times too small.
Undefined, because the temperature does not change
The formula uses the steady temperature T, not a change in temperature.
questions.note: Always use kelvins in ΔS = ΔH/T.
questions.x: Melting ice at 0 °C is reversible, and the temperature stays constant while it happens. So use ΔS = q_rev ÷ T, where q_rev is the heat absorbed and T is in kelvin. Values: q_rev = ΔHfus = 6.0 kJ/mol. 1 kJ = 1000 J, so multiply by 1000: 6.0 × 1000 = 6000 J/mol. T = 0 °C + 273 = 273 K. Plug in: ΔS = 6000 ÷ 273 ≈ 22 J/(mol·K). It's positive because melting absorbs heat and the liquid is more disordered than the ice.

questions.q: A hot metal block cools in a cooler room, and the block's entropy decreases. Why is this process still spontaneous?
o: The room gains more entropy than the block loses, because it receives the heat at a lower temperature
Correct: the same heat divided by a lower temperature gives the room a bigger entropy gain.
The entropy of the universe is conserved
Entropy isn't conserved. It increases in spontaneous processes.
The first law requires heat to flow from hot to cold
The first law conserves energy but says nothing about which way heat flows.
The block's entropy actually increases as it cools
As the block cools, its entropy goes down, just as the question says.
questions.x: A process is spontaneous if the entropy of the universe (block plus room) goes up. The same heat, q, leaves the block and enters the room. An entropy change from heat is about q ÷ T. The block loses q ÷ T_hot, and the room gains q ÷ T_cold. Since T_cold is a smaller number, dividing by it gives a bigger result. So the room gains more entropy than the block loses, and ΔS_universe is positive. The first law only says energy is conserved. It's the second law that says heat flows from hot to cold.

questions.q: A protein folds with ΔH = −80 kJ/mol and ΔS = −200 J/(mol·K). Above about what temperature does unfolding become favored?
o: Correct: T = ΔH ÷ ΔS = 80,000 ÷ 200 = 400 K. Above that, the −TΔS term wins.
This divides 80 by 200 without turning kJ into J.
This flips the ratio, dividing ΔS by ΔH.
It never unfolds because ΔH < 0
At high temperature, the −TΔS term gets big enough to make folding unfavorable.
questions.x: Use ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. A negative ΔG means a process is favored. Folding gives off heat (ΔH negative, helps) but locks the chain into one shape (ΔS negative, hurts). The −TΔS term is positive and grows with T, so at some temperature it cancels ΔH. Set ΔG = 0: T = ΔH ÷ ΔS. Values: ΔH = −80 kJ/mol; 1 kJ = 1000 J, so −80 × 1000 = −80,000 J/mol. ΔS = −200 J/(mol·K). Plug in: T = (−80,000) ÷ (−200) = 400 K. Above 400 K, unfolding is favored.

questions.q: A process has ΔG = −50 kJ. What is the maximum non-expansion (useful) work it can perform?
o: Unlimited work, given enough time
Waiting longer doesn't help. The free energy released caps the work.
Equal to |ΔH|, regardless of ΔG
ΔH includes the TΔS share, which can't be turned into work.
50 kJ
Correct: at constant T and P, the most useful work is −ΔG = 50 kJ.
Zero, because ΔG < 0 means all energy is lost as heat
Negative ΔG is exactly what makes useful work possible.
questions.x: Gibbs free energy (ΔG) is the energy a process has available to do useful work at constant temperature and pressure. 'Useful' (non-expansion) work means anything besides a gas pushing back the atmosphere, like contracting a muscle or running a battery. The most useful work you can ever get is −ΔG. Here ΔG = −50 kJ, so the maximum is 50 kJ. You only reach that limit in a perfect, reversible process; real processes waste some as heat. ΔH isn't the cap, because part of ΔH is tied up in the TΔS term and can't be turned into work.

questions.q: A 100 g metal block at 85 °C is placed in 100 g of water at 20 °C. The final temperature is 25 °C. What is the metal's specific heat? (c_water = 4.2 J/(g·°C))
o: Correct: water gains 100 × 4.2 × 5 = 2100 J, and 2100 = 100 × c × 60 gives c = 0.35.
That's water's specific heat. If the metal matched it, the final temperature would land halfway.
This uses 65 °C for the metal's change. It went from 85 to 25, which is 60.
This swaps the changes: 5 °C for the metal and 60 °C for the water.
questions.note: Heat lost by the hot object = heat gained by the cold one.
questions.x: In an insulated mix, heat lost by the hot object = heat gained by the cold one. Use q = mcΔT, where m is mass, c is specific heat and ΔT is the temperature change. Water: m = 100 g, c = 4.2 J/(g·°C), ΔT = 25 − 20 = 5 °C. So q = 100 × 4.2 × 5 = 420 × 5 = 2100 J. Metal: m = 100 g, ΔT = 85 − 25 = 60 °C, and it lost the same 2100 J. So 2100 = 100 × c × 60 = 6000 × c. Divide: c = 2100 ÷ 6000 = 0.35 J/(g·°C).

questions.q: In a coffee-cup calorimetry experiment on an exothermic reaction, some heat escapes to the room. How does this affect the calculated magnitude of ΔH?
o: It is too small
Correct: lost heat means a smaller temperature rise, so the calculated heat is too low.
It is too large
Lost heat shrinks the measured temperature rise. It can't make it bigger.
It is unaffected
The calculation uses ΔT, and heat loss makes ΔT smaller.
Its sign is reversed
The solution still warms, so ΔH is still negative.
questions.x: A coffee-cup calorimeter finds the heat from q = mcΔT, using the temperature rise of the solution, then uses that to get ΔH. The math assumes every bit of the reaction's heat stays in the solution. If some escapes to the room, the solution doesn't warm up as much as it should. A smaller ΔT gives a smaller q, so the calculated size of ΔH comes out too small. The sign doesn't change, though: the solution still warms, so the reaction still looks exothermic and ΔH stays negative.

questions.q: When 0.020 mol of a solute dissolves in 100 g of solution (c ≈ 4.0 J/(g·°C)), the temperature rises 5.0 °C. What is ΔH of solution?
o: +100 kJ/mol
The temperature rose, so heat was released and ΔH is negative.
−2.0 kJ/mol
This is the total heat. ΔH has to be divided by the moles.
−10 kJ/mol
This divides by 0.20 mol instead of 0.020 mol.
−100 kJ/mol
Correct: q = 100 × 4.0 × 5.0 = 2.0 kJ released, and 2.0 ÷ 0.020 = 100, so −100 kJ/mol.
questions.x: First find the heat with q = mcΔT, where m is mass, c is specific heat and ΔT is the temperature change. Values: m = 100 g, c = 4.0 J/(g·°C), ΔT = 5.0 °C. Plug in: q = 100 × 4.0 × 5.0 = 400 × 5.0 = 2000 J. 1 kJ = 1000 J, so divide by 1000: 2000 ÷ 1000 = 2.0 kJ. The solution warmed, so the dissolving released that heat, and ΔH is negative. ΔH is per mole, so divide by n = 0.020 mol: ΔH = −2.0 ÷ 0.020 = −100 kJ/mol.

questions.q: How much heat converts 36 g of ice at 0 °C into liquid water at 10 °C? (ΔHfus = 6.0 kJ/mol; c = 4.2 J/(g·°C))
o: 12 kJ
This is only the melting step. The water still has to warm from 0 to 10 °C.
About 13.5 kJ
Correct: melting 2.0 mol takes 12 kJ, warming takes about 1.5 kJ, total about 13.5 kJ.
About 1.5 kJ
This is only the warming step. It skips melting, which is the bigger step.
About 7.5 kJ
This melts only 1 mol. 36 g of water is 2 mol.
questions.x: This happens in two separate stages, so find each one and add them. Stage 1, melting at 0 °C: use q = n × ΔHfus. Moles: n = 36 g ÷ 18 g/mol = 2.0 mol. So q₁ = 2.0 × 6.0 = 12 kJ. Stage 2, warming the liquid from 0 to 10 °C: use q = mcΔT, with m = 36 g, c = 4.2 J/(g·°C), ΔT = 10 °C. So q₂ = 36 × 4.2 × 10 = 151.2 × 10 = 1512 J ≈ 1.5 kJ. Total: 12 + 1.5 = 13.5 kJ. Notice melting takes far more energy than warming.

questions.q: A gas sample is held at a temperature below its triple-point temperature, and the pressure is raised steadily. Which phase change occurs?
o: Deposition (gas to solid)
Correct: below the triple-point temperature, the gas region touches only the solid region.
Condensation (gas to liquid)
Liquid exists only above the triple-point temperature.
Freezing (liquid to solid)
The sample starts as a gas, not a liquid.
Sublimation (solid to gas)
Sublimation goes solid to gas, the reverse, and happens when pressure drops.
questions.x: A phase diagram is a map of pressure versus temperature that shows which phase is stable. The triple point is the one spot where solid, liquid and gas can all exist together. Below the triple-point temperature, the map has no liquid region at all: the gas region borders the solid region directly. So if you hold the temperature there and raise the pressure, you move straight up from gas into solid. Gas turning directly into solid is called deposition. Condensing to a liquid can only happen at temperatures between the triple point and the critical point.

questions.q: A substance's solid–liquid line has a positive slope. A liquid sample just above its melting point is compressed at constant temperature. What can happen?
o: It vaporizes
Squeezing favors denser phases. Gas is the least dense, so it isn't favored.
It can freeze, because higher pressure raises the melting point
Correct: a positive slope means the solid is denser, so squeezing favors the solid.
It stays liquid because pressure always lowers the melting point
Pressure lowers the melting point only for a negative slope, like water's.
It sublimes
Sublimation is solid to gas, and it needs low pressure.
questions.x: On a phase diagram, the solid–liquid line shows the melting point at each pressure. Squeezing a substance favors whichever phase is denser, the one that takes up less space. A positive slope means the solid is denser than the liquid, which is true for most substances. So raising the pressure pushes the melting point up. If the liquid is only a little above its melting point, raising the pressure can push the melting point above the current temperature, and the liquid freezes. Water is the well-known exception: ice is less dense than liquid water, so its line slopes the other way.

questions.q: Initial rates: [A] 0.10, [B] 0.10 → rate r; [A] 0.20, [B] 0.20 → 8r; [A] 0.10, [B] 0.20 → 2r. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[A][B]²
This swaps the orders. With B², doubling B alone would give 4r, not 2r.
rate = k[A]³
This gives all of the 8× jump to A, but B alone doubles the rate.
rate = k[A][B]
First order in each gives only 2 × 2 = 4× when both double, not 8×.
rate = k[A]²[B]
Correct: B alone doubles the rate (first order), so A supplies the other 4× (second order).
questions.x: A rate law looks like rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ, where m and n are the orders. Find each order by changing one thing at a time. Runs 1 and 3: only [B] doubles (0.10 to 0.20), and the rate goes from r to 2r, which doubles. So 2ⁿ = 2, and n = 1. Runs 1 and 2: both double, and the rate goes from r to 8r. B accounts for ×2, so A must account for 8 ÷ 2 = 4. So 2ᵐ = 4, and m = 2. Rate = k[A]²[B].

questions.q: Mechanism: Step 1 (slow) NO₂ + NO₂ → NO₃ + NO; Step 2 (fast) NO₃ + CO → NO₂ + CO₂. What is the rate law?
o: rate = k[NO₂][CO]
This reads the rate law off the overall equation instead of the slow step.
rate = k[NO₃][CO]
This uses the fast step and includes NO₃, which is an intermediate.
rate = k[NO₂]²[CO]
CO reacts only after the slow step, so it isn't in the rate law.
rate = k[NO₂]²
Correct: the slow first step sets the rate, and it's two NO₂ molecules colliding.
questions.x: A reaction mechanism is the list of small steps (elementary steps) that add up to the overall reaction. The slowest step is the rate-determining step, the bottleneck, and it sets the overall rate. For an elementary step, the exponents in its rate law equal how many of each molecule collide. Step 1 is slow, and it's two NO₂ molecules colliding, so rate = k[NO₂]². CO only shows up in the fast second step, after the bottleneck, so it doesn't affect the rate and isn't in the rate law.

questions.q: Mechanism: Step 1 (fast, reversible) 2NO ⇌ N₂O₂; Step 2 (slow) N₂O₂ + O₂ → 2NO₂. What is the observed rate law?
o: rate = k[N₂O₂][O₂]
N₂O₂ is an intermediate. It has to be replaced using step 1.
rate = k[NO]²
This uses only the fast step and leaves out O₂ from the slow step.
rate = k[NO][O₂]
Step 1 uses two NO molecules, so NO has to be squared.
rate = k[NO]²[O₂]
Correct: rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂], and step 1 gives [N₂O₂] = K[NO]².
questions.note: Rate laws must contain only reactants (and catalysts), never intermediates.
questions.x: Start with the slow step, since it sets the rate: rate = k₂[N₂O₂][O₂]. But N₂O₂ is an intermediate (made in step 1, used in step 2), and intermediates can't stay in the final rate law. Step 1 is fast and reversible, so treat it as being at equilibrium: K = [N₂O₂] ÷ [NO]². Rearrange: [N₂O₂] = K[NO]². Substitute: rate = k₂ × K[NO]² × [O₂]. Combine the constants into one, k = k₂K, and you get rate = k[NO]²[O₂].

questions.q: In a two-step mechanism, species X is formed in step 1 and consumed in step 2. X is a(n):
o: Catalyst
A catalyst is used up first and remade later. X is the other way around.
Transition state
A transition state is an energy peak, not something made and used between steps.
Intermediate
Correct: an intermediate is made, then used up, so it's missing from the overall equation.
Final product
A final product isn't used up in a later step.
questions.x: In a multi-step mechanism, a species that's made in one step and then used up in a later step is called an intermediate. Because it's made and then consumed, it cancels out and doesn't appear in the overall balanced equation. A catalyst is the reverse: it's used up first and then made again later. A transition state isn't a species you make between steps at all. It's the brief, highest-energy arrangement at the very top of each energy hill, and it can't be isolated.

questions.q: How does the half-life of a zero-order reaction change as the reaction proceeds and [A] falls?
o: It stays constant
A constant half-life is the mark of a first-order reaction.
Each successive half-life gets longer
Half-lives that get longer are the pattern for second order.
It always equals 0.693/k
0.693 ÷ k is the first-order half-life formula.
Each successive half-life gets shorter
Correct: t½ = [A]₀ ÷ (2k), so a smaller starting amount gives a shorter half-life.
questions.x: Half-life (t½) is the time it takes for the concentration to drop to half. In a zero-order reaction, the reactant disappears at a constant rate, the same amount every second no matter how much is left. The half-life formula is t½ = [A]₀ ÷ (2k), where [A]₀ is the concentration at the start of that half-life. As [A] falls, each new half-life starts from a smaller amount, so it's shorter. In fact, each one is half as long as the one before. Only first-order reactions have a constant half-life.

questions.q: A second-order reaction (rate = k[A]²) has a half-life of 20 s when [A]₀ = 0.10 M. What is the half-life when [A]₀ = 0.20 M?
o: A half-life that ignores concentration belongs to first-order reactions.
Correct: t½ = 1 ÷ (k[A]₀), so doubling [A]₀ cuts the half-life in half.
This uses the zero-order pattern, where the half-life grows with [A]₀.
5 s
No common rate law makes the half-life drop with the square of concentration.
questions.x: For a second-order reaction, the half-life formula is t½ = 1 ÷ (k[A]₀), where k is the rate constant and [A]₀ is the starting concentration. Since [A]₀ is on the bottom, the half-life is inversely proportional to it: double the concentration and the half-life is cut in half. Here [A]₀ doubles from 0.10 M to 0.20 M, so t½ goes from 20 s to 20 ÷ 2 = 10 s. It makes sense: with more molecules packed in, they bump into each other more often, so half of them get used up sooner.

questions.q: Reaction X has a larger activation energy than reaction Y. Both are warmed by 10 K. Which is true?
o: k for X increases by a smaller factor than k for Y
This has it backward. A bigger barrier makes k more sensitive to temperature, not less.
Both k values increase by the same factor
Eₐ is in the exponent, so different barriers give different factors.
k for X decreases while k for Y increases
Warming raises k for every reaction with a positive barrier.
k for X increases by a larger factor than k for Y
Correct: a larger Eₐ makes the rate constant more sensitive to temperature.
questions.x: The Arrhenius equation links the rate constant k to temperature: k = A × e raised to the power of (−Eₐ/RT), where Eₐ is the activation energy (the energy barrier), R is the gas constant and T is temperature in kelvin. Because Eₐ sits in the exponent, it controls how strongly k responds to a change in T. A bigger Eₐ means k changes by a bigger factor for the same warming. So both reactions speed up, but X, with the taller barrier, speeds up by more. Heating helps most where the barrier is highest.

questions.q: A catalyst increases the forward rate constant of a reversible reaction 100-fold. By what factor does it change the reverse rate constant?
o: It leaves it unchanged
Then K would go up 100-fold, and a catalyst can't change K.
It increases it 100-fold
Correct: K = k_f ÷ k_r can't change, so k_r rises by the same 100-fold.
It decreases it 100-fold
Then K would go up 10,000-fold.
It increases it 10,000-fold
Then K would drop 100-fold, which a catalyst can't do.
questions.x: For a reversible reaction, the equilibrium constant is K = k_f ÷ k_r, where k_f is the forward rate constant and k_r is the reverse one. A catalyst gives the reaction a lower-energy path, but it doesn't change the energies of the reactants or products, so it can't change ΔG° or K. If k_f goes up 100 times and K has to stay the same, k_r must also go up 100 times: K = (100 × k_f) ÷ (100 × k_r) = k_f ÷ k_r. The lowered hill is crossed in both directions.

questions.q: According to the Hammond postulate, the transition state of a highly exothermic elementary step most closely resembles:
o: The products
Product-like transition states belong to strongly endothermic steps.
An intermediate halfway along the coordinate
Highly exothermic steps have an early transition state, not a halfway one.
Neither, because structure is unrelated to energy
Hammond's postulate links similar energy to similar structure.
The reactants
Correct: an early transition state is close in energy, and in structure, to the reactants.
questions.x: A transition state is the highest-energy point of a reaction step, the arrangement at the top of the energy hill. The Hammond postulate says it looks most like whichever neighbor, reactants or products, is closest to it in energy. In a highly exothermic step, the products sit far below the reactants, so the top of the hill comes early, while things are still close in energy to the reactants. That makes the transition state reactant-like. In a strongly endothermic step it's the reverse: the peak comes late and looks like the products.

questions.q: K = 4.0 for A ⇌ 2B. What is K for 4B ⇌ 2A?
o: This flips K for the reverse reaction but forgets to square it for the doubled coefficients.
This squares K but forgets to flip it for the reverse direction.
Correct: reversing gives 1/4, and doubling squares it: (1/4)² = 1/16 = 0.0625.
This multiplies 1/K by ½ instead of squaring it.
questions.note: Reverse → 1/K; multiply coefficients by n → Kⁿ.
questions.x: Two rules: reversing a reaction flips K to 1/K, and multiplying every coefficient by n raises K to the nth power. 4B ⇌ 2A is A ⇌ 2B written backward and doubled. So the formula is K_new = (1/K)ⁿ. Values: K = 4.0, n = 2. Plug in: K_new = (1/4.0)². Squaring a fraction squares the top and the bottom: 1² ÷ 4² = 1 ÷ 16. And 1 ÷ 16 = 0.0625. Flipping without squaring gives 0.25, the most tempting half-answer.

questions.q: Argon is added to a rigid, fixed-volume vessel containing PCl₅(g) ⇌ PCl₃(g) + Cl₂(g) at equilibrium. What happens?
o: A shift toward PCl₅, because the total pressure increased
Total pressure rises, but each reacting gas's partial pressure stays the same.
A shift toward PCl₃ and Cl₂
Nothing has pushed Q below K, so there's no forward shift.
K decreases
K depends only on temperature.
No shift, because the partial pressures of the reacting gases are unchanged
Correct: at fixed volume, an inert gas doesn't change the reacting gases' partial pressures, so Q stays equal to K.
questions.note: Inert gas at constant V: no shift. At constant P (volume grows): shift toward more moles.
questions.x: An equilibrium only shifts when Q, the reaction quotient (calculated like K but from the current amounts), stops equaling K. Q depends on the partial pressure of each gas that's actually in the reaction. Argon doesn't react. Adding it to a rigid container raises the total pressure, but the volume is fixed and the moles of PCl₅, PCl₃ and Cl₂ haven't changed, so each one's partial pressure is exactly what it was. Q still equals K, so nothing shifts. (If argon were added at constant total pressure instead, the container would expand and the reaction would shift toward the side with more gas moles.)

questions.q: Product P1 forms with Ea = 50 kJ/mol (ΔG° = −10 kJ/mol) and P2 with Ea = 80 kJ/mol (ΔG° = −40 kJ/mol); both form reversibly. After prolonged heating, which product dominates?
o: P1, because it forms faster
Forming faster only matters when products can't turn back. Here they can.
P2, because it is lower in free energy
Correct: reversible plus long heating lets the mixture settle into the more stable product.
Equal amounts, because both pathways are open
Open pathways don't mean equal amounts. Stability sets the ratio at equilibrium.
Neither; both revert to reactant
Both products have negative ΔG°, so both are favored over the reactant.
questions.x: Two different things decide which product wins. The kinetic product forms fastest because it has the lower energy barrier (Eₐ): that's P1, at 50 kJ/mol. The thermodynamic product is the most stable one, with the most negative ΔG°: that's P2, at −40 kJ/mol versus −10. Here both products form reversibly, and the mixture is heated for a long time. That means each product can turn back into reactant and try again, so the mixture reaches equilibrium. At equilibrium, stability decides, not speed. So P2 dominates. Speed only wins when products are locked in.

questions.q: HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene. At −80 °C the 1,2-adduct is the major product; at 40 °C the 1,4-adduct is major. Which inference is correct?
o: The 1,2-adduct is more stable; the 1,4-adduct forms faster
This swaps the roles. The 1,2-adduct is the fast one; the 1,4-adduct is the stable one.
The 1,2-adduct forms faster; the 1,4-adduct is more stable
Correct: cold locks in the fast (kinetic) product; warmth lets the stable (thermodynamic) one take over.
Both adducts have the same stability
If they were equally stable, warming wouldn't favor one over the other.
Temperature changes ΔG° so much that the faster product changes
Temperature doesn't swap which barrier is lower. It lets the products revert.
questions.x: HBr adds to 1,3-butadiene through a carbocation that can be attacked at two spots, giving either the 1,2-adduct or the 1,4-adduct. At −80 °C, there isn't enough energy for the products to turn back, so whichever forms fastest gets locked in. That's the 1,2-adduct, the kinetic product. At 40 °C, the products can revert and re-form, so the mixture reaches equilibrium and the more stable product builds up. That's the 1,4-adduct, the thermodynamic product, because its C=C double bond has more carbons attached, which makes it more stable. The barriers don't swap with temperature; reversibility is what changes.
